The Gear System

On a live call you only need the next block. Tap the gear. Read the black type. Theory stays closed until you have air.
Say this

Name. Pause. Full address. Buyer question.

The mindset before you dial

From the manual, and worth repeating out loud: the purpose of the call is not to win the listing — it's to earn the meeting. Every call is intelligence-gathering disguised as an introduction. Good call = reached the owner and gathered facts. Great call = a clear next step. Best call = appointment set. The moment you try to close a listing on the phone you sound like every other broker who called them this month.

Gear 1 — Make Contact

"[Name]!"
[Yes]

"[Name], this is __________ from Lions Realty Commercial listen… (pause)"

"I was giving you a call regarding the property you have on [Complete Address]?"
[Yes, what about it?]

"[Name], I have several properties in the area near yours for sale… (pause) and I wanted to know if you were interested in buying some more?"
Why this works — the delivery layer

The name alone as an opener is a pattern interrupt. It doesn't sound like a pitch, so the defenses don't come up. Say it with an upward, familiar tone — like you're greeting someone you know — not as a question.

"listen…" plus the pause is the most important second of the call. It signals you have something to say rather than something to sell, and the pause forces them to lean in. Do not fill it. Call-recording research consistently finds that the callers who win are comfortable with silence and the ones who lose rush to fill it.

The address is your credential. Naming the complete address proves in three seconds that this is not a list-blast. Roughly 82% of decision-makers say cold callers are unprepared — it's the number one complaint people have about calls like this — so specificity is your single fastest differentiator. Never say "a property you own." Say the street number.

The buyer question is the honest door. You genuinely have listings, so asking if they want to buy more is true, disarming, and flattering — it treats them as an investor rather than a target. It also opens Gear 2 whether they say yes or no.

Never

Never claim you have a specific buyer for their building unless you can name the buyer and their criteria. "I have a buyer for your property" is the most-told lie in this business, owners have heard it from everyone, and it burns the firm's name — not just yours. The script's construction is honest by design: it offers inventory and asks a hypothetical. Keep it that way.

Gear 2 — Capture the Email

[If YES — build rapport, then:]
"Sounds great — let me get your email address and I'll send you more information on what I have."

[Get the email — this is the micro-commitment]
[Confirm email → send Available Properties + Value Discovery same day → move to Gear 3]
Why this works

The email is a micro-commitment, and that's the entire point. Compliance research is clear that a small yes makes the next yes feel consistent with who the person has already been. Your ladder is: they took the call (yes #1) → they gave the email (yes #2) → they answered a motive question (yes #3) → they took the 20 minutes (yes #4). Nobody jumps from cold call to listing in one leap.

Two upgrades that cost nothing: ask what the subject line should say — it makes them invest in an email they haven't received yet — and ask one qualifying question while you have them ("roughly what size is the building?"). Both feed Gear 3.

Send it the same day, and never send without a callback date. The manual is right and the data agrees: an email that follows a live call gets roughly double the reply rate of a cold one, but only if the call created the reason to open it.

Gear 2 — The 8-Block Radius Variation

"[Name], I actually have a property right around the corner from yours — [Specific Listing Address] — that we just brought to market. (pause)"

"I wanted to make sure you were aware of it, and also to let you know what's happening in your area right now."

[Share 1 relevant detail: asking price, asset type, or market activity]

"Let me get your email address and I'll send you the details."
Why this is the strongest call you will make

This is the highest-converting call in the whole system, and it's worth understanding why. You are calling with information the owner cannot get anywhere else, you are asking for nothing, and the specific address proves the territory claim instantly. Problem- and information-centric language outperforms feature and buzzword language by roughly three to one in large call studies — and this call is pure information.

Work the 8-block radius aggressively every time a listing goes live. It's in the Phase I checklist for a reason: a live listing is a renewable reason to call every owner around it, and those calls carry credibility your general prospecting calls have to earn.

Gear 3 — The Seller Pivot (the three No's)

"By the way… There has been lots of movement in the area. Property values are very high. Have you considered possibly selling your property?"
[No]

"If there was a CASH OFFER that either I or one of my investors could bring you — that would make you reconsider?"
[No]

"Because as I mentioned there has been lots of movement in the area. Property values are very high. There is REALLY no number you would consider?"
[No — third time]

"I hear you. Let me ask you one last thing — setting price completely aside, is the property still doing everything you need it to do? Whether that's the income it's generating, how easy it is to manage day to day, or where it fits in your plans long term?"

[If they respond to any angle:]
"That's exactly why it might be worth a quick 20-minute visit — not to sell, just so you have a clear picture of where things stand. When would be a good time for me to stop by?"
Why the three No's are not stubbornness

This sequence looks aggressive on paper. It isn't, and the data explains why: across hundreds of millions of analyzed cold calls, roughly half of all objections are pure reflex — fired in the first seconds, before the person has processed anything you said. The first "no" to "have you considered selling" is almost never a decision. It's a door closing on autopilot.

Notice the escalation is built correctly. Each pass lowers the commitment rather than raising the pressure: from "would you sell" (a decision) → to "would a cash offer make you reconsider" (a hypothetical) → to "is there really no number" (a curiosity) → to "set price aside entirely" (no transaction at all). That last question is the masterstroke, and it's the one you must never rush, because it converts the call from a sales pitch into a conversation about their life.

The fourth question is the motive question. It names all four Seller Motives without labeling them — income, headaches, and long-term plans — and invites them to pick. Whichever one they react to is your anchor for every future touch. Ask it slowly, and then stop talking.

The two mechanics that decide this sequence

Pause longer than feels natural. Across 67,000 recorded sales conversations, top performers paused roughly five times longer after an objection than weak performers, who practically interrupt. After each "no," count one full beat before the next line. It reads as calm, not as a script advancing.

Slow down instead of speeding up. The same research found that under objection, weak callers accelerate to around 188 words a minute while top producers hold at 176 or below. Your instinct after the second "no" will be to rush the third question. Do the opposite — slower is what makes it land as genuine curiosity instead of pressure.

Anything other than "No"

"When would be a good time to go by your property?"
[You can go by any time]

"Are you ever there so that you can show me around?"

That second line is doing quiet work: it converts a property visit into a meeting with a human being. A drive-by gets you a photo. A walk-through with the owner gets you thirty minutes of unguarded conversation, the motive, and the relationship. Always push for them to be there.

Gear 4 — when "no" is final, open the second door

"Fair enough — and honestly, a lot of the owners I talk to shouldn't sell. (pause) Let me ask you the other question then: is there debt on the property? … When does that loan come due?"

"We also run a commercial loan shop, [Loan Company] — so whether you ever sell or not, I can tell you what a refi looks like at today's numbers. I get paid either way, so I'll tell you straight which one nets you more. Worth knowing?"

The full block, the buyer-side version, the psychology, and the funnel are in the Two Doors tab. Short version: the owner who won't sell still has a loan, a maturity, and equity — and "I get paid either way" is the sentence that makes you the first broker they believe.

Two Doors — The Listing or the Loan

Most brokers have one way to win a call. You have two, and the second one opens exactly where the first one closes. This is the structural advantage the whole system should be built around.

The architecture

Every owner call runs the same Gears — but now a "no" to selling is not the end of the call. It's the handoff to the financing door. And every buyer who says yes in Gear 1 is a buyer you can pre-qualify on the spot. Three outcomes replace one:

  • The listing — Gear 3 lands, the visit is set, the TL closes. Unchanged.
  • The refinance — the owner won't sell, but there's debt on the property. You run a refi analysis, and either you place the loan or you become the last person they trust before a maturity forces a decision.
  • The financed buyer — the owner wants to buy more. You send inventory and a pre-qualification, which makes them a real buyer for your own listings.

The operating system for everything after “Worth knowing?” — intake scripts, soft-read language, term-sheet comparison, listing pre-underwrite, loan clocks, the information wall, and seller paper — is the Loan Companion tab.

The compounding effect is the point: a financed buyer closes on a listing you also hold; a refi client becomes a listing in three years when the next maturity hits; a seller whose buyer you financed refers the next owner. One phone call, three revenue lines, and every line feeds the others.

Gear 4 — The Financing Door Proposed addition — owner's call

Run this after the motive question in Gear 3 whenever the selling answer is final. It's the only new script block in this companion, and since you own both businesses, it's yours to certify.

"Fair enough — and honestly, a lot of the owners I talk to shouldn't sell. (pause) Let me ask you the other question then: is there debt on the property?"
[Yes / No]

[If yes:] "When does that loan come due?" (pause — log the date)

"The reason I ask — we also run a commercial loan shop, [Loan Company]. So whether you ever sell or not, I can tell you what a refinance looks like at today's numbers, or what pulling cash out looks like if you're buying something else. I get paid either way, so I'll tell you straight which one nets you more. Worth knowing?"
[If any opening:]
"What's the balance and the rate you're at now? (pause) Let me run both — what a sale nets you after everything, and what a refi looks like — and you'll have real numbers side by side inside 48 hours. Best email for you?"

[If no debt / free and clear:] "Then you're sitting on a lot of equity doing nothing. If you ever wanted to pull some out to buy the next one without selling this one — that's a conversation I can have in five minutes. Want the number?"
Why it works — the psychology

"I get paid either way" is the sentence that changes the call. Every owner assumes a broker is biased toward whatever pays the broker. When both doors pay you, the bias disappears — and the owner hears someone who can afford to be honest. Perceived neutrality is the rarest thing in this business, and you have it structurally. Say it out loud on every Gear 4.

The alternative-choice close, applied to the business model. "Sell or refi" is two options that are both yes for you. The owner is choosing between doors instead of choosing whether to open one. That's the same mechanism as "Tuesday morning or Thursday afternoon" — it engages the brain in selecting instead of refusing.

Reciprocity at its strongest. A side-by-side of "what a sale nets you" versus "what a refi looks like" is the most valuable free thing you can hand an owner — it answers the question they've been avoiding for years. Owners repay that with the listing, the loan, or the referral. Often all three, over time.

Loss aversion, with a date on it. "Your loan matures next spring into today's rates" is a loss with a deadline. The lending research is blunt: debt maturity is the single most predictable trigger in commercial real estate, and the owner who hears it from you nine months early is the one who calls you when it's time.

The buyer side — Gear 2 with financing attached

[Gear 1: "…interested in buying some more?" → YES]
"Sounds great — let me get your email and I'll send you what I have. (pause) And since we finance most of what we sell, I can tell you what you'd qualify for before you fall in love with anything. Roughly what are you looking to put down, and are you buying in your own name or an entity?"

Two things just happened. You captured the email (the Gear 2 win) and you started a loan application without calling it one. A buyer who knows their number is a buyer who acts — and a pre-qualified buyer on your own listing is the certainty-of-close every seller is quietly praying for.

The listing pitch — certainty of execution

The commercial-lending research is unambiguous about what sellers and their brokers value most: certainty of close outranks price. A reliable buyer 25–50 basis points worse on terms still wins the deal, because a financing fall-through three weeks before closing costs more than any discount. Owners have all lived this. Your firm is now the only one on the block that can say the following honestly:

"We finance our own buyers. When we bring you an offer, the buyer is already underwritten — the deal doesn't die in some bank's credit committee three weeks before closing. That's why our listings close, and it's why they close at a better number: a seller who knows the deal is real doesn't have to give price away for certainty."

This belongs in the TL's listing presentation and in your Appointment Lock value step. It is a differentiator no marketing budget can buy, and it's true.

Those second and third columns come out of the reaches that used to be dead ends — the "not selling" owners with debt and the "yes I'd buy" investors. Track them separately in Salesforce (add dispositions: REFI-ANALYSIS SENT, PREQUAL STARTED, LOAN APP) so you can see which door each call opened. Expect the refinance analysis-to-application rate to run higher than listing appointment-to-signing: a refi asks the owner to change nothing about their life, while a sale asks them to change everything.

Fee math, roughly: a 1% brokerage fee on a $2M refinance is $20,000 from an owner who told you no. Over a year, the refi door alone can out-earn a new agent's listing commissions — and every one of those refi clients is a listing in the pipeline for the next maturity.

Delivery and cadence for the second door

  • Tonality: Gear 4 is delivered entirely in the Consultant register — unhurried, thoughtful, no sales energy. "Fair enough — a lot of owners shouldn't sell" has to sound like you mean it, because you do.
  • The 48-hour promise is the brand. The market benchmark for a soft quote is 48 hours and the credible-terms guardrail is 14 days; deals quoted inside that window close at measurably higher rates. Beat the benchmark and say so.
  • Friday updates on every loan in process, even when the update is "nothing new." The number one reason owners leave a lender is silence, not rates.
  • Maturity calls at nine months out — a Salesforce task, automatic, off the date you logged in Gear 4. This call converts better than any cold call you'll make, because you're calling about their deadline, not your quota.
  • Never push the loan to keep the listing away, or the listing to keep the loan away. Run the side-by-side honestly. The neutrality is the product; spend it once and it's gone.

Keep it clean — disclosure

Wearing both hats on one deal is legal and common in commercial, but it needs to be visible. Disclose the dual role in writing on every file where the brokerage lists and the loan shop finances; never condition a listing on using your financing (or the reverse); and confirm with counsel what Florida's commercial-lending and dual-compensation rules require for your specific structure. The honesty is also the sales strategy — "I get paid either way" only works if it's disclosed and true.

The Buyer Side

The firm lists — it doesn't chase properties around town for buyers. But you work with buyers constantly, and it's worth being precise about why: the buyer pool is the machine that makes your listings sell above market, and now that you finance them, it's also the thing no competitor can copy.

What the buyer relationship actually is here

You are not a buyer's agent hunting the whole market on someone's behalf. You are building and working a pool of qualified buyers for the inventory you control. That distinction matters practically: it keeps your time on listings, it keeps the fee structure clean, and it's the reason Gear 1 opens by asking whether an owner wants to buy more — every owner you call is also a potential buyer, and cataloguing that is free.

Three things a deep buyer pool does for you. It makes a listing presentation credible, because "here is who buys this asset and what they paid" beats any brochure. It produces competitive tension, which is what actually generates above-market pricing. And it turns every closing into two relationships instead of one — the seller who got paid, and the buyer who now owns something and will eventually sell it.

On brokerage relationships: Florida's default is transaction broker, single agency requires written disclosure, and Florida does not permit dual agency. When you're working a buyer on your own listing, be clear in writing which hat you're wearing and make sure the buyer understands you are not their advocate against your seller. Confirm the specifics with your Broker of Record — the disclosure is a form, not a judgment call.

The buyer call — it is not the owner call

The owner call sells information. The buyer call sells access and certainty. A buyer doesn't want to be marketed to; they want first look and a straight answer on whether a deal pencils.

"[Name]! … [Name], this is ______ from Lions Realty Commercial listen… (pause)"
"I've got something on [street/submarket] that isn't out yet — [asset type], [unit count or SF], [rough price]. (pause) Before I put it in front of the market, is that the kind of thing you're still buying?"
[If yes] "Good. Two quick things so I'm not wasting your time — what's your buy box right now, and how are you funding it? … And we finance most of what we sell, so if it's useful I can tell you what you'd qualify for before you spend a weekend on it."

"Before I put it in front of the market" is doing the work. It is true when you say it early in a listing, it costs you nothing, and it is the single most valuable thing a buyer can hear. First look is the currency of this business — spend it deliberately on the buyers who actually close, not on whoever calls loudest.

The buy box — capture it once, use it forever

A buyer who has told you their criteria in writing is a buyer you can match automatically for years. Get these into Salesforce on the first real conversation:

  • Asset type and sub-type — "multifamily" is not a buy box; "8 to 30 units, 1960s-to-1980s vintage, value-add" is.
  • Geography — the specific blocks or submarkets, and just as usefully, where they won't go.
  • Price range and equity available — and whether that equity is theirs or raised, because raised equity adds a decision layer and time.
  • Return requirement — the cap rate, cash-on-cash, or price per unit they need. This is what lets you screen inventory for them instead of blasting them.
  • Leverage and lender — all cash, existing bank relationship, or open to your shop.
  • Timeline and motivation — and specifically, is there a 1031 clock?
  • Decision structure — who signs, who else has a vote, and is there a committee or a partner in another country.
  • What they've actually closed — the last two or three deals, with addresses. This separates buyers from shoppers faster than anything else on the list.

Qualify the buyer — score it

Tick what's true. You're not looking for perfection; you're looking for whether this person should get your first call on the next deal, and what to fix before they do.

Tire-kicker tells

  • "Send me everything you have." A buyer with no criteria has no capital, or no authority, or no intention. Answer with a question: "Happy to — what's the buy box?" Watch what happens.
  • Won't provide proof of funds or a lender contact after a real conversation. Not on first contact — that's reasonable — but after they've asked for a second property, it's a signal.
  • Asks for the full package but never tours. Real buyers get in the car.
  • Wants seller financing for essentially the whole price. That's not a buyer, that's someone asking your seller to be the bank on a deal they can't fund.
  • Has a retrade history. Ask around — this market is small and brokers talk. A buyer who reliably renegotiates after inspection is worth less to your seller than a lower price from someone who closes.
  • Won't say what they've closed. Every real buyer answers this instantly and usually with pride.
  • Goes quiet for a week, then wants an extension. Responsiveness during diligence predicts behavior at closing.

None of these mean you're rude to anyone — this market is too small and people change circumstances. It means you rank your attention. First look goes to proven closers; everyone else gets the package when it goes out broadly.

The 1031 buyer — the best buyer in commercial real estate

An exchange buyer has a statutory clock: 45 days to identify replacement property and 180 days to close, with a qualified intermediary engaged before their sale closed. That clock does something no marketing can — it makes them act, and it makes them pay for certainty.

So ask every buyer, early: "Is this a 1031, and where are you in the clock?" A buyer on day 30 of identification is the most motivated buyer you will meet all year. They will pay a premium for a clean, financeable, on-time closing, because the alternative is a failed exchange and a tax bill that dwarfs the premium.

It also changes what you sell them. Speed and certainty matter more than price. Your ability to finance them is certainty, which is why a 1031 buyer and a firm that owns a loan shop are close to a perfect match. And log the identification and closing deadlines in Salesforce as hard dates — missing one is not a delay, it's a tax event.

Financing the buyer — your unfair advantage, used properly

Every buyer conversation contains a free second product. Offer the pre-qualification as a service to them rather than a pitch for you: "Let me tell you what you'd qualify for before you spend a weekend underwriting something you can't fund." Buyers say yes to that almost universally, because it saves them time and costs them nothing.

What it gets you: a pre-qualified buyer is a real buyer, verified rather than claimed. Their proof of funds and their lender are the same file. And when you take that buyer to your own seller, you can say the sentence no competing broker can — "this buyer is already underwritten; the deal doesn't die in someone's credit committee three weeks before closing." Certainty of execution outranks price for most sellers, which means your financed buyer can sometimes win a deal at a number that wouldn't otherwise have won it.

And the discipline that keeps it clean: never condition access to a listing on using your financing, and never imply you will. Disclose the dual role in writing on any file where both businesses touch the deal. The offer has to be genuinely optional or it stops being a service and becomes a tying problem — and it torches the neutrality that makes the whole two-door model work.

From tour to LOI — running the buyer forward

  • Tour with a purpose. Before the walk, ask what would have to be true for them to write. After the walk, ask it again. The gap between those answers is your negotiation.
  • Push for a letter of intent, not a conversation. An LOI is non-binding but it forces price, deposit, diligence period, closing timeline and financing contingency onto paper — and it exposes a buyer who isn't real, cheaply and early.
  • Get the diligence period short and the deposit meaningful. A long free-look with a small deposit is a free option on your seller's property. Frame it to the buyer honestly: "a tighter timeline and real money makes your offer win against a higher one."
  • Hand them the diligence package on day one — everything from the Environmental & Records tab. A buyer who gets everything immediately has no excuse to extend, and no discovery to renegotiate on.
  • Surface known issues yourself, before the inspector does. Recertification, roof, tanks, open permits. Disclosed problems get priced once; discovered problems get priced twice and shake confidence in everything else you said.
  • Weekly updates through escrow, to both sides. Same rule as the listing: silence is what people fear, and bad news travels from you first with a plan attached.

What buyers complain about — and how you're different

  • "Brokers never send me anything that fits." Because nobody captured a buy box. Yours is in Salesforce, so your matches are real and your emails get opened.
  • "The numbers in the OM never hold up." Because most packages blend in-place with pro forma. Yours labels them separately and sources every figure — which is slower to produce and enormously more credible.
  • "I find out about problems in week three." Because most brokers hope nobody looks. You pull the record before you list.
  • "I never get told about anything early." First look costs you nothing and buys years of goodwill. Spend it on the people who close.
  • "Nobody can tell me what it finances at." You can, on the phone, that afternoon.

Every one of those is a low bar. Clearing all five makes you the broker a serious buyer takes calls from — and buyers who take your calls are the reason your sellers get their number.

Your desk — the reps you already have

This is your own list, filtered to everything that is commercial or business-purpose and dropped into the tool so it is searchable next to everything else. Residential-only correspondents were left out; land, private, DSCR and foreign-national desks were kept, because those are the ones your deals actually need.

Re-verify before the first send. Several of these were logged between 2020 and 2023 and account executives move constantly — the institution is durable, the person is not. Confirm the rep is still there before you put a client’s file in an email, and update the tracker as you go. A bounced email to a lender you are asking to approve you is a bad first impression you only get to make once.

The institutional roster — 117 more, and the exact title to ask for at each

Your desk above is where small and fast gets done. This is the rest of the market — agency, SBA, life companies, CMBS, the Miami banks and the debt funds — for the deals that outgrow a private lender. The “Ask for” line is the important part: it is the title that actually exists inside that kind of shop. Say the title and you get transferred; say “someone in lending” and you get voicemail.

The tracker is this roster as a working spreadsheet — the blue columns are yours: contact name, title, email, phone, status, agreement signed, last contact, notes. Dropdowns and filters are set up, and the second tab names which relationships to build first. Paste your desk contacts above into it and you have one file instead of two lists.

Why direct beats a marketplace — the economics

Any intermediary layer between you and the lender has to be paid, and it gets paid out of the same deal you do. Whether that shows up as a platform fee, a referral split, or pricing that reaches the borrower slightly worse than the lender's actual sheet, the effect on you is the same: the spread you could have earned is already spoken for before you see the deal.

And the compounding problem is that pricing is the most visible thing on a term sheet. If your quote comes back consistently a little worse than the borrower can find elsewhere, you don't just lose the fee — you lose the reputation for being the person who gets deals done at a real number, which is the entire asset you're building.

A direct relationship changes three things at once. You see the lender's actual pricing rather than a version of it. You control the fee conversation with your own borrower instead of inheriting someone else's. And you get a named human who will take your call when a deal is wobbling — which, on a hard file, is worth more than the basis points.

Marketplaces are not useless. They are genuinely good for a deal type you've never placed, a market you don't know, or a one-off where building a relationship isn't worth the effort. Use them as overflow, not as your channel. The goal is that your five or six core lender relationships cover 80% of what you originate, and the platform handles the strange 20%.

The official directories — start here, they are actually maintained

These are the authoritative, current lists. They beat any contact roster because they are updated by the institutions themselves.

  • Freddie Mac Optigo lender directory — every approved conventional, affordable and seniors lender, by geography. mf.freddiemac.com/borrowers/optigo-lenders
  • Fannie Mae DUS lender list — the approved multifamily seller/servicers. Published on Fannie's multifamily site.
  • SBA lender directories — for 7(a) and 504, including which lenders actually do gas stations. One example directory, and SBA publishes participating lender data directly.
  • HUD/FHA multifamily approved lender list — for 223(f) and 221(d)(4).
  • Your state banking association and the Miami-Dade commercial banking community — for the local portfolio banks that do the small-balance and foreign-national work the national shops won't touch.
On names, emails and phone numbers: I'm deliberately not handing you a contact roster. Production officers and broker-relations staff change roles constantly, and a stale list means you email dead addresses and look like you don't know the market — to exactly the people you're asking to approve you. Use the directories above, then use the approach below. It takes an afternoon and gets you a live human whose name is correct.

The outreach playbook — what to actually say, in order

Identifying a lender is the easy half. This is the half that gets you an account. Work it in this sequence — each step is a different conversation with a different goal, and mixing them is why most brokers never get approved anywhere.

The order that works:  1) Submit the broker-approval form where one exists — it costs ten minutes and assigns you a human.  2) Where there is no form, call the main line and ask for the title.  3) Lead your first real contact with a deal, never with a request.  4) Send the one-page summary the same day.  5) Follow the cadence below. Approval paperwork happens naturally once they want the deal — asking for an agreement before you have a deal puts you at the bottom of the pile.

Step 1 — The main-line call, verbatim

Use this when there is no broker form. It works because it is a routine business question, not a pitch, and receptionists answer it freely.

You: “Hi — I'm a commercial mortgage broker in Miami. I'm looking for the account executive who covers South Florida brokers, or whoever handles broker relations. Who would that be, and what's the best email for them?”

If they ask why: “I have deals in their product range and I'd like to get set up to submit. I just need the right person so I'm not sending it to the wrong desk.”

Always close with: “Could you spell the last name for me? And is that a direct line or the main number?”

Swap the title depending on the shop — this is the whole trick:

  • Agency shop or debt fund → “the Production Officer or Originator covering South Florida.”
  • Bank → “the commercial real estate relationship manager for the Miami market.” Call the local commercial office, never the 800 number.
  • Wholesale / non-QM / DSCR → “the account executive for Florida brokers.”
  • SBA lender → “the BDO — business development officer — for Florida.”
  • Correspondent or life company → “your correspondent desk for Florida.” Life companies do not take broker calls directly — you reach them through NorthMarq, Bellwether/BWE, Grandbridge or another correspondent.

Step 2 — The first email, three versions

Short, specific, and it ends with one question. Nobody reads paragraph three. Copy, swap the brackets, send.

A. To a wholesale or small-balance shop — you want an account

Subject: South Florida broker — approval + a [$1.6M] deal in hand

[Name] —

I'm a commercial broker in Miami, [X] deals a year, mostly small-balance multifamily, mixed use and retail in Miami-Dade and Broward.

I'd like to get approved to submit to you. I already have one that fits: [14-unit in Little Havana, $1.6M request, 65% LTV, 1.35 DSCR, sponsor owns three similar assets].

What do you need from me to open the account, and can I send that file over while it's in process?

[Signature — name, firm, license no., direct line]

B. To a bank CRE relationship manager — you want a person, not a product

Subject: Miami CRE broker — [asset type] financing in [submarket]

[Name] —

I broker commercial real estate in [Little Havana / Allapattah / Hialeah] and I place the debt on a good share of what I list. Most of it is [$500K–$5M], [multifamily and mixed use], and a lot of the borrowers are [local operators / foreign nationals with US entities].

I'd like fifteen minutes to understand what you're actively lending on right now — leverage, minimum size, and what you'd rather not see — so I stop sending you things you don't want.

Are you open to a short call this week or next?

[Signature]

Why that one works: it offers to stop wasting their time, which is a bank lender's actual complaint about brokers. It also asks for information rather than a favor, which is far harder to decline.

C. To a private lender or debt fund — lead entirely with the deal

Subject: [$2.4M bridge] — [gas station, Hialeah] — [21-day close]

[Name] —

[Gas station and c-store on 0.8 acres in Hialeah.] Purchase [$3.4M], request [$2.4M], [70% LTV]. Borrower is [an operator with two other stores], [30%] cash in. [Phase I complete, no recognized environmental conditions.] Seller needs to close in [21 days].

Exit is [a refinance into SBA 7(a) once twelve months of operating history is seasoned].

Is this something you'd quote? Happy to send the full package now.

[Signature]

Private lenders and debt funds are deal-flow businesses. They do not want to know about you — they want to know whether the asset, the leverage and the exit work. Give them that in six lines and they answer the same day. Bloomfield Capital publishes the address deals@bloomfieldcapital.com; that is not an accident, it is how the whole channel thinks.

Step 3 — The one-page summary you attach

Send this with the first email, every time. A lender who has to ask for basics puts your file behind the one that came complete.

  • Property — address, folio, asset type, year built, units or square feet, land area, zoning.
  • Request — loan amount, purpose (purchase / refi / cash-out / construction), LTV or LTC, term wanted, and whether rate or speed matters more.
  • The numbers — purchase price or value, NOI, cap rate, and the DSCR at a stated rate. State the rate you used. A lender who disagrees with your rate still respects that you ran it.
  • Sponsor — entity, ownership, net worth and liquidity ranges, credit range, and what else they own. Experience in the same asset class is the single strongest line in the package.
  • The story — two sentences on why this deal exists and why it is priced where it is. Do not hide the hair. A problem you disclose is a condition; a problem they find is a decline.
  • Exit — sale or refinance, and on what timeline. Every bridge lender asks this second.
  • Attachments — rent roll, T-12 or trailing operating statements, purchase contract if there is one, photos, and the Phase I on anything with fuel, dry cleaning or industrial history.
The Underwriting Workbook builds most of this — it is in the Underwriting tab, and the numbers it produces are the numbers this summary needs.

Step 4 — The follow-up cadence

Most brokers send once and quit. The account usually comes on contact three or four, and the reason is boring: the person was busy, not uninterested.

  • Day 0 — email with the one-pager attached.
  • Day 2 — call. Do not leave a long voicemail: “[Name], it's [you] in Miami — I sent a [$1.6M multifamily] Tuesday, wanted to make sure it landed on the right desk. [Number].”
  • Day 5 — reply on your own email thread with one new fact: the appraisal came in, the seller moved, the rent roll updated. Never “just following up” — that is a message with no information in it.
  • Day 12 — a different deal. This is the one that works. It tells them you have real flow and are not a one-deal broker, which is exactly what they are screening for.
  • Then monthly, permanently. One line, one deal, or one market note. Lenders' appetites change quarterly and you want to be in the inbox the week theirs changes.
When they decline, ask two questions: “What would have made this one work?” and “Who do you know who does do this?” The first teaches you their box so you stop wasting sends. The second is free — lenders refer competitors readily, because a deal they cannot do is worth nothing to them. A decline that produces a referral is a good call.

Where the paperwork lands

Once they want the deal, the approval package is routine. Have these ready in one folder and you can turn it around the same day:

  • Broker agreement or correspondent agreement (theirs).
  • W-9, entity documents, and your Certificate of Good Standing.
  • Your real estate license and any mortgage licensing — and see the licensing card below before you accept lender-paid compensation.
  • E&O certificate. Several wholesale shops will not open an account without it.
  • A short statement of volume and what you originate. Be accurate about being newer — lenders would rather have a small honest producer than an inflated number they discover later.
  • How you get paid — borrower-paid, lender-paid, or both, and how it is disclosed. Settle this in writing before you quote anything.

Licensing — the assumption that "commercial means no license" is not reliably true in Florida

Read this before you take a single lender-paid fee. The common belief is that Florida mortgage licensing only touches residential, so commercial brokering is unlicensed activity. That is roughly half right, and the half that is wrong lands directly on the business you are trying to build.

Florida's definition of a "mortgage loan" in F.S. 494.001 does not stop at dwellings. It reaches: (a) residential loans for personal, family or household use secured by a dwelling; (b) loans on commercial real property when the borrower is an individual or the lender is a non-institutional investor; and (c) loans on improved real property with five or more dwelling units under those same conditions.

Read what that actually captures for you:

  • A commercial loan where the borrower signs as an individual rather than through an entity — captured.
  • Any deal funded by a private or hard money lender, because that is a non-institutional investor — captured. That is the entire private-lender channel below.
  • Small multifamily of five units and up with an individual borrower or a private lender — captured.
  • A commercial loan to an entity from an institutional lender is the case that generally sits outside — which is real, but it is narrower than "all commercial."

And the real estate broker exemption does not save you. F.S. 494.00115(1)(f) exempts a Chapter 475 licensee who performs only real estate brokerage activities — "unless the person is compensated by a lender, mortgage broker, or other loan originator." Lender-paid compensation is the standard way mortgage brokers get paid. Take a fee from the lender and the exemption you were relying on is gone.

There is a separate exemption at 494.00115(4)(d) for a person who makes only nonresidential mortgage loans and sells loans only to institutional investors — narrow, conjunctive, and worth understanding precisely. And the statute puts the burden of proving an exemption on the person claiming it.

The distinction almost everyone conflates — worth having precisely, because you are right about half of it. “Business purpose means no license” is a true statement about a different body of law. The business-purpose exemption lives in the federal consumer statutes — TILA / Regulation Z, RESPA, and the SAFE Act's residential definition. It means a business-purpose loan is not a consumer loan, so the consumer disclosure machinery does not apply. That is a separate question from whether Florida requires a state license to broker it. A loan can be plainly business-purpose, exempt from every federal consumer rule, and still sit inside F.S. 494 because the borrower signed as an individual or the money came from a non-institutional investor.

And your Oaktree example is the right one. Institutional lender, entity borrower, commercial collateral — that combination genuinely does sit outside 494, which is exactly why those relationships are the cleanest to build first and why those accounts transfer over the way you expect. The care is needed at three specific edges: the private-lender channel (a non-institutional investor by definition — that is most of your desk), the individual borrower who never formed the LLC, and the DSCR business on one-to-four unit houses, which is residential collateral no matter how business-purpose the loan is. That is where the exposure sits — not in the institutional commercial business. One conversation with counsel prices the whole question.
What to actually do: spend an hour with a Florida financial services regulatory attorney before you sign broker agreements or accept lender compensation. Bring them three questions — how your loan entity should be structured, whether your intended compensation model requires licensure, and whether your DSCR and foreign-national business (often secured by one-to-four unit dwellings) crosses into residential territory. This is a one-time structural decision, not a compliance chore, and getting it right at the start costs a fraction of fixing it later. Nothing on this page is legal advice — the citations are here so your attorney can verify the analysis in ten minutes.

Private and hard money lenders — the channel you will use most

Private capital is where land, gas stations, story deals, distressed sellers and anything with a clock actually get funded. It is also the channel where your speed is the product — a private lender who can close in three weeks is worth more to the right borrower than a bank at half the rate.

What to expect structurally: interest-only, terms of roughly six to thirty-six months, leverage typically in the 55–70% range of value and often lower on land, points charged up front, and an exit that is either a sale or a refinance into conventional debt. Pricing is materially higher than bank debt and that is not the point — availability and speed are the point.

Categories, in the order you will reach for them:

  • Local South Florida private lenders — Miami, Aventura, Boca and Palm Beach shops that know these submarkets and will look at a property the day you call. Names active in this market include BridgeInvest, Forman Capital, LV Lending, and a number of smaller Boca and Aventura funds. Verify current appetite before you send anything.
  • National bridge and debt funds — Ready Capital, Arbor, Lument, Madison Realty Capital, Trez Capital, Bloomfield Capital, Churchill Real Estate. Larger minimums, more institutional process, better pricing than local hard money.
  • Land and pre-development specialists — a short list, because most lenders will not touch raw land. Kennedy Funding is one of the better-known nationwide land lenders; several of the local funds above also do land at low leverage.
  • Small-balance investor lenders — the broker-channel shops that quote sub-$1M commercial and small multifamily with no bank relationship: Velocity Mortgage Capital ($75K–$7.5M, the broadest property-type appetite in the category), Silver Hill Funding ($100K–$3M, to 80% LTV), Stronghill Capital, Revolution Realty Capital, Axos Bank (bank balance sheet, real broker channel, to $20M), AVANA Capital (hospitality, gas and owner-user), Red Oak Capital, BRT / Bayview, Cherrywood, CoreVest, LendingOne, Lima One, Gelt Financial and Emigrant. Every one takes broker-submitted deals — approve with these first, because approval is fast and the sizes match what you actually list.
  • Your own desk and the full institutional roster are both in the filters above, with the title to ask for and a tracker to log the contact once you have it.
How to find the rest, and keep the list current: the Private Lender Link directory filters by state and loan type. The American Association of Private Lenders membership roster is a credibility filter as much as a directory. And once again the best source is free: pull the recorded mortgages on the distressed and fast sales in your comp set — private lenders show up on those documents by name, and a lender who funded three deals on your blocks last year is provably active in exactly what you do.

Vetting a private lender before you send a client: ask how many deals they closed in the last twelve months and in what markets, whether they fund from their own balance sheet or have to raise for each deal, what their actual close timeline has been rather than what they advertise, and whether they have ever retraded terms at the closing table. A private lender who retrades will burn your borrower and it will be your name on it — the same bait-and-switch dynamic the industry is known for. Ask other brokers before you ask the lender.

Wholesale non-QM and DSCR lenders — the residential-collateral channel

Separate from commercial, and worth understanding as its own channel because it is where a lot of your smaller investor and foreign-national business will actually land. These lenders qualify on the property's cash flow rather than the borrower's tax returns, which is exactly what an investor or a foreign national needs.

Active wholesale names in this space include A&D Mortgage (Florida-based, and notable for non-QM and foreign national programs), Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions, Deephaven, Verus, Change Wholesale, Kiavi, Lima One Capital, Visio Lending and Constructive Capital. Most operate a genuine broker channel and will approve a licensed shop without much friction.

But note exactly where this channel sits. Most DSCR and non-QM programs lend against one-to-four unit dwellings — which is residential collateral, squarely inside mortgage licensing territory, regardless of how business-purpose the loan is. This is the part of your plan most likely to require licensure, and it is the specific question to put in front of your attorney. Do not assume that because the borrower is an LLC and the purpose is investment, you are outside the rules.

What a broker agreement actually involves

Most commercial lenders will sign a broker or correspondent agreement with a licensed shop without enormous friction — the barrier is lower than people assume. What they will typically want:

  • Your licensing and entity documentation — and confirm with counsel what Florida requires for your specific activity, since commercial mortgage brokering and consumer lending are governed differently.
  • Company information, principals, E&O coverage, and often a W-9.
  • A sense of your volume and what you originate. Be honest about being newer; lenders would rather have an accurate small producer than an inflated claim they discover later.
  • How compensation works — whether you're paid by the borrower, by the lender, or both, and how that gets disclosed. Get this in writing and understand it before you quote anything, because it determines what you can actually earn per deal.

Broker versus correspondent matters. As a broker you submit the file and the lender does the work, paid a fee at closing. As a correspondent you take on more of the process — and more of the economics, sometimes including servicing. Correspondent status usually requires more track record, so start as a broker and graduate.

One structural note specific to you: because you also own the brokerage, any deal where you list the property and place the loan needs the dual role disclosed in writing, and the financing can never be a condition of anything. Confirm with counsel how your specific structure should be papered — it is worth an hour of legal time to set up correctly once.

Foreign nationals — the Miami specialty worth owning

This is where your market differs from everywhere else, and where a direct relationship is worth the most, because the lender list is short and most brokers don't know it. A foreign national borrower typically has no US credit score, no US tax returns, and often no US entity yet — which eliminates agency debt, most bank programs and anything credit-score-driven.

Who actually lends:

  • Miami portfolio banks with international desks — this is the deepest and most overlooked source. Institutions built around Latin American and European clientele underwrite these relationships routinely and hold the loans on balance sheet, which means they can use judgment rather than a scorecard. Several of the mid-size Miami-headquartered commercial banks are exactly this.
  • Private banks and international banks with a Miami presence — for higher net worth borrowers, often relationship-priced against deposits.
  • DSCR and portfolio lenders with explicit foreign national programs — they qualify on the property's cash flow rather than the borrower's income. Expect lower leverage than a US borrower gets, higher pricing, larger reserves, and a US entity plus an ITIN.
  • Private and bridge lenders — asset-based and the fastest path, at a price. Often the right answer for a purchase with a clock on it, refinanced later once the borrower has US history.

What changes on a foreign national file: lower LTV, a US entity typically required, an ITIN or equivalent, larger interest reserves, verified funds seasoned in a US account before closing, and a passport plus visa documentation. Withholding on a future sale is also a live issue for them, so flag it early and send them to a CPA.

Why this is worth owning: a foreign national buyer who finds a broker who can actually place their loan does not shop you — they bring you every deal, and they refer their entire network. In a market like Miami that's a book of business, not a transaction.

Protecting the relationships once you have them — the NCND

Your lender list is the asset. The failure you are worried about is the predictable one: you introduce a buyer or a borrower to a capital source you spent years building, and they close directly with that lender on the next deal — or on this one — and you never hear about it. The document below is the standard answer, drafted to cover buyers, sellers, borrowers, capital partners and cooperating brokers from one form.

What it does, clause by clause: defines the lender's identity, contact and terms as confidential information (¶1–2); bars the counterparty and every affiliate, nominee, trust or newly formed entity from going around you to any party you introduced, for twenty-four months (¶3, ¶9); and carries a pre-existing relationship carve-out with a five-day written notice requirement — if they do not name the relationship in five days, it is presumed to be your introduction (¶3).

Be honest with yourself about what it is worth. Non-circumvention clauses get signed constantly and enforced unevenly. Courts have voided them where the term was indefinite, the covered parties were not identified specifically, or the “confidential” information turned out to be publicly available — and a lender's name often is. The deterrent value is real; the litigation value is uncertain. That is why this form is drafted the way it is: a definite 24-month term, specifically defined covered parties, a reformation clause so a judge trims it rather than strikes it, and prevailing-party fees so bringing the claim is not automatically uneconomic.
The provision that actually gets you paid is ¶4, not ¶3. A signed fee agreement saying your fee is earned on closing with an introduced party whether or not the deal closes through you, payable at closing, with authority for the closing agent to disburse it directly from closing funds — that is a contract debt with a number attached, and it is enforced far more readily than a restraint on who someone may talk to. Get ¶4 signed before the introduction, every time. Treat ¶3 as the fence and ¶4 as the lock.

Before you use it: it is a drafting sample, not counsel's work product. Have your attorney set the term, confirm the remedies, and check it against your dual role — because when you list the property and place the loan, the disclosure obligations sit on top of this document rather than inside it.

Build the list yourself — the afternoon that pays for years

  • Pull the official directories above and filter to Florida or South Florida.
  • Add the Miami-headquartered commercial banks and credit unions — they are where the sub-$5M and foreign national work actually lives.
  • For every closed deal in your comp set, find out who financed it. The mortgage is recorded and public — the lender's name is right there on the document. That is the single best lender list in existence, because it is proof of who is actually lending on your asset type in your submarket right now, rather than who says they do.
  • Log each one in Salesforce with the asset types they want, their size band, their leverage and pricing, their turn times, and the name of the person you actually talk to.
  • Track which ones close versus which ones quote and then retrade. That record is worth more than any rate sheet — and after a year it is the reason your borrowers trust your quotes.

That last point deserves emphasis: pulling recorded mortgages from the comps you already pull costs you nothing and builds a lender list grounded in evidence. You're already in the Clerk's records for deeds — the mortgage is filed right next to it.

A listing is a fourth outcome, not a replacement. Seller financing is the third door when neither a sale-for-cash nor a refinance pencils. Run them in that order: sell, refi, carry — and never promise a takeout you cannot name.

L1 — Intake. Five minutes. No file yet.

Consultant register. Unhurried. You are classifying the request, not selling a product. The 494 tree lives on — run it in your head before you name a lender.

“Fair enough — let me get the facts so I’m not guessing. (pause)

First: is this a purchase, a refinance, cash-out, or work you want to do to the building?

Who would actually borrow — an LLC, or you personally?

Who uses the property day to day — tenants, your operating business, or will anyone live there?

What do the proceeds actually pay for? I need the real use, not the label.

Is there debt on it now — balance, rate, maturity, and is there a prepay?

What matters more on this one: maximum proceeds, the rate, or the close date?

And the only question that decides whether I should keep talking: when do you actually need this closed?”
Stop the call
  • Anyone will live in a 1–4 unit and they want “DSCR / business purpose.” That is a different product and a different license question.
  • Borrower is a natural person or the likely lender is private / hard money — Chapter 494 may attach. Do not accept a lender-paid fee on a hunch.
  • They will not say what the money is for. Purpose is a fact pattern, not an affidavit.
  • They want you to “just send it to a few lenders” with no engagement. That is how you donate a file.
Capture into Salesforce the same day: purpose, occupancy, borrower type, existing maturity, prepay flag, close date, and which door opened (REFI-ANALYSIS SENT / PREQUAL STARTED / LOAN APP / SELLER-CARRY). The disposition is how you see which door actually pays.

L2 — The soft read. Never a quote.

The 48-hour brand is real only if the words cannot be pasted into a purchase contract as “financing is arranged.” Read this out loud. Then send it in writing.

This is an indicative range only, based on the facts you gave me and current market color. It is not a commitment, not a rate lock, and not lender approval. A real number requires a full package, third-party reports, and the lender’s credit decision. Do not write this range into a contract as proof that financing is arranged. If any fact changes — income, insurance, occupancy, entity, or timeline — the range changes with it.
“I can tell you what this looks like at today’s numbers inside 48 hours — proceeds, a payment, and which constraint binds: LTV, DSCR, or debt yield. (pause)

That is a soft read, not a loan. The lender still has to underwrite it. If you need a number you can take into a contract, that is a different document and it takes longer. Worth the 48 hours so you know whether to keep going?”
Why this wording

Owners and buyers hear “I can get you X at Y%” as a promise. Title companies and opposing counsel will treat it that way when the deal wobbles. The sentence that saves you is the one that names the remaining conditions before anyone spends money on an appraisal.

L3 — Read the term sheet like a loan officer

A term sheet is a menu. A commitment is a reservation with conditions. Funding is the only moment money moves. Most “the lender retraded” stories are conditions nobody translated on day one.

LineWhat to extractWhat “retrade” looks like
AmountLesser of requested, LTV, DSCR, debt yield — say which bindsAppraisal or T-12 comes in light; amount drops, buyer’s equity gap appears
CouponIndex + spread + floor. What is actually being lockedIndex moved, or the “rate” was a teaser without the floor
IO / amortInterest-only months, then amortizing termIO disappears when DSCR is tight
PrepayStep-down, yield maintenance, defeasance, or openBorrower planned a sale in year two against a five-year lockout
RecourseFull, partial, or bad-boy only — and which acts spring full recourseSPE / transfer / bankruptcy carve-outs unsigned because nobody walked them
ReservesTax, insurance, capex, TI/LC, rate-cap, interest reserve — dollars, not monthsProceeds look fine until reserves are netted at the table
FeesOrigination, commitment (earned when?), extension, exit, underwritingCommitment fee “earned upon issuance” on a file that dies in title
ConditionsEvery “subject to” and every “lender’s sole discretion”The MAC clause is how a live term sheet becomes a dead one
LockWhat is locked, for how many days, extension cost, whether it auto-rolls (it does not)Lock expires on a 1031 clock
Do not let the borrower use a term sheet as a commitment, or a commitment as a clear-to-close. Walk the conditions-precedent list the day the paper arrives. If a condition is outside the borrower’s control, say so before they waive a financing contingency.

L4 — Friday update. Even when nothing moved.

Owners leave lenders over silence, not rates. One voice, one chronology, every Friday until funded or dead.

The third door — seller paper

Use this when a cash sale asks the owner to give up the asset and a refinance asks a lender to do something the asset cannot support. A note the seller holds is often the only structure that closes small-balance, gas, land, and foreign-national files.

“If a sale does make sense, there is a third way to get paid: you hold a note. You get a rate a bank will not give a buyer, you may defer some tax with your CPA — I do not advise that — and the buyer can close without waiting on a credit committee. (pause)

The honest version: you become the bank. If they stop paying, you enforce. I will not tell you a takeout is ‘twelve months away’ unless I can name the takeout. Want the structure on one page so you can run it past counsel?”
  • When it is the right tool: DSCR misses by a hair; buyer is foreign or thin on US history; land with no perm takeout; gas the banks will not touch until tanks are clean; seller wants income more than a clean break.
  • Paper the economics: term, rate, IO vs amort, balloon, default rate, due-on-sale, personal guaranty, first vs wrap vs subordinate, who services, what happens on insurance/tax default.
  • Your conflict: if your shop also places a senior loan, the seller is in a junior position you helped create. Disclose it. Get counsel on the stacking. Do not “make the deal work” by leaving the seller naked in second.
  • Never say: “The bank will take you out in a year.” That sentence becomes your problem at month 13.

Pre-underwrite the listing — before the OM goes out

“We finance our own buyers” is true only if the asking price survives LTV, DSCR, and debt yield on in-place NOI after the tax reset and the current insurance quote. If it only works on pro forma rents, say that on the financing page.

Illustrative math only. Replace the rate, LTV, DSCR and debt-yield hurdles with the lender’s current box before anything touches a client. Amortizing payment assumes monthly payments and the entered rate; IO months change year-one cash, not the binding DSCR test used here (underwrite to the amortizing payment unless the lender has confirmed IO through stabilization).

Term-sheet comparison — do not compare rate alone

Two loans at the same coupon can differ by six figures over a hold. Fill three live sheets. Year-1 cash is points + fees + the first-year debt service at the structure you entered.

Speed is a term. A 21-day private quote that funds beats a cheaper bank that misses a 1031 clock.

Loan clocks — the dates that kill files

The Deal Clock tab tracks contract dates. This board tracks the debt file. Stored in this browser only. Export before you change devices. It does not send alerts.

The information wall

When the brokerage lists and the loan shop places debt on the same asset, “I get paid either way” only survives if the files do not leak.

  • Seller financials stay in the listing file until the seller authorizes release — usually under the purchaser NDA plus registration. Do not shop a live OM to lenders “to see if it finances” before you have a buyer or a signed financing engagement from the owner.
  • Do not carry seller commentary into the buyer-borrower file. “They’ll take less” and “the tanks are fine” are not facts unless they are in writing from the seller.
  • Optional use, both sides, in writing. Never condition the listing on using your financing, or the loan on listing with you.
  • Itemize both fees on the settlement statement. Two payments, two engagements, two disclosures.
  • One chronology if anything wobbles. Five agents creating five explanations is how E&O claims get written.
Florida does not permit dual agency. Default is transaction broker unless single agency is established in writing. Designated sales associates exist only in a narrow nonresidential $1M-asset fact pattern — see Licensing & Usury. Conduct can create a relationship the paperwork denies. Stay inside the form your Broker of Record approved.

RESPA / AfBA — when the federal machinery actually attaches

Do not import residential settlement folklore onto a warehouse, and do not skip the disclosure on a 1–4 unit DSCR because “it’s business purpose.” Counsel marks which of your products sit on which side. This card is the question list, not the opinion.

Often in play1–4 unit dwelling + a federally related mortgage loan (most DSCR / non-QM / correspondent). Written affiliated-business disclosure at or before referral. No required use. Pay only for actual services.
Often outside RESPATrue commercial collateral and business-purpose credit. RESPA’s residential settlement scheme frequently does not attach — Florida 475, 494, and your E&O still do.
Always forbiddenA fee, split, gift, or “thing of value” for the referral itself. Volume-based payments between the brokerage and the loan shop are the classic failure mode.
Always documentWho referred, when the disclosure went out, that use was optional, and how each entity got paid. A clean file is the defense.

Chapter 494 still turns on who the borrower is and who the lender is, not on business purpose. Private capital and individual borrowers are the edge. Open the 494 tree on the Licensing tab before you take a lender-paid fee.

Sponsor box — first call, not after the appraisal

Experience in the same asset class is the strongest line in the package. Liquidity after close is the line that actually funds. Ask these before anyone spends money on reports.

A file that fails the sponsor box should not get an appraisal ordered. That is how you stop paying for declines.

Conditions that kill closings

Tick what is already in the file. Unticked items are why term sheets die between commitment and funding.

Bridge, construction, takeout

Land and value-add are not DSCR files. Private lenders ask for the exit second. If you cannot name it, you are brokering hope.

  • Budget + contingency the lender will fund against — not the sponsor’s wish list.
  • Inspect-to-fund mechanics, retainage, change-order protocol, who pays for overruns.
  • Interest reserve sized to the actual construction calendar, not the pitch deck calendar.
  • Completion guaranty and who has the net worth to stand behind it.
  • The takeout: sale, agency, SBA, or perm — with a date and the conditions that takeout will impose (seasoning, occupancy, DSCR at stabilization).
Bridge without a takeout is just an expensive balloon. Write the exit on the one-pager in two sentences. If those sentences are vague, do not send the file.

Farm maturities the way you farm listings

Gear 4 already asks when the loan comes due. That date is a sourcing channel. Pull recorded mortgages on the eight-block and the comp set; sort by maturity year; put Salesforce tasks at 12 / 9 / 6 / 3 months.

“[Name] — your note on [address] looks like it matures [month]. I am not calling to list it. I am calling because the three options are different numbers: sell it, refinance it, or recapitalize it and keep it. I can put sale-net versus refi-net on one page. Which of those do you want to see first?”

That call outperforms cold Gear 1 because you are calling about their deadline, not your quota. Log the maturity when you hear it. If you do not have a task on it, you do not have a pipeline.

Contract language when you wear both hats

Drafting samples for counsel — not forms to send raw. The failure mode is the seller believing you “had the loan,” the buyer believing you “had the deal,” and you holding an indicative range.

  • Financing contingency tied to a defined event and a date: application complete, or written commitment issued, by date X — not “buyer will obtain financing.”
  • Buyer acknowledgment that the affiliated loan shop is optional, that a decline is not a listing-side claim against the firm, and that a soft read is not approval.
  • Seller acknowledgment that a financed buyer you introduce is not a guaranteed close until conditions precedent are satisfied, and that financing is not a condition of the listing.

Have the Broker of Record and Florida counsel set the exact text. Put the approved versions on The Paper tab once they exist. Until then, do not improvise paragraphs into a PSA.

What this tab will not do

  • It will not lock a rate, bind a lender, or decide Chapter 494, RESPA, or usury for a live file.
  • It will not store IDs, tax returns, account numbers, or wiring instructions. Those stay in the approved secure system.
  • It will not replace the Lender Matrix, the DSCR checklist, or the guided deal workspace. Those are still the file-build tools. This is the conversation and comparison layer that sits on top of them.

Prequal desk

Not a consumer approval. Answer the questions, enter the volume, get a lane — and whether you may write an offer. Unknown credit is unverified. A 440 is not “more expensive DSCR.”

Prequal desk — questions, then the dollars

This is not a consumer pre-qual letter. It tells you the lane, whether you may write an offer, and the payment at a street rate and an ugly rate. If credit is unknown, the ugly rate is the one that decides.

“Volume” here is the loan they want. Cash must cover down payment + close + reserves at the rate the lane actually gets — not the rate they wish they had.

DSCR & Business-Purpose Lending — The Submission File

This is the channel where a borrower qualifies on the property's cash flow rather than their tax returns — investors, foreign nationals, self-employed owners, and anyone whose returns do not show what they actually earn. It is also the channel where deals die in underwriting over paperwork, not credit. The checklist below is the fix: collect it up front and the file closes on schedule.

What "business purpose" actually buys you

A business-purpose loan is a loan whose proceeds are used for business or investment, not for personal, family or household purposes. That classification carries real weight: it takes the loan outside the federal consumer machinery — TILA and Regulation Z, RESPA, the ability-to-repay rules, the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure, and the SAFE Act's residential loan originator definition. No consumer disclosures, no ATR analysis, no DTI. That is why the whole DSCR product exists.

What it does for you in practice: the borrower does not produce tax returns, W-2s or a DTI calculation. Underwriting is the rent versus the payment. A file that would take sixty days of income documentation on the conventional side becomes a two-week file here. For an investor buying a fourplex or a foreign national buying a rental, this is often the only product that works at all.
What it does not do: business purpose is a federal consumer-law classification. It is not a state licensing answer. Florida's F.S. 494 definition of a mortgage loan reaches commercial loans where the borrower is an individual or the lender is a non-institutional investor, and five-or-more-unit residential under those same conditions — regardless of purpose. And a DSCR loan on a one-to-four unit house is residential collateral whichever way the purpose falls. The loans that sit cleanly outside are institutional lender + entity borrower + commercial collateral. Everything else is a question for counsel, once, in writing. See the Lender Matrix tab for the full citation trail.

The document that does the classifying is on the checklist below: the Certification of Business Purpose / Non-Owner Occupancy Affidavit, signed and notarized with the closing docs. That affidavit is what the lender relies on to treat the loan as business purpose. If the borrower is going to live in it, this product does not apply — and a borrower who signs that affidavit and then moves in has committed fraud with your name on the file. Ask the question directly, early, and believe the answer only if it is consistent with everything else in the file.

The submission checklist

Work top to bottom. Tick as you collect. Anything not gathered before submission becomes a condition, and conditions are what blow closing dates.

Submission notes — how the file gets built

  • Remove the income, keep the job information. The 1003 still carries employer and position; the income fields come out. Underwriting is not looking at it and a populated income field invites a condition asking you to document it.
  • Update assets and verify three things: the down payment, the closing costs, and the reserves. All three have to be demonstrably in the account.
  • Copies of the leases on the subject property, if there are any. A leased property with real leases underwrites on actual rent; a vacant one underwrites on the 1007 market rent, usually at a haircut.
  • Confirm the borrower owns a home or has rental history. Most DSCR programs want a borrower who has owned property for twelve months. A true first-time buyer usually cannot do a DSCR loan — find that out on the first call, not in underwriting.
  • REO must match credit. REO statements are not needed unless there is a private mortgage on a property, in which case you need the payment history — and a private mortgage is exactly the thing that will not appear on a credit report. Ask.
  • Regular appraisal plus the 1007. The 1007 rent schedule is what produces the rent number the DSCR is calculated from. No 1007, no DSCR, no loan.
The DSCR itself is the whole underwrite. Minimum 1.00 on most programs — gross rent divided by PITIA. Come in below it and the loan gets restructured: more down, a lower loan amount, or a buydown. Run that math on the first call, before anyone orders an appraisal, because a 0.92 does not become a 1.05 by hoping. The Ratios Calculator tab does this arithmetic.

Appraisal standards are stricter than people expect. An approved AMC, the appraiser's license, E&O, AIR certification, and the original first-generation XML — a PDF alone gets rejected. For investment properties the 1007 based on annual tenancy. Lenders frequently order an enhanced desk review on top, at their cost, to support value. Send the appraisal and survey invoices to the lender along with the credit report.

The entity file — where these deals actually stall

Most DSCR loans close in an LLC, and the entity package is the single most common source of last-minute delay, because borrowers assume their LLC paperwork is fine and it usually is not. Pull it in week one.

  • Certificate of Good Standing dated no more than 90 days before the note date. Order it late and it expires; order it early and it expires. Time it.
  • Articles of Incorporation or Organization, and the Operating Agreement — underwriting reads it to determine who can actually sign.
  • A Resolution granting authority for the transaction, subject to compliance review.
  • Landlord or equivalent insurance — dec page with at least six months of rent-loss coverage, confirmation of the replacement cost amount, the invoice or paid receipt, and the correct mortgagee clause. The mortgagee clause is wrong on roughly half of first submissions.
Reserves are a hard stop, not a preference. Six months of reserves is typical and underwriting re-verifies them at clear-to-close, not at submission. A borrower who spends their reserves on the renovation between approval and closing kills their own loan — tell them that out loud, early, in those words.

Where your commercial deals plug into this

The DSCR logic scales. The same cash-flow-over-credit underwrite runs on five-plus unit multifamily, mixed use, retail, warehouse and self-storage at the small-balance commercial shops — the difference is the metric name (DSCR on NOI rather than gross rent), the documents (rent roll and T-12 instead of a 1007), and the fact that no consumer rules were ever in play because the collateral was never residential.

  • 1–4 units, investor — DSCR wholesale. Residential collateral. Fastest, cheapest, most documented. This checklist applies exactly.
  • 5+ units and mixed use — small-balance commercial: Velocity, Silver Hill, Cherrywood, CoreVest, Emigrant, Logan Finance, Hometown Equity. Rent roll and T-12 replace the 1007; the entity package is identical.
  • Commercial by type — retail, warehouse, self-storage, auto, gas — same shops, plus the private desks. Gas requires the environmental report before most of them will look at it (see the Execution Runbook tab).
  • Land — a different animal entirely. No rent means no DSCR. AgAmerica, United AG, FNBA and the private desks, at low leverage against value.

Your DSCR and foreign-national desks are in the Lender Matrix tab, filterable, with the reps you already have.

Fannie Mae reference

The Fannie Mae reference material behind the standard forms — the 1007 rent schedule and related appraisal requirements — is published here: singlefamily.fanniemae.com/media/12351/display. DSCR programs are not Fannie loans, but they borrow Fannie's forms and appraisal conventions, so the standards in that document are what the appraisal gets measured against.

The Land Use Operator — Working Planning, Zoning and the Commission

Zoning is your specialty, and zoning is decided by people in rooms on a published calendar. The brokers who win land and entitlement work are not the ones with better comps — they are the ones who know what is on next month's agenda, who sits on which board, and what the rules are for talking to them. This tab is how you become that person legitimately, and how you avoid the three mistakes that end careers here.
Read this before anything else on this page. Everything below is researched and sourced, but it is not legal advice, and two of the rules turn on questions I could not resolve from public sources. Miami-Dade's Commission on Ethics and Public Trust issues free written advisory opinions — ask before you act, keep the answer, and have a Florida land use attorney review your registration decision once. That one hour is the cheapest insurance in this business, and if a complaint is ever filed, a written opinion in the file is the strongest evidence of good faith you can have.

The one distinction that governs everything: is the matter legislative or quasi-judicial?

Florida law splits local land use decisions into two kinds, and the same commissioner is a politician on one and a judge on the other. Treating a quasi-judicial item like a political one is the single most common way people get into real trouble here.

LegislativeQuasi-judicial
What it isComprehensive plan amendments, code text changes, area-wide rezonings — policy setting, affecting a broad publicSite-specific rezonings, variances, special exceptions, appeals — policy application to a limited number of people
Contacting officialsPolitical persuasion is legitimate. Call, meet, advocatePresumed prejudicial unless disclosed on the record. See the next card
What winsVotes, coalitions, constituent pressureCompetent substantial evidence in the record — testimony, studies, expert opinion
Court reviewDeferential — “fairly debatable”Certiorari in circuit court on the record
Right to speakF.S. 286.0114 guarantees a reasonable opportunity to be heard286.0114 expressly does not apply. The right comes from due process and the local code, and the format is evidentiary

The controlling case is Board of County Commissioners of Brevard County v. Snyder, 627 So. 2d 469 (Fla. 1993). It holds that rezonings affecting a limited number of persons are quasi-judicial, and it sets the burden: the landowner first shows the proposal is consistent with the comprehensive plan and meets procedural requirements — then the burden shifts to the board to show that keeping the existing zoning serves a legitimate public purpose.
