Written findings are not required; the ruling must rest on competent substantial evidence.

Why this is commercially useful, not just legal trivia. On a quasi-judicial item, consistency with the comprehensive plan is the whole ballgame. If you can show a seller or a buyer that their parcel's CDMP or comp-plan designation already supports the use they want, you have told them something worth real money — and you have told them before the attorney does. That is the land use conversation nobody else on the phone is having.

Ex parte contact — the mistake that voids the approval your client paid for

Jennings v. Dade County, 589 So. 2d 1337 (Fla. 3d DCA 1991) arose from exactly this fact pattern: a lobbyist hired by a zoning applicant contacted Miami-Dade commissioners before the hearing. The court held that once an aggrieved party proves an ex parte contact occurred, its effect is presumed prejudicial unless the other side proves otherwise. Unrebutted, the decision is vacated and the hearing starts over.

Read what that means in dollars. An undisclosed hallway conversation does not just create an ethics problem. It hands an opponent a ready-made certiorari argument and can void an approval your client spent a year and six figures obtaining — and your name is on the file. This is not a theoretical risk in Miami; it is the case the rule is named after, and it came out of this county.

F.S. 286.0115 was the legislature's answer. It lets a city or county adopt an ordinance establishing a disclosure process that removes the presumption of prejudice. Where such an ordinance exists, the procedure is:

  • Oral communications — the subject of the communication and the identity of the person or group are disclosed and made part of the record before final action.
  • Written communications — placed in the record before final action.
  • Site visits, investigations and expert opinions — their existence is placed in the record.
  • Timing — disclosure must occur before or during the meeting at which the vote is taken, so opponents have a real chance to respond.
The open question, stated plainly. The statute is enabling, not self-executing — it only helps if the local government actually adopted an ordinance under it. I could not verify that Miami-Dade or the City of Miami has adopted one. Until you confirm that with the County Attorney, the City Attorney or your own land use counsel, assume Jennings governs and that ex parte contact on a pending quasi-judicial item is presumptively prejudicial.

The working rule that keeps you clean either way: once a specific application is filed, stop having private conversations about it with anyone who will vote on it. Put your position in a written submission that goes into the record, and make your case at the hearing where it can be tested. Build the relationships before there is an application and on matters that are legislative — that is both legal and, as it happens, more effective.

Lobbyist registration — assume you must, in both jurisdictions

This is the rule people get wrong most often, and the penalty is not a fine — it is a ban on lobbying, which for someone building a land use practice is the whole business.

Miami-Dade County — Code Sec. 2-11.1(s)

  • Register with the Clerk of the Board, through the LORIS online system.
  • When: within five business days of being retained, or before any lobbying activity — whichever comes first.
  • Fee: reported at $490 annually per company per lobbying employee, plus a $100 ethics course fee. Confirm the current-year amount with the Clerk.
  • Renewal: calendar year; renew by January 15, window opens in December.
  • Expenditure report: due July 1 for the prior calendar year — and it is due even if you spent nothing. Items over $25 itemized.
  • Ethics course required after registering.
  • Penalties: late report $50 per day per client, automatic suspension if not filed by September 1. Ethics Commission enforcement escalates to a 90-day, one-year, then five-year lobbying ban; civil penalties $250 then $500; three or more violations can trigger contractor debarment.

City of Miami — Code Sec. 2-651 to 2-658

  • Register with the City Clerk. miamilobbyists@miamigov.com  ·  (305) 250-5361
  • When: within five business days of retention, or before lobbying.
  • Fee: reported at $525 annually, plus $105 for each principal for each issue lobbied. The per-issue add-on is easy to under-pay — confirm with the Clerk.
  • Renewal: expires December 31, calendar-year basis. Amendments within 15 days of any change; withdrawal notice within 30 days of ceasing.
  • Expenditure report: reported as due January 15 — a different date from the County's July 1. Late penalty $50/day plus removal from the active list.
  • Ethics course within 60 days of registering, refresher every two years, administered by the County Ethics Commission.
The three traps — this is the part worth reading twice.

Trap 1. The County's quasi-judicial exemption may not protect you. The County excludes representatives appearing at quasi-judicial proceedings “where the law prohibits ex-parte communications.” But in Florida practice ex parte is generally not prohibited — F.S. 286.0115 permits it with disclosure. If that is the case here, the exemption arguably does not reach ordinary rezoning and variance hearings at all. Unresolved. Get it in writing.

Trap 2. The County exemption does not carry over to the City. The Miami-Dade Commission on Ethics addressed this directly in Inquiry 15-133: an architect representing a condominium association at a quasi-judicial zoning appeal before the Miami City Commission was required to register and take ethics training, because City Code Sec. 2-653 is stricter and has no equivalent carve-out. Municipalities may set stricter standards than the County. The only City exception noted was for someone limited to providing factual information requested by board members.

Trap 3. A compensated broker is not “self-representing.” The self-representation exclusion requires appearing in your individual capacity without compensation or reimbursement. A broker earning a commission who advocates for a client's application does not fit it. A property owner appearing personally and unpaid on their own property probably does.
The practical posture: register in both jurisdictions and treat it as a cost of doing business. A few hundred dollars a year against a five-year lobbying ban is not a close call — and registration has a second benefit almost nobody thinks about: it puts your name on the public list that developers and land use attorneys search when they need a broker who works entitlements. The registration is marketing as much as compliance. The City's own hearing application checklist lists “lobbyist registration (if applicable)” among required uploads, so the question comes up on every file anyway.

One correction worth having: F.S. 112.3261, which people cite as the state lobbying statute for local government, does not reach counties or cities — its operative definition covers water management districts only. Florida has no general state registration requirement for local lobbying. The Miami-Dade and City of Miami ordinances are the operative law, which is exactly why they differ from each other.

Sunshine Law — and the one thing you must never do

F.S. 286.011 requires that all meetings of a county or municipal board at which official acts are taken be open to the public, with notice and minutes. No formal action is binding unless taken at such a meeting. Violations are punishable by a fine up to $500, and a board member who knowingly attends a non-compliant meeting commits a second-degree misdemeanor.

The conduit problem — the classic and most dangerous mistake for someone building influence. Two members of the same board may not privately discuss a matter that will come before them. That prohibition cannot be evaded by routing the conversation through you. If you carry the message — “Commissioner A is prepared to support this if you are” — you have created a de facto meeting between two officials outside the Sunshine. You have exposed both of them to criminal and civil liability and potentially voided the action. You will not be thanked for it, and you will not be called again.

The safe practice, which is also the professional one: talk to each official independently; never report one official's position, vote count or negotiating posture to another; never convene a call or meeting that includes two members of the same board; and put positions on the record at the public hearing, which is where they belong anyway.

Public records — the research weapon nobody uses

F.S. Chapter 119 gives any person the right to inspect and copy public records, and you do not have to say who you are or why you want them. Copies run up to 15¢ per one-sided page; an agency may charge a reasonable special service charge if the request requires extensive IT or clerical work. For land use work this is the highest-yield, lowest-cost research available:

  • Staff reports and recommendations on pending and decided applications — this tells you how the planning department actually thinks about a use in a district, before you advise anyone.
  • Correspondence between applicants, their representatives, and planning staff or commissioners. This is where the real story of a project lives.
  • Complete application files — plans, traffic and concurrency studies.
  • Code enforcement history and open violations on a parcel. The City requires proof of no open violations to get a hearing, so this is a deal-killer you can find first.
  • Lobbyist registrations and expenditure reports — see the intelligence card below.
  • Pre-application meeting notes.
It cuts both ways. Your own emails to government staff are public records, and your competitors and your client's opponents can request them. Write every email to a public employee as if it will be read aloud at the hearing — because it can be.

Money — contributions, gifts, and the disclosure that voids approvals

  • Contribution limit. Under F.S. 106.08, the limit for county and municipal candidates is $1,000 per election — and primary and general count as separate elections, so each can receive the limit. I did not verify whether Miami-Dade imposes a lower local limit; confirm with the Elections Department.
  • Straw donors are a crime. “A person may not make any contribution through or in the name of another, directly or indirectly.” Reimbursing employees, family or partners for contributions is the single most common way real estate figures get prosecuted in Florida. Do not do it, do not let a client do it through your office, and do not be the person who collected the checks.
  • Gifts. Miami-Dade Sec. 2-11.1(e) defines a gift as any transfer of economic value without adequate consideration — a meal counts as one gift. It is unlawful to offer a gift to covered County personnel for or because of an official action, not merely to accept one. The ordinance reaches the giver. You are exposed even if they decline. Gifts over $100 from one source trigger disclosure obligations on the official.
  • Cone of silence is procurement, not zoning. Sec. 2-11.1(t) covers RFPs, RFQs and bids — it starts at advertisement and ends at the written recommendation, and it bars oral communication with staff, commissioners and selection committee members. Written communication copied to the Clerk is permitted at all times. You will hit this on County or City land dispositions, P3s, unsolicited proposals and brokerage-services solicitations — all squarely your business. You will not hit it on a private rezoning; there, the ex parte doctrine is the constraint.
City of Miami Ordinance 12918 — know this one cold, because it is aimed at a practice that is common here. Anyone requesting approval or relief from the City Commission or its boards must disclose any consideration provided or committed to any person for an agreement to support, or to withhold objection. “Consideration” is defined extremely broadly — gift, payment, contribution, donation, fee, commission, promise, service, credit, or financial assistance of any kind, direct or implied, present or future. It is filed at the commencement of the hearing. Non-compliance renders the application or order void without further force or effect, and bars review of related applications for one year.

Settling with an objector or a neighborhood association is not itself illegal. Failing to disclose it destroys the approval. If your client is negotiating with an opponent, that is the moment to say this out loud.

City of Miami — how an item actually moves

The Planning, Zoning and Appeals Board (PZAB) is the City's local planning agency — eleven regular members, one alternate and a school board representative. It meets the first and third Wednesday of each month at 6:30 PM at City Hall. The code is Miami 21, form-based, adopted 2010; the procedures are in Article 7.

ApplicationWho decidesAppeal
By-rightZoning AdministratorDe novo to PZAB within 15 days
Waiver (minor deviations)Zoning Administrator, 30+ days after NET noticeDenial appealable de novo to PZAB, 15 days
WarrantPlanning Director, 30+ days after NET notice; over 200,000 sf goes to the Coordinated Review CommitteeDe novo to PZAB, 15 days
ExceptionPZAB — quasi-judicial, Planning Director recommendsDe novo to City Commission, 15 days
VariancePZAB — quasi-judicial. Only lot size, coverage, setbacks, parking, open space, and only on proof of special hardshipDe novo to City Commission, 15 days
Rezoning / Special Area Plan / comp plan amendmentPZAB recommends; City Commission decides, minimum two hearings—

Two timing facts worth more than they look. Warrants, Waivers, Exceptions and Variances are valid two years. And rezoning applications are limited to twice-yearly cycles (except CS zones and city-initiated changes) — so missing a cycle deadline costs your client roughly six months. Knowing the cycle dates is a reason for an owner to take your call.

The flow: mandatory pre-application meeting with the Zoning Administrator or Planning Director (nothing said there binds anyone) → submit plans via ePlan → on batch stamp, referred to Hearing Boards → upload 18 categories of documents, including legal descriptions, affidavits, lobbyist registration if applicable, ownership disclosures, corporate resolutions, proof of no open code violations, and a property owner list within 300 feet (Excel, no older than six months) → fees are 50% upfront, 50% after batch stamp → hearing date in roughly 45 days. An authorized representative must attend. Hearing Boards: (305) 416-2030, 444 SW 2nd Ave, 3rd floor.

Notice: certified mail to abutting owners and registered neighborhood associations through the NET office at application; Exception and Variance hearings require certified mail to owners within 500 feet, at least 10 days before. Decisions posted within five days and distributed by NET to registered associations.

Miami-Dade County — the bodies and the thresholds

Community Councils / Community Zoning Appeals Boards — ten council areas serving unincorporated Miami-Dade, six elected members each plus one BCC appointee, all residents of the area.

A genuine conflict in the County's own sources — resolve it before you file anything. The County's Community Councils web page describes them as advisory, making recommendations rather than final decisions. But Code Sec. 33-311 grants the CZAB authority to “hear and grant or deny” district boundary changes, use and non-use variances, special exceptions and unusual or new uses, except where the BCC has direct jurisdiction. Confirm with the Clerk of the Board or a land use attorney which body actually decides your application type today. Filing in the wrong forum costs months.

Board of County Commissioners — direct jurisdiction over developments of regional impact and specified modifications; appeals under §§ 33-313 and 33-314. Zoning meetings roughly monthly at the Stephen P. Clark Center, 111 NW 1st Street, 2nd floor chambers.

Developmental Impact Committee (DIC) — Code § 33-303.1. A multi-department body that reviews large-scale zoning actions and, as the Executive Council, serves as the Land Development Regulation Commission, making recommendations to the BCC. Executive Council meets monthly in person; Lower Council monthly virtually; both at 10 a.m.; no meetings in August.

Screen every deal against the DIC thresholds early — DIC adds months, and telling a client that up front is worth more than telling them a price:

  • Residential over 250 units
  • Business uses over 10 acres or 100,000 sf of retail
  • Office over 125,000 sf
  • Industrial on over 50 acres
  • Public schools and airport zones
  • Development agreements and vested rights matters

County flow: the Zoning Evaluation Unit reviews plans for sufficiency and against the Comprehensive Development Master Plan and Chapter 33, prepares the finalized request for advertisement and mailed notice, and presents the department recommendation to the appropriate board. There is a formal pre-application process. At the hearing the chair explains the rules, your item is called, you or your attorney present, supporters and objectors speak, the board votes to approve, deny or approve with conditions, and a Resolution documents it. A boundary survey updated within one year is mandatory.

Speaking time at the BCC: five minutes on public hearing items; two minutes on other propositions with a ten-minute cap per side and four minutes for representative speakers when more than five people register. Zoning applications are expressly excluded from that rule and governed by Chapter 33. City of Miami limits are published per meeting on the calendar page rather than in one rule — check the specific meeting.

Where to watch — the links that matter

  • City legislative portal — agendas for PZAB and the Commission: miamifl.iqm2.com. Select Planning, Zoning & Appeals Board from the dropdown.
  • PZAB board page and meeting calendar: miami.gov PZAB  ·  Zoning Boards Calendar
  • City hearing application requirements: Request a Hearing
  • Miami 21 Article 7 (procedures) — the source for everything in the table above: miami21.org Article 7
  • County BCC zoning hearings and agendas: miamidade.gov zoning hearings
  • Community Councils, calendars and the area map: Community Councils
  • Developmental Impact Committee: DIC
  • County Commissioners by district: Board of County Commissioners — 13 districts, each with its own contact page.
  • City Commissioner district offices: District Offices — 5 districts. Appointments go through the chief of staff or district aide.
  • Miami-Dade Commission on Ethics and Public Trust: ethics.miamidade.gov — free written advisory opinions, ethics training, and a 24-hour hotline at 786-314-9560. It has jurisdiction over both County and municipal government, including the City of Miami.

The intelligence play — map the network without one improper conversation

Both jurisdictions publish their lobbyist registries, and this is the best competitive intelligence available in this market, for free. A registration discloses the lobbyist, the principal, and the issue lobbied.

  • Miami-Dade LORIS — searchable registrations: LORIS  ·  Clerk of the Board
  • City of Miami — searchable registered lobbyist database through the City Clerk: Lobbyist Information

What it tells you, read properly: who represents whom on what; which firms dominate which districts; who is already working a project you are chasing; and — because County registration requires disclosing anyone holding 5% or more of a registering entity and any business relationships with County personnel — who is actually behind an entity. Combine that with expenditure reports and a Chapter 119 request for staff correspondence and you can map the real influence network on any project without a single improper call.

And the obvious use nobody makes of it: the registry is a list of everyone in Miami who does entitlement work for a living — land use attorneys, expediters, planners, the firms whose clients are buying and selling land. Those are your referral sources and your buyer list. They need a broker who understands zoning; you need their deal flow. Reading the registry as a prospecting list rather than a compliance document is the single highest-leverage thing on this page.

The monthly routine — how you actually stay on top

None of this works as a project. It works as a standing appointment on your calendar, the same way the Perfect Calendar tab handles prospecting. Two hours a month, permanently.

  • First Wednesday, morning — pull the PZAB agenda for that night from the legislative portal. Read the item list. Every applicant is a lead and every objector is a lead.
  • Same morning — pull the BCC zoning agenda and the DIC Executive Council agenda for the month.
  • Pick two items in your submarkets and read the staff report. That is where you learn how the department is currently thinking — which is what makes you sound like a specialist on the phone rather than a broker with a script.
  • Go to one hearing a quarter, in person. Sit through it. You will learn more about who actually decides things in three hours than in a year of reading, and the same twenty people are in that room every month. Being a recognizable face is most of what “connected” means.
  • Once a month, run the lobbyist registry for new registrations in your submarkets. New registration means a new project, usually before anything is public.
  • Introduce yourself to your district commissioners' offices — the chief of staff and the district aide, not the commissioner. On no pending matter, with nothing to ask for. Say what you do, what submarkets you cover, and that you are a resource on property questions in the district. That call costs nothing and is remembered.
  • Register with the NET offices and get on the neighborhood association notice lists in your farm. You will see applications at the same time the neighbors do — which is earlier than the market does.
What this compounds into. In twelve months you will know the calendar, the staff, the recurring objectors, the attorneys and the thresholds. When an owner asks “can I put this on my land?”, you will answer from the code and the comp plan instead of saying you'll find out. That is the entire difference between a broker who lists land and a broker who gets called about land — and it is built out of public agendas and showing up, not out of favors.

Confirm before you rely — the open items

These are the things I could not settle from public sources. Each one changes what you should do, so take them to the Ethics Commission or counsel rather than guessing.

QuestionWhy it mattersAsk
Has Miami-Dade or the City adopted an ex parte disclosure ordinance under F.S. 286.0115?Determines whether pre-hearing contact is permissible at all, and whether the County lobbyist exemption appliesCounty / City Attorney; land use counsel
Does the County's quasi-judicial lobbyist exemption cover a compensated broker?Registering unnecessarily is cheap; failing to register is a 90-day to 5-year banClerk of the Board + written COE opinion
Current-year fees — County $490, City $525 + $105 per principal per issueUnderpayment can invalidate the registrationClerk of the Board; City Clerk
City expenditure report due date (Jan 15) vs County (Jul 1)$50 per day penaltiesCity Clerk
Do Community Councils decide or only recommend today? The web page and Sec. 33-311 conflictFiling in the wrong forum costs monthsClerk of the Board; land use counsel
Any Miami-Dade rule on contributions from persons with matters pendingPotential ethics violationCommission on Ethics
Any local contribution limit below the state $1,000Over-limit contributions are a campaign finance violationMiami-Dade Elections Department
The standing move: the Commission on Ethics issues free written advisory opinions, and the published inquiry letters are exactly that — real people asking real questions and getting an answer they can rely on. Ask before you act, in writing, and keep the answer. Nothing on this page is legal advice; the citations are here so an attorney can verify the analysis quickly.

Winning the Contract — Getting the Exclusive Signed

Everything else in this system produces conversations. This tab produces signatures — the exclusive listing from a seller, the exclusive representation from a buyer. Without that signature you are doing unpaid research for someone who will transact around you, and you will never know it happened. This is the highest-leverage skill in the business, and it is almost entirely psychological.
The premise this whole tab rests on, and you should agree with it or stop reading. These techniques work because the exclusive genuinely serves the client when you actually perform — a broker with an exclusive runs a real process, spends real money, and gets them a better number. Used by someone who will not perform, the same techniques are manipulation, and in a referral business that is a slow-motion way to end your career. Persuade people into agreements you will honor. Everything below assumes you mean it.

Why the open listing is worse for them than for you

Most agents defend exclusivity as though it is a favor the seller does for them. It is not, and arguing it that way is why they lose. Here is the actual case, and it is a strong one:

  • Nobody spends money on a listing they might not get paid for. An open listing gets a sign and a portal entry. An exclusive gets professional photography, an offering memorandum, a targeted campaign to a buyer list, calls to every 1031 buyer in the market, and someone willing to spend forty hours on a rezoning analysis. The seller does not get less service on an open listing — they get a different product entirely.
  • Open listings suppress the price. When three brokers are racing, every one of them is incentivized toward speed, not number — because a slower higher offer might close with someone else. You get whoever calls first, not who pays most. An exclusive is the only structure where the broker’s interest is a higher price rather than a faster one.
  • It signals distress. A property a buyer sees from three different brokers reads as shopped and stale, and buyers price that in. The listing that looks hard to get sells for more than the listing that is everywhere.
  • Nobody is accountable. With three brokers, no one owns the outcome, no one reports, and no one will tell the owner the price is wrong. One throat to choke is a feature for the seller, not for you.
Say it as a question, not a lecture: “Can I ask you something? If four brokers are all working it, who’s actually accountable for the result? And who’s going to spend eight thousand dollars marketing a property they have a one-in-four chance of getting paid on?” — then stop talking. They will answer it themselves, and an argument they reach on their own is one they will not later resist.

The seven levers — Cialdini, applied to this specific signature

Robert Cialdini’s work on influence is the most heavily replicated body of research in persuasion. Here is each principle translated into something you actually say at a kitchen table in Hialeah.

LeverWhat it isHow you use it here
ReciprocityPeople return what they receive — and the effect is strongest when the gift is unexpected, personalized, and given firstDo the work before you ask. Walk in with the comp set already pulled, the folio history, the zoning read, the payoff math on their current loan. Hand it over and say “this is yours either way.” Saying that out loud is what makes it a gift rather than a pitch.
Commitment & consistencyPeople act consistently with what they have already said — especially when it was said out loud, voluntarily, and in their own wordsMake them state the goal. “What would this have to sell for, for you to be happy you did it?” Write the number down in front of them. Every later step is now consistency with their number, not compliance with your ask.
Social proofWe look to similar others, and the closer the similarity the stronger the pullNot “we sold 40 properties.” “The two buildings behind yours on 14th both traded in the last year. Both were exclusives. I can tell you what they got and what the buyer pool looked like.” Same street, same asset, same kind of owner.
AuthorityDemonstrated expertise, not claimed — and credentials land hardest when delivered by someone elseOne specific fact they did not know about their own property beats a page of credentials. The zoning change, the assemblage next door, the recertification year. Have your assistant or partner introduce you: “he does the land use work in this corridor.”
LikingSimilarity, genuine compliments, and cooperating toward a shared goalFind the real similarity — the neighborhood, the family business, the operator’s problem. Then physically sit on the same side: pull up beside them with the numbers between you, not across a desk. “Let’s figure out what this is worth” is a different posture than “let me show you what I do.”
ScarcityLoss of an opportunity motivates more than gain of the same size — but only real scarcity survives contactUse only what is true, and there is usually plenty: the 1031 buyer with a 45-day identification clock, the rate window, the twice-yearly rezoning cycle deadline, the buyer who just lost out on a similar deal. Manufactured urgency is detected and it costs you the file.
UnityNot similarity — shared identity. The “we” categoryThe strongest lever in Miami and the most underused. Same neighborhood, same immigrant family business story, same operator class. “People like us” is a category, and once someone is inside it the persuasion stops being persuasion. Co-create the plan with them so it becomes ours.

Pre-suasion — the sixty seconds before the ask

Cialdini’s later work makes a point most people miss entirely: what you do immediately before the request changes the answer to it. Attention channeled onto one idea makes whatever follows feel connected to that idea. So the question is not just what do I ask — it is what is on their mind when I ask.

  • Before asking for the exclusive, put control on the table. “Before we talk about anything else — how much control do you want over this process? Some owners want to know everything; some want it handled.” Whatever they answer, the exclusive is now the answer to a question they raised.
  • Before talking about the term, ask about time. “When would you want to be done with this?” A six-month term stops being a long commitment and becomes the time required to hit your date.
  • Before the commission conversation, talk about the marketing budget. Not as a defense — just describe what you will actually spend and do. The fee then arrives as a cost of that program rather than as a number out of their pocket.
  • Before the buyer rep, ask what happened last time. “When you looked before, how did that go?” Almost every commercial buyer has a story about losing a deal or being ignored by a listing broker. Let them tell it. The representation agreement is then the answer to a problem they just described, not a form you produced.
The mechanism is simple and it is worth internalizing. A request that arrives as the answer to a question already in their head feels like a solution. The identical request arriving cold feels like a sales pitch. Same words, different result, and the only variable is the sixty seconds before.

Loss aversion — and why you must frame the cost of not signing

Kahneman and Tversky’s central finding is that a loss hurts roughly twice as much as an equivalent gain feels good. Almost every agent pitches the gain — what they will do, how hard they work. The gain frame is the weak one.

  • Weak: “If you list with me I’ll run a full marketing campaign and get you the best price.”
  • Strong: “The risk in an open listing isn’t that it doesn’t sell. It’s that it sells — to the first buyer who calls, at the first number they offer, because nobody had a reason to go find the second and third one. You never see the offer you didn’t get.”
  • Buyer side, weak: “I’ll send you everything that comes up.”
  • Buyer side, strong: “Right now you’re seeing what’s on the portals, which is what everybody sees. The deals that trade well in this market don’t get there — they go to the three or four brokers who have a buyer under agreement, because those are the calls that are worth making. Without that, you’re bidding against the whole market on the leftovers.”
The discipline: loss framing must be true and specific, or it reads as fear-mongering and destroys the trust you spent an hour building. Name a real mechanism — the offer you never see, the off-market call that never comes — not a vague threat about “missing the market.”

The commitment ladder — the yeses before the yes

Nobody goes from stranger to signature in one step. They go up a ladder, and each rung is a small commitment they made voluntarily. Your job is to never skip a rung and never ask for a rung they are not standing under.

  • Rung 1 — they give you information. The rent roll, the debt, the reason. Someone who has answered three real questions is invested.
  • Rung 2 — they state a goal in their own words. A number, a date, a reason. Write it down in front of them.
  • Rung 3 — they agree with a piece of your analysis. “Yeah, that’s about right.” That is a public commitment to your competence.
  • Rung 4 — they help build the plan. “Would you want the tenants to know, or do we keep it quiet?” Once they have made a decision inside your process, it is their process. People value what they helped build far more than what they were handed.
  • Rung 5 — they agree to the next step. Not the signature — the walk-through, the rent roll, the pricing meeting.
  • Rung 6 — the signature, which at this point is the administrative expression of five things they already said.
The tell that you skipped a rung: “let me think about it.” That almost never means I need time. It means you asked for rung six while they were standing on rung three. The recovery is not to push — it is to go back down: “Fair enough. Can I ask what part you’d want to think hardest about — the price, the timing, or me?” All three are answerable. Vague hesitation is not.

Tactical empathy — the moves that do the most work

These come out of hostage negotiation and they transfer to this conversation almost unchanged, because both situations share one feature: the other person is afraid of being trapped.

  • The accusation audit. Say their objection before they can. “You’re probably thinking that six months is a long time to be locked in with somebody you met an hour ago. And that every broker who sits here says the same things I’m about to say.” An objection you name is defused. An objection they raise is a fight.
  • Labeling. Name the emotion, do not argue with it. “It seems like you’ve been burned by a broker before.” “It sounds like the timing is the real issue, not the price.” Then stay silent. Labels make people elaborate, and elaboration is where the real objection comes out.
  • Chase “That’s right,” not “yes.” Summarize their position so accurately that they say “that’s right” — that is the moment they feel understood, and it is the hinge of the whole meeting. “You’re right” is the opposite: it means they want you to stop talking.
  • Calibrated questions instead of demands. “How am I supposed to market this properly if I might not be the one who sells it?” puts the problem in their hands without a confrontation. “How” and “what” questions make them solve your problem for you.
  • No-oriented questions. People feel safe saying no, and safe people talk. “Is it a bad idea to put a date on the calendar?” “Have you given up on selling it this year?” “Would it be ridiculous to look at what an exclusive process actually gets you?” A “no” to those is a “yes” to you — and this is the same mechanic that makes the three-No rule work in the Gears.
  • Mirroring. Repeat their last three words as a question. “Too long a commitment?” It costs nothing, it is nearly invisible, and it reliably produces another paragraph.

The structure that beats closing technique on big-ticket deals

Neil Rackham’s research, built on observing roughly 35,000 sales calls, found something uncomfortable for traditional sales training: hard closing techniques increase success on small transactions and decrease it on large ones. On a big-ticket decision, pressure raises the buyer’s perceived risk, and perceived risk is the thing that kills the deal. What works instead is building value until the decision is obvious. That is done with four kinds of question, in order.

QuestionWhat it doesOn a listing
SituationFacts. Ask few of these — do the research first, and ask only what you could not find“How long have you owned it?” “Is it all on one folio?”
ProblemSurfaces a difficulty or dissatisfaction“How are the tenants performing?” “What’s the hardest part of holding it right now?”
ImplicationWhere the value is actually built. Makes the cost of the problem concrete“If the two month-to-month tenants leave before a sale, what does that do to what a buyer will pay?” “What does the recertification cost if you’re still holding it next year?”
Need-payoffMakes them articulate the value of the solution“If we could get those two on real leases before we go to market, what would that be worth to you?”
The need-payoff question is the most valuable sentence in this tab. When they answer it, they say the benefit out loud in their own words — and a benefit they stated is one they will not argue against later. You never have to close what they have already justified to themselves.

Choice architecture — never present one option

A single option invites a yes-or-no decision, and no is always the safer answer. Two or three options change the question from whether to which, and that alone materially raises your close rate. It also preserves their autonomy, which is the thing they are actually protecting.

  • Three terms, not one. “Twelve months is what I’d normally do on a land or zoning play, because entitlement takes that long. Nine is standard. Six is aggressive but doable if we price it right from day one. Which fits how you’re thinking?” Anchor at twelve and most people land on nine.
  • Two service levels. A full campaign with an offering memorandum and a marketed process, versus a quiet off-market approach to a targeted buyer list. Both are exclusives. The choice is real, and the exclusivity is no longer the decision on the table.
  • The honest retreat. Open with the larger ask, and when they push back, concede visibly to the one you wanted. “I’d normally ask for twelve. Given the timing you described — let’s do nine, and if it’s moving we won’t need it.” A concession triggers reciprocity, and it works only if the first number was defensible. Ask for something absurd and you have taught them your numbers are made up.

Autonomy — the counterintuitive one

People resist being controlled more than they resist the actual request. Explicitly returning the decision to them raises compliance — it is one of the most reliably replicated findings in the literature, and it costs you nothing.

Use these constantly, and mean them:

“But it’s completely your call.”
“You’re free to say no to this — I’d rather you did than sign something you’re not sure about.”
“I’m not going to chase you. If it’s not right, tell me and I’ll stop.”
“Feel free to do whatever you want here — my job is to make sure you’re deciding with the real numbers in front of you.”

And the cancellation clause is the strongest version of this move, which is why the sample listing agreement contains one. “There’s a clause in here that lets you cancel in writing at any time. I put it there on purpose. If I’m not doing what I said, you shouldn’t be stuck with me — I’d rather earn the six months every month than be owed them.” Handing them the exit is what makes them willing to walk in. And it is not a giveaway: the protection period still covers the buyer you produced.

The listing close — the full sequence

Run it in order. It takes forty to sixty minutes and it is the same every time.

  • 1. Arrive with work already done. Comps, folio history, zoning, debt. Hand it over: “this is yours either way.”  reciprocity
  • 2. Sit beside them, not across. Numbers between you.  liking · unity
  • 3. Ask about control and timing before anything else.  pre-suasion
  • 4. Run the question sequence. Few situation questions, then problem, then implication, then need-payoff. Let them say the number and the date. Write both down in front of them.  SPIN · commitment
  • 5. Deliver one fact about their property they did not know.  authority
  • 6. Give the street-level social proof. Same block, same asset, same kind of owner, real numbers.  social proof
  • 7. Build the plan with them. Ask two decisions into it — tenant confidentiality, timing, whether to approach the neighbor about assemblage.  co-creation
  • 8. Run the accusation audit before the ask. Name the lock-in fear, the “every broker says this” fear, the commission.  tactical empathy
  • 9. Frame the loss, once, specifically. The offer they never see.  loss aversion
  • 10. Present the choice of terms, anchored high.  choice architecture
  • 11. Hand them the cancellation clause deliberately.  autonomy
  • 12. Ask, then stop talking. “I’ve got it filled out to the nine months and the number you gave me. Shall we start it Monday?” — then say nothing at all until they speak. Whoever breaks the silence concedes, and after twelve steps of doing this properly you have earned the right to wait.
Have the agreement physically present and filled in from the start of the meeting. Not produced at the end like a trap — on the table from minute one, with their name and their property already on it. A document that has been visible for an hour is furniture. A document produced at the end is an ambush, and everyone can feel the difference.

The buyer representation close — why it is harder, and what changes

Sellers understand listing agreements; almost no commercial buyer has ever signed a representation agreement and most will ask why it exists. Three things change.

  • Lead with what it costs them, because the answer is usually nothing. “On almost every deal I’m paid by the seller or out of the listing broker’s fee. This agreement doesn’t add a cost — it says that when I bring you something, I get paid out of the deal, so I can afford to go find you the ones that aren’t listed.” The shortfall clause is your credibility: you told them before they made the offer, and they could walk with no obligation.
  • Sell access, not service. Every buyer has been told “I’ll send you listings.” Nobody is impressed. What they cannot get elsewhere is the off-market call — and the honest reason you only make those calls for a client under agreement is that they take days of work.
    “If I spend three days finding the owner of a building that isn’t for sale and talking him into a conversation, I need to know you’re not going to take that introduction to another broker. That’s the whole agreement.”
  • Use the loss frame, because it is literally true here. “The buyers who get the good deals in this market aren’t smarter. They just get called first. And brokers call the people they have an agreement with, because those are the calls that pay.”
  • Shorten the first term. Six months, or even ninety days on a first engagement. A short first term closes far more buyers than a long one, and the renewal after you have produced something off-market is nearly automatic. The goal of the first agreement is the second one.
The single best buyer-rep line, and it works because it is honest: “I’m not asking you to be loyal to me. I’m asking you to be exclusive with me for ninety days so I can justify the work. If in ninety days I haven’t shown you something you couldn’t have found yourself, don’t renew it — and I’ll have deserved that.”

The objections — tap what they just said

Every answer follows the same shape as the Objection Map: acknowledge, reframe, return the decision, end on a question. One rebuttal per objection, never two.

Say this
Why it works

What actually loses the contract

  • Presenting instead of asking. The agent who talks for forty minutes and asks four questions loses to the one who asks twenty and talks for ten. If you are doing most of the talking, you are losing.
  • Defending the commission. The moment you justify your fee you have accepted the frame that it is a cost rather than part of a program. Answer it once, factually, then return to the number they will net — which is the only number that was ever relevant.
  • Arguing with the price they want. They are attached to it and the attachment is real — people systematically overvalue what they own. Do not attack it; make it testable. “Let’s go out at your number for thirty days with a real campaign, and I’ll bring you every piece of feedback. If the market agrees, you were right and I was wrong. If it doesn’t, we’ll both know why.” That closes listings the argument never closes.
  • Pressure at the end. On a decision this size, pressure raises perceived risk and perceived risk is what kills it. Nine-tenths of the work happens before the ask; the ask itself should be almost boring.
  • Leaving without a next date. If they genuinely need time, never leave without a specific day and time on both calendars. “I’ll call you next week” is how a listing becomes someone else’s.
  • Sending the agreement instead of sitting with it. “Email it over and I’ll look at it” converts at a fraction of the rate. Offer to walk it through in ten minutes — in person, or on a screen share.

The hour after they sign

Post-decision doubt is real and it is strongest immediately after a large commitment. The cancellation that comes three days later was created in the ten minutes after the signature, by an agent who packed up and left.

  • Confirm the decision out loud. “You made a good call. Here’s what happens Monday.” Never let the last thing said be about the paperwork.
  • Give them something concrete within twenty-four hours — the photographer booked, the draft offering memorandum, the first three buyer calls made. Speed of first action is what converts a signature into a relationship.
  • Set the reporting rhythm before you leave. A fixed day, every week, whether there is news or not. The 14-Day Report tab is built for exactly this. Owners cancel over silence far more often than over price.
  • Tell them the bad news first and early. The broker who reports the disappointing feedback on day nine is the one who is believed on day sixty when they recommend the price change.

Where this comes from — and how much to trust it

Worth being straight about the evidence, because “psychology says” gets used to sell a lot of nonsense.

  • Cialdini’s principles are drawn from a large experimental literature and are among the better-supported findings in social psychology — though, as with much of the field, individual studies vary in how well they replicate, and effect sizes in the wild are smaller than in the lab.
  • Loss aversion (Kahneman and Tversky) is one of the most robust findings in behavioral economics, and it won a Nobel Prize. The roughly 2:1 ratio is a rule of thumb, not a constant.
  • SPIN came from observation of roughly 35,000 sales calls — a genuinely large field study, though conducted by a consultancy with a commercial interest in the result.
  • Tactical empathy — labeling, mirroring, calibrated questions, the accusation audit — is practitioner wisdom from hostage negotiation, not controlled research. It is extremely useful and it is not peer-reviewed. Treat it that way.
The part that is not in any of the books: all of this is amplification. It makes a real case land harder and a false one collapse faster, because a sophisticated commercial owner who feels handled will not merely decline — they will tell three other owners. Use it on deals where you are genuinely the right answer, and it compounds. Use it anywhere else and it is the fastest way to burn a market this small.

The Paper — Every Agreement, and Which One Protects You Where

Eight documents covering every seat you sit in: seller-side, buyer-side, lender-side, broker-to-broker, and inside your own firm. Each one downloads as a Word file you can edit and a print-ready PDF. The common thread: the paper goes out before the information does. Once you have made the introduction or sent the rent roll, you have given away the only leverage you had to get it signed.
Case law audit, September 2026 — read this before you rely on the NCND on this page.
Research found not one Florida appellate decision enforcing or striking down a non-circumvention agreement. Every source located was a law firm marketing page citing zero cases — including one asserting “a long history of courts enforcing” them while citing nothing. Multiple secondary sources characterize an NCND as a type of non-compete governed by § 542.335 — and if that is right, a perpetual, worldwide, all-counterparties NCND with no identified confidential information is the classic § 542.335 casualty. This is the highest-priority item for your lawyer.

And note what is verified: your strongest protection is not the NCND at all. It is the procuring-cause intentional exclusion doctrine from Sheldon Greene and Easton-Babcock, which punishes exactly the conduct an NCND targets — “dealing with one another directly and in secret” — and requires no restrictive-covenant analysis whatsoever. Plead procuring cause first and the NCND second. Full detail on the Case Law Audit tab.
All of these are drafting samples, not counsel’s work product. They are written to be close enough that your attorney is editing rather than starting, which is where the savings are. Have a Florida attorney review each one before you use it, and have your Broker of Record approve anything a client signs. Nothing here is legal advice.

Which paper, when — the decision table

The question is always the same: what am I about to give away, and to whom? Find the row, send the document, then send the information.

The momentWhat you are protectingSend this
A buyer wants the OM, rent roll or T-12Your seller’s financials, their tenants, their staff, and the fact they are sellingConfidentiality Agreement — Prospective Purchaser
An owner is deciding whether to trust you with their numbersNothing yet — you are buying trust, and this is what buys itBroker Confidentiality Undertaking — Owner Information
You are introducing your buyer to an owner or a listing brokerYour buyer, your fee, and the introduction itselfBuyer Registration & Broker Protection Agreement
A buyer wants you to start working for themYour time, and the deal they close without youExclusive Buyer Representation Agreement
An owner wants you to market their propertyEverything — this is the one that pays for all the restExclusive Right of Sale Listing Agreement
The same firm may list and arrange the loanThe dual role, optional use, and the fact that a soft read is not a closeOptional-use acknowledgment + PSA financing rider
You just gave an indicative rangeBeing quoted as if you committed the lenderSoft-read disclaimer letter
You are sending a file to a bank or capital sourceYour borrower, from being solicited directly for the next loan or the deposit relationshipNon-Solicitation & Broker Protection Addendum — Lender
A principal is being introduced to your lendersThe lender relationships themselves, plus your feeNon-Circumvention, Non-Disclosure & Fee Agreement
Another brokerage is working a deal with youThe split, and your client from being approached directlyCo-Brokerage, Commission Sharing & Non-Circumvention
You are bringing on an agent or staffYour database, your lender contacts, your comps, your clientsAgent Confidentiality & Restrictive Covenant Agreement

Dual-hat set — listing and loan on the same file

Counsel-blessed working drafts. Fill the blanks, keep the SAMPLE banner until Broker of Record initials the form, then send. The paper still goes out before the information does.

Use order: optional-use acknowledgment first → soft-read letter with the range → PSA rider when a contract is drafted → wall protocol in the internal file the same day both hats are on.

The library

Each downloads as .docx to edit and .pdf to send or print. Every one carries a SAMPLE stamp — remove it only after counsel signs off.

The four clauses that do the actual work

Most of what is in these documents is furniture. Four provisions are load-bearing, and if you understand only these you will still be better protected than most brokers in this market.

  • 1. The five-day carve-out notice. Every non-circumvention provision has to allow for a genuine pre-existing relationship, or a court will call it unreasonable. The fix is not to drop it — it is to put a clock on it: they must identify the pre-existing relationship in writing within five business days, and anyone they do not name is conclusively presumed to be your introduction. That single sentence converts a vague argument four months later into a document they either sent or did not send.
  • 2. The affiliate-and-nominee sweep. Circumvention almost never happens in the counterparty’s own name. It happens through a new LLC, a partner, a family member, a trust. Every restriction in this library reaches affiliates, principals, nominees, trusts and newly formed entities, and says plainly that they cannot do indirectly what the clause prohibits directly.
  • 3. Earned-and-payable, disbursed at closing. A fee that is earned on closing whether or not the deal closes through you, payable at closing, with authority for the closing agent to disburse it directly from closing funds, is a contract debt with a number attached. It is enforced far more readily than a restraint on who somebody may talk to. This is the clause that actually gets you paid.
  • 4. Reformation, not severance. A restrictive covenant that is too long or too broad gets struck entirely in some states. Florida courts will reform an overbroad covenant to what is enforceable — but the agreement should say that is what the parties intended. Every document here says it.
And the honest counterweight. Non-circumvention clauses get signed constantly and enforced unevenly. Courts have voided them where the term was indefinite, the covered parties were not specifically identified, or the “confidential” information turned out to be publicly available — and a lender’s name often is. The deterrent value is real; the litigation value is uncertain. Which is why clause 3 matters more than clause 2, and why getting the fee agreement signed before the introduction beats every enforcement theory in this tab.

Non-competes in Florida — what actually changed

Worth knowing precisely, because the ground moved recently and most people are working from old information.

  • F.S. 542.335 remains the framework: a restrictive covenant must be in writing, signed, and supported by a legitimate business interest — confidential business information, substantial relationships with specific clients, or extraordinary and specialized training — and must be reasonable in time, area and line of business.
  • The CHOICE Act took effect July 1, 2025 and is strongly employer-favorable. It permits non-compete and garden leave agreements of up to four years for “covered” workers — employees and independent contractors earning more than twice the annual mean wage of the Florida county involved, roughly $80,000 to $150,000 depending on the county. It also directs courts to issue a preliminary injunction unless the worker shows by clear and convincing evidence that the agreement is unenforceable.
  • But the formalities are strict and unforgiving. The agreement must be in writing, must advise the worker in writing of the right to consult counsel, and must give at least seven days to review before signing, plus a written acknowledgment of access to confidential information. Miss the seven days and you may have lost the protection you paid for. The form in this library carries the acknowledgment language, but the sequencing is on you.
  • The federal FTC non-compete rule is gone. It was set aside by a federal court, the FTC moved to accede to that vacatur in September 2025, and the rule was formally removed from the federal regulations in early 2026. State law governs. Note that the FTC has said it will continue case-by-case enforcement against particular non-compete practices, so “the rule is dead” is not the same as “anything goes.”
Do not use the agent form without a Florida employment attorney. This is the one document in the library where getting it slightly wrong does not mean a weaker agreement — it can mean no agreement at all, at the exact moment you need it, which is the week a producer leaves with your database. An hour of counsel is cheap against that.

How to send these without killing the deal

The document is not the hard part. Handing it to someone without making them feel accused is the hard part — and the same move works every time: name the discomfort before they feel it, and make the paper about protecting them.

  • To a buyer, before the OM: “Before I send the numbers — my seller runs this building with staff and tenants who don’t know it’s on the market. I need a one-page confidentiality before I release the rent roll. It’s standard, it’s two minutes, and honestly you’d want the same thing if it were your building. I’ll send it now and the full package the second it’s back.”
  • To an owner, unprompted: “One thing before you send me anything — here’s my confidentiality undertaking. You’re about to hand a stranger your rent roll and your debt. I’d want that in writing, so I’m giving it to you before you ask.” Offering it before they ask is the single highest-trust move in this entire system.
  • To another broker: “Send me the co-broke and I’ll send the address. Nothing personal — I just don’t want either of us reconstructing the split from memory at the closing table.”
  • To a lender: “I’ll send the file today. One thing in my submission packet is a short non-solicitation addendum — my borrowers are my business and I need to know they won’t get called directly about the deposit relationship. Mark it up if you need to; I’d rather know now than find out later.” Inviting the markup is what makes it land — institutional lenders will strike parts of it, and asking for the edit is far better than getting silence.
The accusation audit — use it every time. Say the objection out loud before they can: “This is going to look like I don’t trust you. That isn’t it — it’s that I send the same paper to everybody, and the day I make an exception is the day it costs a client.” An objection you name yourself is defused; an objection they raise is a negotiation.

Contract Builder — The Agreement, Tuned to the Asset

A listing agreement that works on a fourplex will lose you the fee on a land deal. The term is wrong, the protection period is wrong, and the five ways a land seller can pay you nothing are not addressed anywhere in it. Pick the side and the asset class and this builds the rider that attaches to the base agreement — the warranties you demand from them, and the clauses that protect you.

How the pieces fit

This is a rider, not a replacement. The structure is the way it is actually done:

  • The base agreement — the Exclusive Right of Sale Listing Agreement or the Exclusive Buyer Representation Agreement, both in the Paper tab. Commission, term, cancellation, arbitration, the standard machinery.
  • The asset rider — what this builder produces. It attaches, it is referenced in the base agreement, and it controls where the two conflict.
  • The confidentiality agreement — separate, signed by the other side before information moves.
Every one of these is a drafting sample, not counsel’s work product. Have a Florida attorney review the rider once per asset class — you will use the same seven riders for your whole career, so that is seven reviews total, not one per deal. Your Broker of Record should approve anything a client signs. Nothing here is legal advice.

Development & Construction Cost — Build the Budget

Hard costs, soft costs, permit fees, impact fees, carry and the developer fee — then the three numbers that decide whether a deal happens: yield on cost, the development spread, and what the land is actually worth. Every default below is sourced and dated. Nothing here is invented — where a number could not be verified from an authoritative publisher, the field is blank and says so.
Read this before you quote anything. A calculator is only as good as the $/SF you feed it. The defaults are Rider Levett Bucknall’s published Miami figures (January 2026 data) — a real cost consultancy that publishes a Miami index — but they are broad ranges for gross floor area, not a bid. On a live deal, replace them with a GC’s number. Use this to size a deal in ten minutes, screen a land parcel, or sanity-check what a developer tells you. Do not use it as a construction budget.

1. The project

2. Hard costs

 

3. Soft costs

Built line by line, not as a percentage — deliberately. The two sources that publish a soft-cost-as-a-percentage rule define the denominator differently (one includes land, one does not) and cannot be reconciled. The Miami fee items below are hard numbers from the County and City schedules, which is far more defensible than any rule of thumb. Permit and impact fees compute automatically from the jurisdiction and the inputs above.

4. Land, financing and the developer fee

5. The answer

The formulas, stated plainly

WhatHow it is computed
Total development costLand + hard + soft + financing + contingency + developer fee. The fee is computed on cost before the fee — otherwise it is a circular reference and the answer is wrong.
Yield on costStabilized NOI ÷ total development cost. Also called the development yield or the going-in return on cost.
Development spreadYield on cost − market exit cap rate, in basis points. The institutional threshold is roughly 150–200 bps. Below about 150, most developers conclude the risk is not compensated versus simply buying an existing cash-flowing building.
Residual land value(Stabilized NOI ÷ target yield on cost) − every cost except land. This is the number that tells a land seller what their dirt is actually worth to a builder — and it is the single most useful calculation in this tab.
Interest reserveLoan × average % outstanding × rate × months ÷ 12. 50% outstanding is the documented default. Raise it if draws are front-loaded; add contingency because delays are close to inevitable.
Profit margin((NOI ÷ exit cap) − TDC) ÷ TDC. What the developer makes if it sells at stabilization.
LTC vs LTVLTC = loan ÷ total cost. LTV = loan ÷ completed appraised value. Construction lenders size to the lesser of the two — LTC governs during construction, LTV governs the takeout.

Where these numbers come from — and what I could not verify

The defaults, with vintage:

  • Rider Levett Bucknall, Quarterly Construction Cost Report, Q1 2026 (January 2026 data, published March 2026) — the $/SF defaults. RLB publishes a Miami index specifically: 20,848 at January 2026, +4.74% year over year, and their Q2 2026 release puts Miami at +4.99% annual, third-highest of the cities cited. Current pressure is attributed to transportation and fuel, not materials or labor. rlb.com — cost report archive
  • ICC Building Valuation Data, August 2026 — the permit-valuation table, updated every February and August. National average with no regional adjustment, and conservative against real bids in coastal markets. Use it for permit valuation, never as a construction budget. iccsafe.org — BVD
  • Miami-Dade permit fees — Implementing Order IO-04-63, effective June 26, 2026. Note the surprise: Miami-Dade charges by square foot, not by valuation. Commercial new construction is $0.40/SF to 100,000 SF, $0.15/SF above, $147 minimum, plus roughly 10% in stacked surcharges (7.5% RER, 1% DBPR, 1.5% DCA). miamidade.gov — permit fees
  • City of Miami permit fees — Exhibit C, adopted April 2026. The City does the opposite: 1.00% of construction cost to $30M and 0.50% above, $110 minimum, plus a 2.50% commercial solid waste surcharge (capped at $10,500) and $0.11/SF energy conservation. County and State surcharges stack on top. miami.gov — fee schedule
  • Miami-Dade impact fees — schedule effective December 31, 2023 through December 30, 2027, mobility rates updated December 2024. Five fees: mobility, fire, police, parks, educational facilities. Mobility rates vary across four benefit districts. miamidade.gov — impact fees
  • Developer fee 3–5% of total project cost including acquisition; GC fee 3–4% of hard costs only; affordable/LIHTC developer fee 5–7% of eligible costs. When the developer is also the GC, the fee belongs at the low end. General conditions 5–10%; hard cost contingency 5–10%.
  • Development spread 150–200 bps and the 50% average outstanding balance convention for the interest reserve.
What I could not verify — do not let a calculator invent these.

Miami-Dade water and sewer connection charges. The charge categories are published (verification letter fee, water allocation fee, service charge, recording fee) but not the amounts. MDWASD invoices per project, typically per gallon of allocated capacity. Call 305-665-7477 and enter the number in the field above.

The school, parks, fire and police impact fee amounts. The County’s own PDF shows those columns but the published version I could reach had them blank, and the one aggregator that lists them does not reconcile with the County’s mobility figures. The County assesses impact fees case by case — you bring the permit plan set to the Impact Fee Section, Permitting and Inspection Center, 11805 SW 26th St, 786-315-2670.

Multifamily $/SF split by construction type (wood-frame walk-up vs concrete high-rise). No published South Florida source breaks it out. The tool derives a split from the ICC BVD ratio between construction types and labels it as derived — that is defensible as a method, but it is not a published Miami figure.

Industrial shell-only versus finished, retail freestanding and QSR, office tenant-improvement $/SF for Miami, and renovation light/medium/heavy gut. None are published by an authoritative source for this market. Get these from a GC or a project manager.

Gas station line items are national trade-source averages, not Miami-adjusted — and Miami runs high because of the water table, DERM requirements and double-wall secondary containment. Treat them as order of magnitude.

RSMeans’ Miami city cost index is behind a subscription (roughly $400 to $1,000 a year for the tiers a broker would use). ENR’s current absolute index values are paywalled; only the 2025 annual changes are public (BCI +4.2%, CCI +3.6%). And a caution worth carrying: ENR’s indices are input indices — no contractor margin, no market conditions — which is why they read low. Turner and RLB are final-cost indices and better for budgeting.

The other index readings, current: Turner Building Cost Index 1552 at Q2 2026, +5.15% year over year. Mortenson +5.60% over twelve months at Q3 2026 — but note Mortenson tracks only eight metros and none of them are in the Southeast, so do not use it to localize Miami. Marshall & Swift, now Cotality, is what tax assessors and appraisers use for the cost approach — worth knowing, because it is the dataset on the other side of the table in an assessment appeal.

Tax — Federal, State, County and What Is Hiding on the Bill

Answer the questions, enter the numbers, and this computes closing taxes, the post-sale property tax reset that wrecks more pro formas than any other single item, and the depreciation position. Every rate is sourced and dated below. Nothing here is tax advice — it is the arithmetic, so you can have the conversation and then send them to a CPA.
Two things are moving right now and you should know both.

1. Florida Amendment 3 is on the November 3, 2026 ballot. It would cut the non-homestead assessment cap from 10% to 5%, effective January 1, 2027 — first appearing on August 2027 TRIM notices and November 2027 bills. It needs 60% approval. The cap is a field below so you can model it either way.

2. Miami-Dade’s FY2026-27 millage was not adopted as of this build. The final budget hearing was set for September 17, 2026. The rates below are the FY2025-26 adopted rates, which are what is on the bills currently outstanding. Confirm the new millage before you quote a forward year.

1. The deal

2. The answer

Before you underwrite — the thirteen checks

Federal — what changed, and what it means

  • Depreciation lives. Residential rental 27.5 years, nonresidential 39 years, qualified improvement property 15 years — straight line, mid-month. Under ADS those become 30, 40 and 20. IRC §168(c); IRS Pub. 946.
  • 100% bonus depreciation is back and it is permanent. Restored by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025. The catch is a two-part test: property must be both acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025, and acquisition means the binding written contract date. IRS Notice 2026-11 removed the old sunset. A taxpayer may elect 40% instead for the first year ending after that date. Buildings themselves never get bonus — only the 5, 7 and 15-year components a cost segregation study carves out, plus QIP.
  • Cost segregation is therefore worth far more than it was. It reclassifies building basis into 5-year (carpet, decorative lighting, dedicated electrical, removable partitions), 7-year (furniture and fixtures) and 15-year land improvements (paving, parking, sidewalks, landscaping, site utilities, fencing). With 100% bonus, all of it is deductible immediately. IRS Publication 5653, the Cost Segregation Audit Techniques Guide, is the standard the IRS examines against — and it expects a study prepared by someone with both construction and tax expertise.
  • But understand the trade. Components moved to §1245 personal property recapture at ordinary rates up to 37%, not the 25% unrecaptured §1250 rate that applies to the building. Aggressive cost segregation accelerates deductions and converts future gain from 25% to ordinary. Netting that correctly is the most common modeling error in this entire area.
  • Section 179 for 2026: deduction limit $2,560,000, phase-out beginning at $4,090,000. Qualified real property is eligible — expressly including roofs, HVAC, fire protection and alarm systems, and security systems on nonresidential property already placed in service. Capped by business taxable income, so it cannot create a loss.
  • Section 199A survived and is permanent, effective 2025 forward, still at 20% (the 23% version did not make it out of the House draft). Phase-in ranges widened to $75,000 single / $150,000 joint. The rental safe harbor in Rev. Proc. 2019-38 excludes triple-net leases — which is most commercial. A NNN owner may still qualify as a trade or business on general facts, but not through the safe harbor.
  • Section 163(j) got materially better. EBITDA-based adjusted taxable income was restored for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, and made permanent — depreciation is added back, which raises the 30% interest ceiling substantially. Small business exemption is $31 million of average gross receipts.
  • Which means the real property trade or business election is often now a mistake. Electing out of the interest limit forces ADS depreciation — 40-year nonresidential, 30-year residential, 20-year QIP — and ADS property is not bonus-eligible. With EBITDA-based ATI back and 100% bonus permanent, the election frequently costs more than it saves. Rev. Proc. 2026-17 lets a taxpayer withdraw elections made for 2022, 2023 or 2024 by amended return — deadline the earlier of October 15, 2026 or the statute of limitations. If you have a client who elected, that is a phone call worth making today.
  • Passive losses. Rental activity is per se passive under §469(c)(2). Real estate professional status requires both prongs: more than half of all personal services in real property trades or businesses with material participation, and more than 750 hours. The $25,000 active-participation allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of AGI and is not indexed.
  • Net investment income tax 3.8% above $250,000 joint / $200,000 single of modified AGI. Those thresholds have not moved since 2013 and are not indexed.
  • Section 1031 is unchanged and remains real-property-only post-TCJA. 45 days to identify; 180 days to close — or the return due date including extensions, whichever is earlier. That earlier-of clause is what catches fourth-quarter closings.
  • Opportunity Zones are permanent. New designations are made beginning July 1, 2026 and take effect January 1, 2027 on a ten-year recurring cycle; the original TCJA zones run through December 31, 2028, so there is a two-year overlap. The fixed 2026 recognition date is replaced by a rolling five-year deferral, and rural zones get a 30% basis step-up at five years versus 10% standard, plus a substantial-improvement threshold cut to 50%.
  • FIRPTA on a foreign seller: 15% of the gross amount realized — the sale price, not the gain. On commercial property it is always 15%; the reduced residence tiers require the buyer to take it as a residence. The exits are a non-foreign affidavit from a domestic seller, or a withholding certificate on Form 8288-B, which is the standard move when 15% of gross wildly exceeds the actual tax on the gain.

Florida — and the two traps everyone gets wrong

  • Documentary stamps on the deed. Miami-Dade is not like the rest of Florida. Every other county is $0.70 per $100. Miami-Dade is $0.60 per $100 — plus a $0.45 surtax on anything other than a single-family residence. So commercial, multifamily, industrial, retail and land all pay $1.05 per $100. On a $5,000,000 commercial sale that is $52,500 in Miami-Dade versus $35,000 in Broward. Ch. 201, F.S.
  • Documentary stamps on the note: $0.35 per $100 — and the $2,450 cap does not apply. The cap is for unsecured notes only. There is no cap on a mortgage recorded in Florida. On a $10,000,000 mortgage that is $35,000, not $2,450. This is a frequent and expensive error. §201.08, F.S.
  • Nonrecurring intangible tax: 2 mills — $2 per $1,000 — on the obligation secured by the mortgage. §199.133(1), F.S. Combined, Florida mortgage taxes run about 0.55% of the loan amount.
  • The commercial rent tax is gone. Repealed effective October 1, 2025 by HB 7031; §212.031 fully repealed. The prior rate was 2% state plus the 1% Miami-Dade surtax — 3% all in. Tax still applies to rent attributable to occupancy through September 30, 2025, regardless of when it was paid. Any comp or pro forma built before that date has a 3% gross-up on rent that no longer exists — check it.
  • What the repeal did not touch. §212.03 still taxes parking and vehicle storage, boat slips, aircraft hangars and tie-downs, and transient rentals of six months or less, plus rentals of tangible personal property. A mixed-use asset with a paid garage still has a taxable revenue line at 7%.
  • Tangible personal property tax. Anyone owning business TPP on January 1 files a DR-405 by April 1. First $25,000 of assessed value is exempt. It is a separate folio and a separate bill from the real property — and a buyer of an operating business asset inherits the obligation.
  • Florida corporate income tax is 5.5%, and there is no personal income tax. But Florida decouples from federal bonus depreciation. Per DOR TIP 26C01-01 issued July 7, 2026, a Florida C corporation must add back bonus depreciation taken under §168(k) for assets placed in service before January 1, 2027, and recover it as a one-seventh subtraction over seven years. So 100% federal bonus is not a 100% Florida deduction in year one. This hits entities subject to the Florida corporate tax, not individuals or most pass-throughs.

Ad valorem — how the number is built

  • January 1 fixes everything — value, ownership, use and exemptions. A sale on January 2 does not touch that year’s roll; it lands on the following January 1.
  • Just value → assessed value → taxable value. Just value is market value under the eight factors in §193.011. Assessed value is just value reduced by any cap. Taxable is assessed minus exemptions — and commercial property generally has no exemptions, so taxable equals assessed.
  • The 10% cap lives in §193.1555 for nonresidential property. Annual reassessment may not exceed 10%. But it expressly excludes school district levies — school millage applies to full just value every single year. In Miami-Dade the school board is 6.633 mills of a roughly 16.9 to 20.0 total, so a third or more of the bill was never capped at all.
  • The cap resets on change of ownership or control — and control includes the cumulative transfer of more than 50% of the ownership of the entity that owns the property. A membership-interest deal resets the cap with no deed recorded. It also resets on a qualifying improvement that raises just value by 25% or more.
  • Portability is homestead only. There is none for commercial. When a commercial property sells, the entire accumulated cap differential is simply lost.
  • TRIM notice is mailed by August 24. It is not a bill — it is the only document showing proposed taxes before they are final, and the only thing that starts the appeal clock. VAB petition deadline is 25 days after the TRIM mailing. Filing fee is $15 per folio. Evidence is due 15 days before the hearing, which is before a special magistrate.
  • To keep a VAB petition alive you must pay, before delinquency, 100% of non-ad valorem assessments and at least 75% of the ad valorem taxes. Miss that and the petition is denied. §194.014, F.S.
  • Bills mail around November 1. Discounts: 4% in November, 3% December, 2% January, 1% February, gross in March, delinquent April 1. On a $200,000 annual bill the November discount is $8,000 a year — it belongs in the pro forma.
  • Agricultural classification under §193.461 assesses land at agricultural use value, which can be a fraction of just value. Application deadline is March 1, it is reviewed annually, and it is not transferable on sale — the new owner must reapply. A development-site listing with a tiny tax bill is almost certainly greenbelt, and the assessment jumps to full just value on conversion. There are potential back-assessment consequences; that is a question for counsel.

Non-ad valorem — what is hiding below the line

These sit on the same bill under §197.3632, are collected by the Tax Collector, and carry the same lien and the same enforcement as taxes. They appear on the August TRIM notice and the November bill in a separate section. They do not show up in a cap-rate calculation unless you look for them.

  • Fire rescue in Miami-Dade is ad valorem, not a flat assessment. Worth knowing, because most Florida counties do it the other way. Miami-Dade funds it through the Fire Rescue District at 2.3965 mills — which means fire cost scales with value and resets on sale along with everything else. The thirty municipalities with their own fire departments, including the City of Miami, sit outside the district and do not pay that millage.
  • Community Development Districts.
