Two components: a debt service assessment that is fixed, amortizing over 10 to 30 years and often prepayable, and an O&M assessment that recurs forever and resets annually with the district budget. The Property Appraiser notes that subsequent sellers are often not required to disclose a CDD — unlike special districts and PACE, where disclosure is mandatory. Never rely on seller disclosure for a CDD. Pull the bill. Economically it is off-balance-sheet leverage that runs with the land: capitalize the O&M, treat the debt like assumed debt.
  • PACE is the one that kills deals at closing. Under §163.08 and §163.081, the recorded agreement creates a lien of equal dignity to county taxes from the date of recordation — which puts it senior to a first mortgage. Terms run about 30 years and it runs with the land, but an acquisition lender will very often demand full payoff at closing, turning an assumable annual line into a six or seven figure cash requirement days before closing. Seller disclosure is mandatory and a mortgage clause accelerating solely because of PACE is unenforceable — but none of that helps you if you find it at title instead of in week one. Search for PACE early.
  • Special taxing districts and MSTUs. Over 1,000 active districts serving roughly 390,000 households in Miami-Dade — street lighting, security and guard services, landscape and multipurpose maintenance, capital improvements. Assessments run with the land, and the Property Appraiser says it plainly: “the sales price of the property does not include the financial obligation of the non-ad valorem assessment unless it is negotiated into the price.” Nothing prorates automatically. Negotiate it explicitly.
  • Water, road and sewer assessments — districts such as OJUS — are currently collected in 30-year annual installments.
  • Solid waste in Miami-Dade is a residential assessment; commercial properties contract with permitted private haulers under the County franchise system. I could not verify the current commercial treatment or amount — check the actual bill. Stormwater billing method is also unverified — check the parcel.
Where to actually look. Property Appraiser search gives you values, characteristics, sales history and the folio. The PA Tax Estimator takes a purchase price — that is the official post-sale projection. Tax Comparison shows current versus prior year by taxing district, which isolates what actually changed. But the itemized non-ad valorem detail is on the Tax Collector bill, not the PA site. The PA shows values; the Tax Collector shows what is actually charged. Get the folio from one and the bill from the other.

Where to List It — The Distribution Stack

You won the listing and you papered it. Now it has to reach buyers. Pick the asset, the price band and whether the seller will let you advertise, and this gives you the launch order, what each channel costs, and what your association membership already pays for. Most brokers in this market pay twice for something membership already includes — that is the first thing this fixes.

The base layer — what MIAMI membership already buys

This is the part people get wrong. Verified current dues for the 2026–27 year, from the live application portal:

MembershipCost
Commercial REALTOR® add-on — if you are already a MIAMI member$87.50
Commercial REALTOR® — primary$1,014.33
Commercial Designated REALTOR® (broker)$1,228.50

There is no separate CIE fee. Commercial MLS access is bundled into those numbers. If you already hold a MIAMI membership, $87.50 is the entire cost of getting into the only dedicated commercial MLS in South Florida — which claims 80% of the commercial MLS business across Miami-Dade and Broward and 3,400+ commercial members.

What comes with it at no extra cost:

  • Crexi syndication — listings imported from your MIAMI dashboard to the Crexi marketplace and refreshed daily, at no cost to members, plus 35% off Crexi PRO. Verify this before you rely on it — the 35% discount is confirmed live today, but the automatic daily feed is documented only in the original 2020 announcement and is not restated on the current help pages. Call MIAMI Commercial at 305-468-7074 and confirm the feed still runs. Associations quietly change these at merger time, and there was a merger.
  • Brevitas — MIAMI is a named syndication partner, and members get a free basic account plus 33% off the full suite when you link your NAR account.
  • Member2Member (M2M) — a free email blast to 2,600+ MIAMI commercial members. This is the single best broker-to-broker channel in this market and it costs nothing.
  • CompStak — 20 lease and sale comparables, free.
  • iMapp — plat maps, tax data across 33 Florida counties, MLS integration, demographics. Free.
  • RPR Commercial — on-market and off-market property data.
  • Terra-Fly aerial photography and demographics, International MLS membership, Global Referral Connect, Data Co-Op via Matrix.
  • Discounts: CREOP 20%, NARR / Commercial Resources 15%.
  • Monthly Commercial Marketplace meetings and luncheons with live listing presentations — a room, not a portal.
The association changed on May 11, 2026 and it matters. MIAMI REALTORS® and RWorld completed a merger — 56,000 + 37,000 members, roughly 93,000 combined, now the third-largest MLS in the nation, with IDX feeds carrying both MIAMI MLS and BeachesMLS. Broward and Palm Beach commercial (the RCA) is now the same organization you are in. Your listing sits in a materially bigger footprint than it did last year — and the commercial MLS rules were almost certainly rewritten, which is the second reason to make that phone call.
What membership does NOT buy you: LoopNet. CoStar takes no association feed — it competes with association CIEs. Nothing you enter into the MIAMI commercial MLS reaches LoopNet. That is a separate purchase, every time.

The paid platforms — and what nobody will tell you the price of

LoopNet tiers, from their own current materials. The old “Basic/Silver/Gold/Platinum/Diamond” naming is partly outdated; the current public structure is:

TierWhat it addsClaimed vs Silver
SilverCoStar Market Advantage, Marketing Center, CDX Mail, company and broker pages, CityFeet / Showcase distribution, flyer creation, Data Room. Priority placement above the free listings. 1–10 listings. Distributes to 150+ partner CRE websites.baseline
Gold Signature+ architectural photography to 20 photos, aerial drone, 1 Matterport tour, 1 Matterport 3D exterior, call tracking, dedicated marketing support5×
Platinum Signature+ featured CoStar placement, retargeting ads, prospect targeting, contact upload targeting, 2 Matterport tours17×
Diamond Signature+ HD video tour, 4 Matterport tours, maximum exposure49×
LoopNet publishes no prices, and I am not going to invent one. Every tier page says contact sales; pricing varies by property type, location and package. There is a widely circulated table on the trade sites running $69.95 to $3,300 a month — it is roughly 2014 vintage, it predates the entire Signature structure, and quoting it would mislead you. Go into that call knowing the tier names and the claimed multipliers, and nothing else, because that is genuinely all that is public.

CoStar and LoopNet are separate purchases. Definitively — CoStar Group reports them as separate revenue segments in SEC filings: LoopNet $87M in Q2 2026 (up 14% year over year), the CoStar data subscription $337M (up 9%). A LoopNet upgrade is marketing spend on one asset. A CoStar subscription is a research seat for you. Neither includes the other. CoStar does not publish subscription pricing either; the one third-party dataset puts the average around $15,000 with a $3,000–$23,000 range, but it rests on three deals, which is not a market rate.

PlatformCostRead
CrexiFree to list. Paid tiers not publishedFree tier includes unlimited listings, lead info, basic analytics. 35% off PRO as a MIAMI member — if you buy one upgrade, this is the cheapest one available to you.
BrevitasFree basic for members, 33% off the suiteThe confidential-listing tool. See the off-market card below.
Buildout$125 / user / month starting — publishedOM generation, CRM, and syndication to 13 channels including CommercialEdge (10M monthly visitors), Catylist, OfficeSpace, Brevitas, TenantBase, RI Marketplace. But LoopNet and Crexi are not on its syndication list — do not buy it expecting it to solve those two.
OfficeSpace.comFree to list, alwaysCovers sale and lease broadly, not office only. Featured upgrade price not published.
MyEListingFreeNo downside, no published traffic data either. Do it because it is free, not because you expect leads.
RealNexNot published — has a free MarketPlace tierBuildout competitor. The free tier is worth claiming at zero cost.
Catylist (Moody’s)Not publishedPowers other associations’ CIEs — not MIAMI’s. Reach it through Buildout if at all.
Biproxi—Stop. It is not a listing marketplace anymore. It pivoted to an invitation-only institutional capital network. Wrong tool.
42Floors—No longer a destination. Acquired by Knotel in 2018, Knotel failed; it survives as an endpoint inside CommercialEdge. You get it free if you syndicate through Buildout. Do not target it.

The business-for-sale channel — gas stations and anything with an operation

When you are selling a business plus real estate, the CRE portals are half the answer. The buyer for a gas station is often shopping business marketplaces, not LoopNet.

BizBuySell is the only platform in this entire tab that publishes an honest rate card. On six-month terms:

PackagePrice
Basic$74.95 / month
Showcase$99.95 / month
Diamond$199.95 / month

Three-month terms cost more per month; twelve-month terms are discounted; monthly renewal is available after the initial term.

The leverage nobody uses: BizBuySell, BizQuest and LoopNet are all CoStar. LoopNet acquired BizQuest in 2010 and all three sit under CoStar today. On a gas station you are dealing with one vendor across both sides of the transaction — the business listing and the real estate listing. Ask explicitly whether one package cross-posts to all three before you buy three things. I could not verify that it does, and it is exactly the question a salesperson will answer if you ask and will not volunteer if you do not.

Auction — when speed beats price

PlatformCostNotes
Ten-X (CoStar)Flat 3% buyer transaction fee, min $20,000, max $300,000 — effective September 15, 2025Replaced a variable model that ran about 5%. The 3% is explicitly the buyer’s number — what the seller pays to list is not disclosed. Do not assume it is zero.
Crexi auctionNo cost to sellers. Buyer’s premium not publishedClaims a 30-day close on cash terms, deals signed within 24 hours.
RI MarketplaceNothing published at allBroker-centric, ~28 days launch to close. Claims $6B+ volume, 100K+ investors, 17 average registered bidders per asset. A Buildout syndication partner.
All three sell speed and certainty, not price. Twenty-eight to thirty day timelines. Auction suits a motivated seller, a lender-driven disposition, or an asset with a genuine bidder pool. For a well-located Miami asset with a normal seller, a conventional listing will usually clear at a better number — and there is no independent data comparing auction outcomes to conventional listings. If a seller raises auction, that is the honest answer to give them.

The listing the seller will not let you advertise

An estate, a family partnership, an operator whose staff and tenants do not know — this comes up constantly and most brokers handle it by doing nothing. There are real channels.

  • Brevitas private listings — free at basic tier for you. Marking a listing Private hides photos, address and documents; the public sees a teaser only. Full access requires a request approved by you, and documents sit behind a signed NDA. And the feature that makes it genuinely usable: “Principals (Buyers Only)” excludes unsolicited broker requests — so a seller who does not want the brokerage community knowing can still get in front of buyers. You can preview the teaser to see exactly what others see.
  • MIAMI Member2Member. A free blast to 2,600+ local commercial brokers. You control what is in it — asset type, submarket, price band, no address. This is how an off-market Miami listing actually gets shopped.
  • The monthly Commercial Marketplace meeting. Present it in a room instead of publishing it. Free with membership and nobody does it.
  • RPR Commercial — free with membership, covers on-market and off-market, useful for sourcing the buyer side quietly.
  • theBrokerList — free CRE broker database, a Buildout syndication partner.
  • Crexi private listings — generally understood to exist, but I could not confirm the mechanics, visibility rules or cost from Crexi’s own materials. Ask them.
One compliance item you must check yourself. NAR’s Clear Cooperation Policy governs residential MLS. I could not verify how the MIAMI commercial MLS rules treat office-exclusive, pocket or delayed-marketing listings — the rules document I could reach is 2020 vintage and predates the May 2026 merger. Get the current commercial rules from MIAMI before you take a confidential listing. A merger of that size almost certainly triggered a rewrite.

Before you launch anything

Going live before this is ready is how a listing burns its first two weeks of attention — which are the only two weeks where a new listing gets free traffic.

What actually works — the honest answer

There is no credible independent data on which CRE listing platform generates the most leads or closes. None. It is entirely marketing claims. I searched for it specifically. Every “LoopNet vs Crexi” comparison that surfaces is vendor marketing, affiliate-monetized SEO, or AI-generated aggregator content with no methodology. NAR’s 2025 technology survey is residential-weighted and does not rank commercial platforms. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.

NAR’s own position is the most revealing thing I found. Their commercial listing platforms page names exactly four — RPR, Brevitas, Crexi and CompStak — and attaches this: “These products and the companies that offer them are not endorsed and have not been vetted by the National Association of REALTORS®.” It is a self-submitted list that invites companies to apply. LoopNet/CoStar is absent from it entirely, and NAR publishes zero adoption or performance data.

The self-reported traffic claims, so you know what is being said to you:

  • LoopNet: 13 million unique monthly visitors; searchers signed $400 billion in leases and sales last year; listings sell or lease 14% faster; 169× ROI.
  • Crexi: $815.6 billion in active for-sale listings through November 2025, up 16.7%; more than 2 million monthly active users, up 6.3%; $1 trillion+ facilitated to date.
Do not compare those two numbers directly. LoopNet reports unique monthly visitors; Crexi reports monthly active users. Different metrics, different denominators — MAU implies registered and engaged, unique visitors counts anyone who loads a page. Neither is third-party audited. The gap is real but almost certainly nowhere near the 6-to-1 the raw numbers suggest.

The one genuinely independent signal is CoStar’s SEC-filed revenue — and it measures what brokers spend, not what works.

Two phone calls to make before you spend anything

  • MIAMI Commercial — 305-468-7074 (or commercial@miamire.com). Two questions: is the automatic daily Crexi feed still running post-merger, and what are the current commercial MLS rules on confidential and office-exclusive listings. Both answers change what you do, and both are unverifiable from outside.
  • BizBuySell. One question: does a single package cross-post to BizQuest and the LoopNet business-for-sale section, or are those separate buys. They are all CoStar, so the answer should be yes — but it is not published, and it is the difference between one subscription and three.

Everything else in this tab is verified and dated. Where a price is not shown it is because the company does not publish it — not because I could not be bothered to look. In this industry that is most of them, which is itself worth knowing before you walk into a sales call.

The Launch Campaign — The 30 Days After You List It

Posting to the portals is about four percent of the work. A listing gets one launch and roughly two weeks of free attention, and what you do inside that window decides whether it sells in sixty days or sits for nine months. This is the shot list, the call list, the international play, what to spend on ads, and the three ways you can get in real trouble advertising commercial property in Florida.

The shot list — and yes, always the drone

Photography is the cheapest lever you have. A $400 drone shoot changes what a buyer believes the property is. Skipping it to save four hundred dollars on a $2M listing is not thrift, it is self-sabotage.

  • The straight-down aerial with the parcel lines drawn on it. This is the hero image on land, industrial and anything with a yard. It is the only image that answers “what am I actually buying.”
  • The oblique aerial showing the corridor. What is next door, where the traffic comes from, how far to the highway. Buyers underwrite context, not buildings.
  • Exterior stills — front, both sides, rear, street approach in both directions, and the parking.
  • Interior stills — wide, corrected verticals. For industrial: the clear height with something for scale, the dock doors, the electrical panel, the sprinkler heads.
  • The twilight shot on retail and multifamily. It is a cliché because it works.
  • A 360 / 3D tour on anything with an interior a buyer would want to walk. See the Stack tab — you can do this for a dollar an image rather than a Matterport subscription.
  • Video above $5M. A two-minute walk-and-talk shot on a phone gimbal beats no video, and beats a slideshow with music.
If you want to fly the drone yourself, you need a Part 107 certificate. This is not optional and it is not a gray area. Shooting a listing you are paid to market is commercial operation — the recreational exception does not cover it.

What it takes: be 16 or older, pass the Unmanned Aircraft General (UAG) knowledge exam at an FAA-approved testing center, apply through IACRA, clear a TSA background check. Recurrent training every 24 months, and that course is free. Register the drone through FAADroneZone — $5, good for three years — and register it under Part 107 from the start, because registration cannot be transferred between recreational and Part 107. Remote ID is mandatory. The test fee is charged by the testing center, not the FAA, and is widely reported around $175 — I could not confirm that from an FAA or PSI source, so verify it when you book.

The Miami-specific catch nobody mentions: a large share of Miami-Dade sits in controlled airspace — MIA, Opa-locka, Tamiami, Homestead. You will need LAANC authorization on a lot of your listings. It is free and it is fast, but it is a step you cannot skip.

Worth it? Roughly $180 one time against $300–$600 per shoot. If you list more than a handful of properties a year, this is the highest-return certification on the list.

The property website, the sign, and the tracked number

  • A single-property website above about $2M. Yes. Not because buyers browse it — because it is the link you put in every email, every text and every WhatsApp message. One page: address, aerial, photos, the numbers, your name and your brokerage. Buildout generates them; a one-page site works just as well.
  • A sign on the property, with a phone number. Especially on land and retail. The buyer for a corner parcel is frequently the person who drives past it every day. Check the municipality’s sign permit rules before you plant it — they vary and code enforcement does look.
  • A tracked number if you are running more than one paid channel. Otherwise you will never know whether the Crexi promotion or the sign or the postcard produced the call. Call tracking runs about $50 a month — only worth it when you are actually spending on multiple channels. If everything comes from your sphere, skip it.
  • Your brokerage name on every single one of these. See the compliance card below — this is a real FREC rule and it is the easiest violation in the business.

The call campaign — this is the part that actually sells it

Portals are passive. They work while you sleep, which is another way of saying they work slowly. The buyer who closes in the first three weeks comes from a phone call, and these are the calls, in order of yield.

  • 1. The adjacent owners. Literally the parcels that touch it. Pull them off the Property Appraiser in ten minutes. The neighbor has assemblage logic nobody else has, he already knows the block, and he has been wondering about that property for years. This is the highest-yield call you will make on any listing, and most brokers never make it.
  • 2. The eight-block radius. You already run this play in the Gears tab for prospecting. Run it on the listing. “I just listed the building on the corner — before it goes out to the market, does it interest you, and do you know anyone it should go to?” That second half is the point.
  • 3. Everyone who bought this asset type in this submarket in the last 24 months. Pull it from your comp set. These are proven buyers with proven financing — not people who told you they were looking.
  • 4. The brokers. Member2Member blast to 2,600+ commercial members, free. Then call the three or four who actually work this asset class. A blast is not a call.
  • 5. Net-lease brokers and qualified intermediaries if it is retail or NNN. A 1031 buyer on a 45-day clock is working a broker, not a search box.
  • 6. Your lenders. Nobody does this and it is your edge.
    You have 71 contacts in the Lender Matrix. A lender who just financed a similar deal knows a buyer who lost that deal. Call and say: “I’ve got a 12-unit in Little Havana at $1.6M, 1.35 DSCR — do you have a borrower who missed on something similar?”
    It costs nothing, nobody else in this market can make the call, and it works because the lender wants the loan. You are not asking a favor. You are bringing him business.

Colombia and the international question — the honest version

The buyers are real and Colombia is number one. MIAMI’s international report, released January 2026: foreign buyers did $4.4 billion across roughly 5,300 South Florida properties in 2025 — 15% of South Florida sales by dollar volume against 2% nationally. By origin: Colombia 15%, Argentina 12%, Mexico and Brazil 7% each, Venezuela and Canada 5% each. Colombia and Argentina together are 27% of all international closed sales.
Now the caveat that matters, and I am not going to bury it: all of that data is residential. I searched for a credible figure on the Latin American share of Miami commercial investment and there isn’t one published. The buyer pool is obviously real — you see it on every deal — but do not quote the 15% to a seller as if it describes commercial. It describes homes.

Can you syndicate a commercial listing internationally? Mostly no, and this surprised me.

  • MIAMI has 308 international partners across 78 countries, and the Colombian ones are real and named: FEDELONJAS, La Lonja de Propiedad Raíz de Bogotá (2023), Lonja de Cali y Valle del Cauca (2018), and AFYDI (2013). Venezuela, Brazil, Argentina and Mexico all have multiple named counterparties too.
  • But these read as referral and networking agreements, not listing-distribution pipes. I could not verify that any partnership obligates a partner to distribute MIAMI listings, and the association’s own materials describe “resources, visibility and connections” rather than a feed.
  • The global program and its tooling are residential-oriented in every document I could find. The Commercial division’s published services are regional — South Florida search, M2M email, luncheons. No international distribution of commercial listings is described anywhere.
  • International MLS is free with your membership, so enable it — but its reach numbers are entirely self-reported vendor marketing with no independent audit. Zero cost, so no downside. Just never promise a seller it will produce a buyer.
  • Juwai is the only confirmed commercial-capable international portal — and its audience is Chinese. Wrong continent for you. Realtor.com International looks deprecated, WorldProperties appears defunct, and Proxio, Point2 and LuxuryEstate could not be confirmed for commercial.
So what actually works? The highest-value action is also the most old-fashioned: call the named Colombian partner organizations directly. FEDELONJAS and the Lonja de Bogotá are real institutions with real members who broker real estate for real clients, and MIAMI has a standing relationship with them. That is a warm introduction you already paid for with your dues.

Then: a Spanish version of the one-page property site, and WhatsApp as the actual channel — because that is how business gets done with Latin American clients and email is not. I could not find a single credible study on Spanish-language marketing ROI or WhatsApp conversion in this market, so I am telling you what the market does, not what the data proves.

One thing to have straight when a foreign buyer asks: FIRPTA withholding — 15% of the gross price — hits a foreign seller, not a foreign buyer. The buyer is the withholding agent and is liable for failing to withhold. So it is a future-exit consideration for your buyer, and a reason their counsel gets careful when the current seller is foreign. Entity structuring, blocker corporations and EB-5 are cross-border tax attorney questions, not marketing questions. Know enough to refer, not to advise.

Paid digital — Facebook, Google, LinkedIn

Read this before you boost a single post. Meta has a “Housing” Special Ad Category and it exists because of the Fair Housing Act.

If your ad is classified as Housing, you lose: age targeting (fixed 18–65+), gender targeting, ZIP codes, neighborhoods and metro areas (minimum 15-mile radius), location exclusions, most detailed targeting, and lookalike audiences entirely.

Does it apply to commercial property? I could not get a definitive answer and I am not going to pretend otherwise. Meta’s own policy pages are blocked from automated reading and the archives were unavailable. What I can tell you is the legal basis: the category exists because of the DOJ’s June 2022 settlement with Meta over housing ads, and the Fair Housing Act governs “dwellings.”

The practical rule: multifamily and the residential half of mixed-use are dwellings — assume Housing applies. Pure office, retail, industrial and land are probably outside the FHA, but Meta’s classifier is automated and reads your keywords, your images, your landing page, your pixel events and your Page category. It can flag you regardless of intent, and misdeclaring carries account-level risk.

Get it in writing from a Meta rep or fair-housing counsel before you spend. Do not let a marketing vendor make this call for you. If the listing has any residential element at all, declaring Housing is the conservative path — losing ZIP targeting is a much cheaper outcome than an FHA complaint.

Google Ads. The only benchmark with disclosed methodology — 13,474 US search campaigns, April 2025 to March 2026: real estate averages $3.22 cost per click, 7.61% click-through, 3.70% conversion, and $102.51 cost per lead — with CPC up 27% year over year, the largest increase of any industry. But “real estate” is one undivided category with no commercial breakout, so treat it as directional.

My read: don’t run search ads for a single listing. Search demand for one specific commercial asset is too thin to justify $100 a lead. If you spend on Google at all, spend it on category and geography terms that feed your whole pipeline — “sell my building Miami,” “commercial broker Little Havana” — not on one address.

LinkedIn. The targeting is genuinely right for this business — job title, company, industry, seniority, plus uploaded company and contact lists. You can put an ad in front of acquisitions officers and family office principals by name. But LinkedIn publishes no CPC, and every benchmark I found was an agency blog with no disclosed methodology, so I won’t quote you a number. Expect multiples of Google’s CPC and validate with a small live test rather than a published figure.

Retargeting. LoopNet’s Platinum tier includes property retargeting (people who already viewed your listing) and prospect targeting (people who have not — matched from the CoStar ownership and tenant database). The second one is the genuinely differentiated product, because that dataset has no independent equivalent. Google, Meta and LinkedIn all do pixel retargeting; none of them can do prospect targeting, and that data moat is what Platinum actually sells. LoopNet publishes no price and no performance data for either.

And the honest bottom line on all of it: there is no credible, independent, CRE-specific digital advertising benchmark in existence. LoopNet publishes no cost per lead. LinkedIn and Meta publish no industry CPC. The abundant “CRE marketing benchmarks” content comes from agencies selling CRE marketing. Any cost-per-lead figure quoted to you for commercial real estate specifically is unverified vendor marketing until someone shows you the methodology. The defensible approach is a small test with your own tracked numbers.

Three ways to get in real trouble

  • 1. Leaving the brokerage name off an ad. This is the easiest violation in the business and it is a real rule. FREC Rule 61J2-10.025: all advertising must make clear a reasonable person is dealing with a licensee, and must include the licensed name of the brokerage as registered with DBPR. On internet and social media the brokerage name must sit adjacent to, or immediately above or below, the point of contact information — the phone, email or address. Your last name must appear as registered.
    That means every Instagram post, every WhatsApp blast, every portal listing, every sign. And team names cannot include Agency, Associates, Brokerage, Company, Corporation, LLC, Properties or Realty, and cannot be printed larger than the brokerage name. I found no commercial exemption and none is stated — assume it applies to you.
  • 2. Fair housing on multifamily and mixed-use. The FHA governs dwellings. The residential component of a mixed-use listing pulls your advertising into FHA territory and into Meta’s Housing category. This is the highest-risk item on this page, and it is the one most commercial brokers have never thought about because they think of themselves as doing commercial.
  • 3. Email and cold calling. See below — both are legal, and both have teeth.

CAN-SPAM, for your listing blasts. Accurate headers, honest subject line, identify it as an ad, a valid physical postal address, a working opt-out, and opt-outs honored within 10 business days. Two things worth knowing: it is opt-out, not opt-in — prior consent is not required, which is why cold listing blasts are legal. And “the law makes no exception for business-to-business email” — you are fully in scope. Penalties run to $53,088 per email.

Cold calling owners — Florida’s mini-TCPA. Good news first: F.S. 501.059 is limited to “consumers” buying “consumer goods or services,” and commercial brokerage sold to a property-owning business is not that. Better: F.S. 501.604(25) expressly exempts a person licensed under Chapter 475 soliciting within the scope of that chapter from telemarketing licensure. You are exempt.

The risk is not Florida — it is federal, and it is three specific things. The federal TCPA does not care that your call is B2B: an autodialer or prerecorded voice to a cell phone needs consent regardless. Small commercial owners overwhelmingly list personal cell numbers in public records and skip-trace data. And multi-line predictive dialing into skip-traced cells is exactly the configuration plaintiffs’ firms look for — at $500 per call, trebled to $1,500 for willful, that compounds fast.

What keeps you clean: manually dialed, human-initiated calls, to business numbers, screened against the federal and Florida do-not-call lists, between 8am and 9pm, with a suppression list you actually maintain. If you buy a dialer, buy a power dialer (one line, you press the button) rather than a predictive or multi-line one — that architecture alone is worth the higher price. Have a Florida TCPA attorney look at your actual list and dialer config once before you turn it on.

The Stack — What to Subscribe To, and What Not To

Every price here was pulled from the vendor’s own page and dated. Where a company does not publish its pricing it says NOT PUBLISHED — not a guess, not a number from a review site. That distinction matters more than it sounds, because most CRE software hides pricing specifically so you have to take a sales call, and knowing which ones do is half the negotiation.
The headline finding, and it is not what you would expect. A working Miami commercial broker can run a complete, professional operation for $26 a month in verified cost — plus a laptop, a license and a phone. Everything above that line should be justified by a specific deal you could not have done otherwise. Most brokers buy the $1,000 stack and make 8 calls a day. The $26 broker making 30 calls beats them every time.

The free tools you should be fluent in before you buy anything

This is the honest floor of the whole business. Folio → property search → comparable sales → official records → permits and violations reconstructs ownership, basis, debt and physical condition for zero dollars. A broker fluent in these five needs materially less paid data than one who is not.

Note the Property Appraiser moved domains — it is miamidadepa.gov now, not miamidade.gov/pa.

  • Property Search — folio, address, owner, mapping: apps.miamidadepa.gov/propertysearch
  • Comparable Sales — interactive sales maps: apps.miamidadepa.gov/ComparableSales
  • Tax Estimator — takes a purchase price, gives the post-sale number: Tax Estimator  ·  Tax Comparison
  • Clerk Official Records — deeds, mortgages, liens, lis pendens. This is where your lender list comes from: onlineservices.miamidadeclerk.gov/officialrecords
  • Permit records: RER ePermitting
  • Code violations and unsafe structures — search by folio, address, owner or permit: Regulation Support Viewer  ·  Code Violations GIS map
The unsafe-structures and recertification search is a live deal-killer in this market. Run it before you underwrite, not during diligence. An open unsafe-structure case on a 1970s Miami building can cost more than the equity in the deal.

The one paid data product that does something free tools cannot

Reonomy — $400/month starting, published on their own pricing page. Annual saves 30% per Altus, though the annual figure itself is not published. Free trial available, length not stated.

Why it is the one: LLC-piercing. Miami-Dade commercial property is overwhelmingly held in entities, and the Property Appraiser will show you “1234 NW 7TH LLC” and stop there. Reonomy resolves the entity to a human and gives you a number. That is the single thing the free county stack genuinely cannot do, and owner-direct prospecting is your whole business.

The cheaper thing to try first: Prospect by Buildout (formerly ProspectNow) has a self-serve free trial — no sales call — which means you can test it against Reonomy before anyone quotes you anything. Pricing not published. Predictive likelihood-to-sell scoring is the pitch; the underlying owner data is the actual value.

And the free version of this that most brokers never do: your Trace Board tab plus the Clerk’s Official Records. The mortgage tells you the lender, the deed tells you the entity, Sunbiz tells you the registered agent and manager. It takes ten minutes per owner instead of ten seconds — but it costs nothing and it teaches you the market in a way a database never will. Run it manually for ninety days. If you are still bottlenecked on it after that, buy Reonomy and you will know exactly what you are buying.

Dead, moved, or not worth your time

ToolStatus
RealMassiveDefunct since 2020. The domain now serves an unrelated online gambling site. Do not include it in any stack.
CherreAcquired by RealPage, July 2026. Was never a broker tool — it is an enterprise data pipeline.
ProspectNowNow Prospect by Buildout — the old URL redirects.
AptoNow Buildout (acquired January 2022, along with Rethink in 2021). Do not shop it standalone.
ClientLookNow LightBox. Still sold, and it is one of the few CRE CRMs that publishes: $129/user/month, or $1,068/year (~$89/mo). 10-day free trial.
PropertySharkReal, but its depth is NYC and the Northeast. Thin in Miami-Dade. Skip.
LandVisionPricing not published, site blocks automated reading. At your deal size the free county parcel tools cover it.
BiproxiNo longer a listing marketplace — pivoted to an invitation-only institutional capital network.
42FloorsNot a destination anymore. Survives as a syndication endpoint inside CommercialEdge.

The 3D tour line item — the smartest small purchase on this page

EyeSpy360 charges $1 per 360 image, pay as you go, 15-image minimum, twelve months of hosting included. No subscription. You pay only when you actually have a listing. Monthly plans start at $12.99 and only make sense above roughly eight tours a year.

CloudPano is $27/month, or $33 on the Pro Plus annual plan, with a $9.99 per-publish Google Street View add-on. Kuula has a free tier good for 300 posts but hides its paid pricing behind a JavaScript calculator.

Matterport is a brand-signal purchase, not a necessity — and its pricing is a mess. The live plans page shows no dollar amounts at all; the only published table sits in a support article whose plan names do not match the current site and which carries no date. Do not budget off it. Also note the free tier cannot share or embed, which makes it useless for a listing. Get a real quote before you commit.

The CRM decision, since you already have Salesforce

You already run Salesforce, which changes this calculation entirely. The relevant tier is Pro Suite at $100/user/month — note Salesforce renamed its editions, so “Enterprise” and “Unlimited” no longer exist as names. Starter Suite is $25, Core $195.

So the honest question is not “which CRM” — it is what you would be paying Buildout for.

  • Buildout for marketing and OM production: worth it. $125/user/month starting, published. It collapses offering memoranda, property websites, email campaigns and syndication to 13 channels into one line item. That genuinely replaces a Canva workflow plus a separate email tool.
  • Buildout for CRM: redundant with Salesforce. Don’t pay twice for a pipeline.
  • ClientLook, Apto standalone: skip. You already own the CRM layer.
  • HubSpot free is genuinely good — but the 1,000-contact cap is fatal for owner prospecting. A Miami owner list blows through it immediately, and it has no property records, no lease expirations, no commission splits.
Buildout does not syndicate to LoopNet or Crexi. Its 13 channels are CommercialEdge, Catylist, TenantBase, OfficeSpace, Brevitas, RI Marketplace and the rest of the long tail. Do not buy it expecting it to solve the two portals that matter. Buy it for OM production, or don’t buy it.

If you buy a dialer, buy the right architecture

PhoneBurner — $140/user/month annual, $165 monthly. Mojo — $10/user platform fee plus $89 single-line or $139 triple-line, with skip tracing at $49. BatchDialer — $95 to $199 per agent, 3 to 5 lines, 7-day trial.

The price difference is not the point. The architecture is.

PhoneBurner is a power dialer — one line, you press the button, a human initiates every call. Mojo Triple Line and BatchDialer’s 3–5 lines are multi-line, and multi-line dialing into skip-traced cell numbers is exactly the configuration plaintiffs’ firms look for.

Federal TCPA does not care that your call is business-to-business: an autodialer or prerecorded voice to a cell phone needs consent regardless — and small commercial owners overwhelmingly list personal cells in public records and skip-trace data. At $500 per call, trebled to $1,500 for willful, that compounds into a certified class fast.

The extra money for the power dialer is insurance, and it is cheap insurance. Full compliance detail is in the Launch Campaign tab.

Who publishes, who hides — and why you should care

Publishes real numbers: Buildout (floor only), Reonomy (floor only), ClientLook, CloudPano, EyeSpy360, Canva, Adobe, HubSpot, Salesforce, DocuSign, Dotloop, Calendly, CallRail, PhoneBurner, Mojo, BatchDialer, Microsoft 365.

Hides pricing entirely: CoStar, Placer.ai, LandVision, RealNex, Apto, Crexi Intelligence, Prospect by Buildout, CompStak paid tiers, LoopNet every tier, Matterport in any usable form.

Why this matters going into a sales call: a company that hides pricing is pricing by what it thinks you will pay — per market, per seat, per your firm’s size. That means the number is negotiable and the first quote is not the price. Ask for the annual, ask what a single-market seat costs, ask what they do for a solo shop, and be willing to leave the call without buying. The ones who publish have already given you their floor; the ones who hide are waiting to find out yours.

Vintage and sourcing

Every figure on this page was retrieved from the vendor’s own pricing page on September 17, 2026, except where noted otherwise. A few honest gaps worth knowing about:

  • Zoom — prices render in JavaScript and could not be read off Zoom’s own page. Not quoted rather than guessed. Basic is free.
  • Google Workspace — only Business Standard at $14/user/month is confirmed, from Google’s own January 2025 announcement of the Gemini-inclusive repricing. The older $6 / $12 / $18 table is superseded — do not use it.
  • Mailchimp and Constant Contact — the $13, $20, $10.20 and $29.75 figures are entry-band prices at roughly 500 contacts. Both price by contact band through a calculator. At 2,500 to 5,000 contacts your actual cost is materially higher and is not published. Run both calculators at your real list size before choosing. Constant Contact’s explicit send multiplier — 12× contacts on Standard — is the more transparent model for monthly blasts.
  • CompStak — the MIAMI member benefit is 15 free leasing comps, not 20, and that announcement is from June 2020. Treat it as six years stale and confirm current terms. The permanent free Exchange tier, where you earn credits by submitting your own closed comps, is the real value and it does not expire.
  • Part 107 test fee — widely reported at $175, charged by the testing center rather than the FAA. I could not confirm it from an FAA or PSI source. Verify at booking. The $5 drone registration and the free recurrent training are confirmed.

The Marketing Budget — Real Dollars, By Asset and Price

Set the deal and this builds the budget with actual vendor prices. Every number came off a vendor’s published page and is dated September 2026. The rule underneath all of it: marketing spend should be a visible fraction of your fee, you should be able to say what each line bought, and the seller should never pay a dollar of it.

Before you order the biggest sign — the law caps it, and the cap is small

You said you want the biggest signs. The binding constraint is not your budget, it is the sign ordinance — and it is much tighter than people expect.

City of Miami — Miami 21, Article 10. Real estate signs on private property need no permit, but in the commercial and industrial transects (T5-L, T6-L, CI, CI-HD, D1, D2, D3) the cap is 15 square feet. Residential transects: 4 square feet. Must come down within 30 days of the sale.
A 4′×8′ panel is 32 square feet — more than double the City cap. The biggest compliant real estate sign in a City of Miami commercial transect is roughly 3′×5′.

Unincorporated Miami-Dade — and here the sources genuinely conflict. Code §33-94 allows 40 square feet in BU and IU districts with no sign permit (one sign, 10 feet max height, 5 feet off the right-of-way, 90-day display). But the County’s own Neighborhood Compliance page says real estate signs may be up to 4 square feet and that fixed signs visible from the street require a Zoning Improvement Permit. The primary code text could not be retrieved to settle it.

Call Miami-Dade Zoning Information at 305-375-1806 and get the answer in writing for your specific folio before you order panels. The difference between those two readings is the difference between a legal 4×8 and a code violation.

What it costs to be wrong: civil citations from $60 to $810+, with immediate fines up to $510 per sign for right-of-way violations.

And banners: Miami-Dade lists banners as prohibited except for temporary grand-opening announcements. Same phone call.

Two honest workarounds inside the rules: (1) Multiple compliant signs beat one illegal one. If the cap is 15 sq ft, a 3′×5′ on each street frontage of a corner parcel is legal and doubles your visibility. (2) On a land parcel in unincorporated BU/IU, if 40 sq ft holds, a 5′×8′ is the largest single panel available to you — and on land, a big sign genuinely is the highest-ROI marketing item there is, because the buyer is often driving the corridor.

But be honest about what a billboard is for. It is not for selling one listing. 1.37 million impressions of a warehouse listing is almost entirely wasted. These are not substitutes and the price difference is misleading. EDDM is two and a half times cheaper per piece and completely useless for commercial prospecting, because it hits residents on a mail route, not the owners of commercial parcels. Targeted mail at $1.20 a piece to 300 hand-picked owners of industrial buildings in Medley is worth more than 3,000 EDDM pieces at forty cents. Pay for the list, not the postage.

The principle underneath all of it

  • Budget as a percentage of your fee, not as a flat number. The tool above does this — it shows what you are spending against what you are earning. If marketing is more than roughly 8–10% of the fee, you are either over-marketing or under-priced.
  • The seller pays nothing, and say so out loud. This is in your objection map already for a reason: cost absorption is one of the strongest commission defenses there is. But it only works if you actually spend the money.
  • Spend on production, not on placement. Photography and drone make every channel work better, forever. A paid listing upgrade improves one channel for ninety days. At every budget level, buy the pictures first.
  • The most expensive item on every one of these budgets is free. Six call lists, the adjacent owners, and your lenders. No line item on this page outperforms the phone.

The Channel — You Asked Me to Dictate It, So I Will

No options, no “you could consider.” Here is the channel: the language, the name, the format, the first twelve episodes, the gear, and the rules. Every decision below is made. If you disagree with one, change it — but change it on purpose, not by drifting.

Decision 1 — Spanish. Not English.

This is the most important call on the page and it is not close.

  • English CRE YouTube is saturated and the ceiling is low. The biggest commercial real estate channel in the world has 266,000 subscribers. Break Into CRE has 104K, Tyler Cauble 98K. In residential, million-subscriber channels are routine. You would be entering a crowded room with a low roof.
  • There is essentially no Spanish-language commercial real estate YouTube of consequence. Not a thin field — an empty one. Nobody is teaching commercial underwriting, Miami zoning or commercial financing in Spanish to a Miami audience.
  • Your own county is the argument, not overseas buyers. Miami-Dade, per Census QuickFacts: 75.3% of households speak a language other than English at home, 70.6% Hispanic or Latino, 54.5% foreign born. Three out of four households in the market you farm do not speak English at home.
  • And the channel’s job is listings, not buyers. Buyers come from portals, the broker network and the six call lists. Listings come from owners — the man who owns the twelve-unit in Hialeah, the family holding the Allapattah warehouse since 1988, the operator with three stations in Westchester. Older, first-generation, Spanish-dominant, and holding twenty years. That is the entire listing pipeline and it is Spanish-first. A video in English does not reach him. A video in Spanish reaches him, his son who handles the paperwork, and the three friends he forwards it to on WhatsApp.
  • The foreign buyer pool is the bonus, not the case. Colombia is the number one foreign buyer source for South Florida at 15%, Argentina 12%, Mexico and Brazil 7% each. Real, and worth having — but you would make this channel in Spanish even if not one overseas buyer ever watched it.

Where English genuinely wins — and this is real, not a consolation prize: institutional and out-of-state capital, lenders and the broker layer, and deals over $10M where the buyer is an entity rather than a person. But notice what that list is: all buy-side and capital-side. None of it is where listings come from, and you reach those people through the Lender Matrix and the broker network, not YouTube.

The one thing that overrides all of this, and only you know the answer: which language are you actually better on camera in? If you are sharper, funnier, more yourself in English — do English. On camera, natural beats demographic every time. A stiff broker in Spanish loses to a relaxed broker in English, and no amount of market data fixes stiff.
Spanish first, English subtitles, and let YouTube’s auto-dub handle an English track later if you want one. The content is natively Spanish because the audience is natively Spanish. Do not make an English channel and translate it — that always reads as translated.

And do not run both. Two channels means two half-channels. Run Spanish for 52 weeks and reassess with a year of real data instead of a guess. If it works, the English version is easy — you will have fifty-two episodes of proven formats to remake.

Decision 2 — Your face and your name. Not the firm.

The evidence on this is brutal and unambiguous. CBRE — the largest commercial brokerage on earth, with a global marketing department — has 12,300 subscribers. Tyler Cauble, one guy in Nashville, has 98,100. Chad Griffiths, one industrial broker, has 12,100 — matching all of CBRE by himself.

Corporate brand channels underperform individuals by roughly an order of magnitude, every time. Nobody subscribes to a logo. Put Lions Realty Commercial in the description and on the end card — and put your name and your face on the channel. The firm benefits either way; the channel only works the one way.

Decision 3 — The format. This is what makes it not boring.

The failure mode of every CRE channel is a man at a desk explaining cap rates. Flat, generic, and indistinguishable from the next one. Here is the format instead:

You stand in front of a real Miami building and underwrite it on camera, live, using only free public records.

Address on screen. Folio pulled up on your phone. “This sold in 2019 for $1.2 million. Here is the deed. Here is the mortgage — recorded, public, I will show you the document. The taxes were $14,000; here is what they are now and here is why they jumped. It has an open permit from 2021 — here is where I found that. And here is what I think it is worth today, and here is exactly how I got there.”

Why this works when a desk video does not:

  • It is visual. Street, building, phone screen, drone pull-back. Something moves every eight seconds.
  • It is specific. A real address people recognize. “That is the building by my cousin’s shop.” Specificity is what gets shared.
  • It is verifiable. Every source is free and public. The viewer can go do it themselves — and that is the point. You are giving away the method and keeping the judgment.
  • It teaches one usable thing every episode. That is your contract with the viewer.
  • It generates leads structurally, not by asking. Every owner whose building you feature either calls you or gets called by three friends who saw it. The video is the prospecting letter.
  • Nobody can copy it without your knowledge. A residential agent cannot read a comp plan designation or explain why the DSCR does not work. The moat is the thing you already know.

And it costs you nothing extra, because you are already standing in front of these buildings pulling these records for your own underwriting. You are filming work you already do.

Decision 4 — The five series

SeriesLengthWhat it is
¿Cuánto vale?
What’s it worth?		8–12 minThe flagship. Walk a real building, underwrite it live off public records, land on a number and defend it. One per week, forever.
El Folio3–5 minOne free tool per episode. How to find who really owns that building. How to see if it has an open permit. How to check the recertification. Pure utility — this is what gets shared in WhatsApp groups.
La Zona6–10 minZoning explained through one parcel. “This lot is worth $400,000 as it sits and $1.8 million if you know what you can build on it.” This is your moat and nobody else in Spanish is doing it.
El Banco6–10 minThe financing door. “The bank said no. Here is who says yes.” Lender types by deal, DSCR explained, what a foreign national actually needs. You own a loan brokerage — nobody else can make this series.
El Error5–8 minDeal post-mortems. What killed it — the open permit, the environmental, the tax reset nobody modeled. Fear content converts, and these are true stories that help people.

Rotation: ¿Cuánto vale? every week. The other four rotate in the second slot if you get to two a week. Do not start at two a week. Start at one and never miss.

Decision 5 — The first twelve episodes, in order

Do not start with your best idea. Start with the one that is easiest to make, because the only thing that matters in month one is that episode two exists.

Episode 1 is deliberately not about you or your firm. It is a free tool that makes a stranger’s life easier in four minutes. That is how you earn the right to episode twelve.

Decision 6 — The gear. Under $150, and stop shopping.

Decision 7 — The rules I would impose on you

  • 1. Never a desk. Always on location, always in front of the actual building. The moment you sit down at a desk you become every other CRE channel.
  • 2. Every episode names a real address. No hypotheticals, no “let’s say a building.” Specificity is the whole product.
  • 3. Every episode teaches one free tool the viewer can use tonight. That is the contract. Break it and the channel is an advertisement.
  • 4. Never pitch. The pitch is a five-second end card. If the video is good the pitch is unnecessary, and if it is bad the pitch will not save it.
  • 5. Cut a vertical Short out of every long video. One clean idea, 45 seconds. This is where the reach actually comes from — the long video is where trust comes from.
  • 6. One a week, same day, for one year. Fifty-two episodes. Batch four in an afternoon if you have to. Consistency beats quality for the first year and it is not close.
  • 7. Your brokerage name in every description and on every end card. This is not optional — FREC Rule 61J2-10.025 requires the registered brokerage name adjacent to your contact information in advertising, and a YouTube channel with your phone number in the description is advertising.
  • 8. Do not chase monetization. See below.

On monetization — ignore it, and here is the arithmetic

The YouTube Partner Program currently requires 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 qualified public watch hours in twelve months, or 1,000 subscribers plus 10 million Shorts views in ninety days.

On February 1, 2027 that changes: watch hours double to 8,000, Shorts views double to 20 million, and the subscriber requirement is removed entirely. So if you start now you have roughly four and a half months at the easier threshold.

And you should not care even slightly. A channel at 10,000 subscribers in this niche might make a few thousand dollars a year in ad revenue. One $2.5 million listing at 5% is $125,000. The channel is not a media business — it is the most scalable version of the eight-block radius call you already make. Judge it on listings and buyer calls, not on AdSense. If it produces one deal a year it has outperformed almost anything else on your marketing budget.

What I can actually do here

You said dictator, so to be straight about the division of labor: I can write every script, plan the calendar, build the episode list, draft the titles and descriptions in Spanish, and tell you which building to shoot and what to say standing in front of it. I cannot film it, upload it, or be on camera. That part is you, and it has to be you — the whole strategy rests on it being your face.

Say the word and I will write the first twelve scripts in Spanish — shot by shot, with the on-screen text, the public-records steps to pull up on camera, the exact phrasing for the underwriting, and the end card. Give me one real address you have already underwritten and episode two writes itself.

Objection Map — Tap What They Just Said

Every response here runs the manual's framework: Isolate → Acknowledge → Reframe → Ask. Isolate with a hypothetical to find the real objection, acknowledge with "I hear you" (never "I understand" — it sounds submissive), reframe to the dominant motive, and always end with a question to keep them talking. One rebuttal per objection, never two.

Why it works

Next move

The 4 Seller Motives — and the Triggers Underneath Them

The manual's four motives are what the owner feels. Underneath each one is a life event that created it. Learn to hear both: the motive tells you what language to use, the trigger tells you when the listing is coming.

💧 Liquidity

Needs cash · refinancing · bills · funding another project

🌿 Legacy

Estate planning · family · long-term wealth transfer

📈 More Income

Underperforming · better reinvestment exists

🔧 Fewer Headaches

Aging asset · tenants · certifications · time drain

Liquidity — and the trigger that creates it: debt

Listen for: "things coming up," "the loan's getting expensive," "need to simplify," any mention of another project or a partner buyout.

Anchor question: "Is there anything coming up where access to capital would be helpful?"

The trigger question that predicts the listing: "Is there debt on the property — and when does that loan mature?"

Loan maturity is the single most predictable seller trigger in commercial real estate, and it's the only one with a date attached. An owner facing a maturity into a higher-rate environment has to choose between a cash-in refinance and a sale — and most haven't run the numbers. Log every maturity date you learn in Salesforce and set the task for nine months out. That call writes itself: "Your loan comes due next spring — worth knowing what a sale looks like next to a refi at today's rates. Want me to run both?"

Legacy — and the triggers: death, family, and the estate

Listen for: "had it twenty-plus years," "my father built it," "it's in the trust," "the kids aren't interested," "we inherited it."

Anchor question: "When you think long-term, what do you want to happen with this asset?"

The trigger question: "Who else is on title with you — partners, family, a trust? Are you all on the same page about holding it?"

Two of the most reliable forced-sale events in this business live inside this motive: an estate that needs liquidity and heirs who don't want to co-own a building, and a partnership that stops agreeing. Partnership disputes create more sales than market cycles do. When you hear "I'd have to talk to my partners" or "there are four of us," you have not hit an obstacle — you have found a fault line. Log the names.

More Income — and the trigger: the rent gap and the tax clock

Listen for: "returns aren't what they were," "I could do better elsewhere," "my accountant says…"

Anchor question: "Is this property still performing the way you want it to?"

The implication question that does the work: "If market rents on your block are [X] and yours are [Y] — what's that gap costing you a year? And over the next five?"

Let them do that arithmetic out loud. The largest study ever conducted on selling behavior — twelve years and 35,000 observed calls — found that in big-ticket transactions the top performers barely pitch; they ask questions that make the buyer compute the cost themselves. An owner who says "huh, that's about ninety grand a year" has just sold himself, and nothing you could have said would have worked better.

Watch for the tax version of this motive too: depreciation runs out, the shelter dies, and suddenly they're paying tax on income they used to shield. "I'd get killed on taxes" is not an objection — it's a motive announcing itself.

Fewer Headaches — and the trigger: every complaint they make

Listen for: "tired of dealing with it," "tenants are exhausting," "the certifications are killing me," anything about a roof, an inspector, a manager, or a vacancy.

Anchor question: "How much time and energy does this property take from you every month?"

The one that opens people up: "What's the most annoying part of owning it these days?"

That last question is the highest-yield sentence in your entire arsenal, and it doesn't sound like selling at all. Every complaint an owner makes about their building is a confession. In South Florida specifically, milestone inspections, recertification, and insurance are turning a lot of tired owners into sellers who haven't said it out loud yet. Ask it, then write down every word.

The rule that makes motives worth finding

From the manual, and it's the part most new agents skip: once you identify the motive, anchor everything to it. A liquidity-driven seller does not respond to legacy language. A legacy seller isn't moved by income arguments. Put the motive in the Salesforce note on the first call, and let it choose the language for every email, every follow-up, and every word the TL uses in the meeting. An agent who hands a TL "Reached — OTI — legacy, three siblings on title, father built it in 1974" has done more for that listing than one who hands over "seemed interested."

Asset Playbooks — Multifamily · Gas Stations · Land & Zoning

The Gears are the same. What changes by asset is what you research before the dial, the one market fact you lead with, which motive is most likely, and which door — listing or loan — the owner is most likely to walk through. Specialization is what gets your call returned: "the multifamily guy" gets a callback; "a commercial broker" gets voicemail.

Multifamily

Before you dial: unit count, year built, last sale date and price, current loan and maturity, and rough rents versus the block. In Miami-Dade, also check the building's recertification status — a 40-year-old building facing recertification is a headache motive with a deadline attached. And know the insurance story: Florida premiums have reset the economics of small multifamily, and every owner is feeling it.

The one market fact to lead with: a per-unit comp on their block, or the rent gap. "Units on your street are renting at [X]; yours are listed at [Y]" is a sentence that makes an owner do math on the spot.

Most likely motives: More Income (the rent gap), Fewer Headaches (insurance, recert, tenants), and Liquidity (a maturity into higher rates). Legacy on the 20-year-plus owners.

Questions that open it:
"How many units, and are you at market on rents or is there room?"
"What did the insurance renewal do to you this year?"
"What's the loan on it — bank, agency, and when does it mature?"
"Anything big coming — roof, recert, a rollover of tenants?"

Which door: both, and this is where the two-door system shines. A stabilized building with a maturity is a refi candidate at agency terms (typical lenders want debt coverage around 1.25x and lend into the 65–80% range of value). A tired owner with a rent gap is a value-add listing — and the buyer you bring can be financed by you on a bridge. "Sell to a value-add buyer we finance, or refi and raise rents yourself — let me show you both numbers" is the whole pitch.

Objection you'll hear: "Cap rates are too high to sell right now."
Say: "You might be right — so let's not sell. What does the refi look like, and what's the building worth if you push rents to market first? If the answer is 'hold two years, then sell,' I'd rather tell you that now than list it at the wrong time."

Gas Stations & C-Stores

Before you dial: whether the owner holds the real estate, the business, or both; the fuel brand and supply agreement term; underground storage tank registration and age (Florida DEP records); any Phase I environmental history; and rough inside sales. Gas stations are the most research-sensitive asset you'll call on — an owner can tell in one question whether you understand the business.

The structural fact that makes this your best niche: most banks won't touch gas stations because of environmental exposure, so the buyer pool is starved for financing and deals die at the lender. A brokerage that can place gas station loans — SBA 7(a) and 504, and the specialty lenders who actually understand tanks — is the only call that makes a sale possible. That's not a pitch; it's the reason owners in this category should be talking to you and no one else.

Most likely motives: Fewer Headaches (tanks, compliance, 24-hour operations, staffing) and Legacy (owner-operators aging out with kids who don't want the station). Liquidity when the fuel contract renewal or a tank replacement is coming.

Questions that open it:
"Do you own the dirt and the business, or just one of them?"
"When does the fuel agreement come up?"
"How old are the tanks — and has anyone done a Phase I on it recently?"
"Are you still running it yourself, or is someone running it for you?"

Which door: the listing — because you're one of the few who can bring a financed buyer — and, for the owner-operator who wants out of operations but not out of the real estate, a sale of the business with you financing the operator, which keeps them as landlord. That second structure is a conversation almost no other broker can have.

Objection you'll hear: "Nobody can get a loan on these anyway."
Say: "That's exactly why I called. Most banks won't — and that's why the last three stations on your side of town sat for a year. We place gas station loans, which means the buyer I bring you is a real buyer, not a guy hoping his credit union says yes. Want to know what a financed buyer would pay for yours?"

Land Use & Zoning

Before you dial: current zoning and the future land-use designation, lot size, any recent rezonings or entitlements on adjacent parcels, and comp sales of entitled versus raw land nearby. Also check whether recent state land-use legislation (the kind that allows residential density on commercially zoned parcels) touches their site — for some owners that quietly multiplied what their land is worth and nobody told them.

The one market fact to lead with: the entitled-versus-raw gap. "Raw land on your corridor is trading at [X] a square foot. Entitled for [use], it's trading at [Y]." Entitled land is routinely worth multiples of raw, and most owners are sitting on the raw number in their head.

Most likely motives: Legacy — land is the asset most often "held for the kids" — and More Income, once they realize the land is producing nothing while its highest-and-best use is producing a number. Liquidity when they need capital for another project and don't realize the land can be borrowed against.

Questions that open it:
"What's it zoned now — and have you ever looked at what it'd be worth rezoned?"
"Is it producing anything, or just holding?"
"What's the plan for it long-term — build, sell, or leave it to the family?"
"Has anybody approached you about the parcel next door?"

Which door: the zoning work itself is the door. You take the owner through the entitlement, and then they either sell entitled at the higher number (a listing) or build, which needs a land loan and then a construction loan you place. Land loans run conservative — often 50–65% of value and lenders want entitlements in hand — which is exactly why the entitlement conversation comes first.

Objection you'll hear: "I'm holding it for my kids."
Say: "Then let's make sure they inherit entitled land, not a rezoning project. Getting it entitled while you own it is the single biggest thing you can do for its value — and you can still hold it. Want me to show you what it's worth zoned for what it should be?"

Industrial right now — and why the headline number is lying to you

The single most useful fact in this tool, and almost nobody in Miami is quoting it. County industrial vacancy is 6.4% — a number that describes big-box distribution product you do not trade. Broken out by building size (Newmark, Q2 2026):

10,000–49,000 SF → 3.3% vacancy.   50,000–99,000 SF → 4.0%.   100,000–249,000 SF → 7.8%.   250,000+ SF → 11.3%.

Small-bay vacancy is roughly one third of big-box vacancy. And by vintage it inverts what everyone assumes: modern 0–20 year buildings sit at 12.3%, while 40+ year old infill runs 3.7%. The 2021–23 spec big-box wave has not absorbed. The old warehouse on a Hialeah side street has.

The numbers, Q2 2026: county vacancy 6.4%, down 10 bps and plateauing after climbing from a 2.6% record low in 2022. Asking rent $15.91 NNN — but flex and R&D runs $19.92, a 27% premium. Absorption positive at +429,712 SF in the quarter. Pipeline down to 2.8M SF and falling 6.6% per quarter, with deliveries at roughly a third of the 2024–25 run rate.

The submarkets. Hialeah is the value play — 4.9% vacancy, the best YTD absorption in the county at +292,898 SF, and the cheapest rent at $13.54. Medley posted the single best absorption number, +307,160 SF. Airport West / Doral commands the top rent at $18.06–$18.34 and its small-bay segment runs under 3%. South Miami-Dade is the tightest overall at 3.2%. Weakest: North Central and Northeast Dade.

And institutional money is buying exactly your segment. Three portfolio trades between July and September 2026: Longpoint at $267/SF (729,901 SF, 74 tenants, average tenant 9,865 SF), Midtown Capital at $296/SF (14 Doral small-bay buildings, units of 600–2,500 SF), Ares at $280/SF. Two of the three largest industrial trades in Miami this year were small-bay infill, not big box.

The honest bear case, because you should be able to give it. Sublease space is at an all-time high — 3.9M SF, 1.8% of inventory, shadow supply that does not show in headline vacancy. Asking rents have fallen three consecutive quarters, 2.1% off the Q3 2025 peak, and one brokerage puts them down 5.3% year over year. Landlords are conceding — free rent and TI are back. And the real risk is trade volume, not real estate: global trade growth is forecast at 0.5–1% for 2026, down from 4.2%, and PortMiami grew only 2.35% in FY2025. Tariffs are the thing to watch.
Two data cautions that will save you an argument. (1) CoStar-derived sources show Miami industrial at 8.0% vacancy with negative absorption, against the brokerages’ 6.4% and positive — the difference is inventory definition (285M SF vs 215M SF). Know which one your client is looking at before you contradict them. (2) In-place rents are up 7.3% while asking rents are down — both are true, because old leases are rolling to higher rates while new asking rates soften. Do not get caught on that one.

Not verified, so do not quote: a Miami-specific industrial cap rate (no brokerage published one), remaining developable UDB acreage, SBA 504 owner-user volume, and insurance cost per SF. And data centers, film production and nearshoring appear only in marketing content, never in a brokerage research report. Do not cite them to a client.

Sources: Newmark 2Q26 Miami Industrial; Cushman & Wakefield Miami Industrial MarketBeat Q2 2026; CBRE Miami Industrial Figures Q2 2026; Connect CRE and CRE-Sources on the 2026 portfolio trades; Marcus & Millichap Miami-Dade 2Q26.

The rule across all three

Say the asset class in the first ten seconds of every call — "I sell gas stations in Miami-Dade," "I do multifamily in [neighborhood]," "I work on land and zoning along [corridor]." Owners return calls from specialists because a specialist might know something they don't. And log the asset-specific facts in Salesforce with the motive, so the TL walks into the visit already knowing the tank age, the rent gap, or the zoning designation.

Underwriting — The Numbers, The Ask, The Give

For each asset class: the metrics that actually determine value, exactly what you request from the seller, and what you hand the buyer. The live math is in the Underwriting Workbook (the .xlsx) — this tab is what you say and ask while you're standing in the building.

The rule that governs all of it

Every number in your offering memorandum must trace to a document the seller gave you. Rent traces to a lease or an estoppel. Expenses trace to tax returns or an operating statement. A number you cannot source is a number that blows up in due diligence — in front of the buyer, the lender, and your client at the same time.

And never blend in-place with pro forma. Label them separately, every time. Buyers catch a blended number instantly and it costs you the credibility you spent months building.

The universal ask — request these on day one, every asset

  • Rent roll — dated and signed. An undated rent roll is an opinion.
  • Trailing 12-month operating statement, month by month.
  • Last three years of tax returns or P&Ls — this is where the operating statement gets verified.
  • Current tax bill and assessed value. Taxes reset on sale — underwrite the new number, never the seller's frozen basis. This one line kills more deals in diligence than any other.
  • Insurance declaration page and a current quote. In Florida, last year's premium is fiction.
  • Every lease plus all amendments. Verbal lease terms are not lease terms.
  • Service contracts — some survive the sale whether the buyer wants them or not.
  • Survey, title policy, capital improvements, open permits and violations, environmental reports.

Estoppels — the document that separates you from most brokers

A tenant estoppel certificate is a short statement each tenant signs confirming what they actually pay, what deposit is held, when the lease ends, and that no side agreements exist. It is the single most valuable thing you can collect on an income property.

Why it matters: a seller's rent roll is what the seller believes or wishes. An estoppel is what the tenant will sign their name to. The gap between those two is where deals die at the eleventh hour — a "rented at $1,800" unit that turns out to be $1,500 with two months free changes the NOI, changes the value, and changes the loan. Collect them early rather than letting the lender discover the discrepancy for you, because the lender will require them anyway.

How to ask without alarming the seller: "Standard part of the package — the lender's going to require each tenant to confirm their own terms in writing, so let's get it done now rather than three weeks before closing when it becomes a fire drill. It also protects your number: once a tenant signs it, nobody can renegotiate what they were paying."

Multifamily

What drives value: price per unit is the headline and NOI is the truth. The gap between in-place and market rent is the entire value-add thesis. Year built governs the buyer pool. In Miami-Dade, recertification status and the insurance number can move value more than rent does right now.

Ask the seller, beyond the universal list: unit mix with in-place rent per unit · signed estoppels from every tenant · security deposit ledger (it transfers at closing and shortfalls get credited to the buyer) · delinquency and aging report — occupancy means nothing if half of it isn't paying · 40/50-year recertification status · twelve months of owner-paid utility bills · any rent-regulated or subsidized units, which change the buyer pool entirely.

Give the buyer: the unit mix table showing in-place versus market and the annual gap · recertification and capital status stated plainly · a real insurance quote rather than last year's premium · and the leveraged return, because multifamily buyers decide on cash-on-cash, not cap rate alone.

What to ask an owner on the phone: "How many units, and are you at market on rents or is there room?" · "What did the insurance renewal do to you this year?" · "Where are you on recertification?" · "What's the loan, and when does it mature?"

Industrial / Warehouse

What drives value: price per square foot, and then the three things that never appear in a tax record — clear height, loading, and power. Under about 18 feet of clear height your buyer pool shrinks dramatically. Land-to-building ratio matters too: under 2:1 means tight truck maneuvering, over 3:1 means excess land carrying its own value.

Ask the seller: lease abstract and a signed estoppel · clear height, dock-high and grade-level door counts, and electrical service (amps and phase) · roof age, warranty and last inspection — the biggest capital item in the asset class · Phase I environmental, and Phase II if it's recommended, because prior industrial uses leave things behind · floor thickness and column spacing, which govern racking.

Give the buyer: the full spec sheet, the mark-to-market analysis, truck court dimensions, and the land-to-building ratio. Industrial buyers are technical and they reward a package that speaks their language.

Retail / NNN

What drives value: the leases are the asset. Two numbers dominate — WALT (weighted average lease term) and the recovery structure. Under three years of WALT lenders get nervous; under two, many won't quote at all. And an occupied NNN box and a vacant one will never comp to each other, so never average them.

Ask the seller: full lease abstracts for every tenant — options, exclusives, co-tenancy and kickout clauses each move value · estoppels from every single tenant, non-negotiable · CAM reconciliations for two years, which reveal whether recoveries are real or chronically under-billed · tenant sales reports if there's percentage rent, which also tell you who is about to fail · the anchor lease in full, because one exclusive clause can make a vacant suite unleasable · parking count and any shared-parking agreements.

Give the buyer: the tenant roll with WALT and a rollover schedule, the anchor lease summary with co-tenancy exposure, and an honest statement of what is actually recoverable versus what the seller calls recoverable.

Gas Station / C-Store

What drives value: two assets in one, and you must value them separately or you'll be wrong about both. The real estate earns a market rent and caps like real estate. The business earns whatever is left after that rent and trades on a multiple — typically 2.5 to 4 times, depending on brand, volume trend and remaining supply term.
