Ask the seller: twenty-four months of fuel invoices, because verbal gallon counts are worthless · inside sales by category, since cigarettes and food service carry very different margins · the full fuel supply agreement with term remaining · UST registration, tank age and the last tightness test — tanks past twenty years are a live replacement cost · Phase I, and Phase II if flagged · the state financial-responsibility certificate · the franchise agreement, since transfer rights are never automatic · and an equipment list separating what conveys from what is leased, because dispensers and coolers are usually leased.

No environmental report means no lender. Full stop. That's also your opening: most banks decline this asset class entirely, which is why stations sit for a year. Because you can place the loan, the buyer you bring is a real buyer — and that is the reason an owner should list with you instead of anyone else.

Give the buyer: the twenty-four-month volume trend (trend matters more than level), the real estate and business values shown separately — which almost no competing broker will do — environmental status and tank age stated plainly, and a named financing path.

Land — Highest & Best Use

What drives value: zoning in, buildable out. The metric that matters is price per buildable square foot, not price per lot square foot — entitled land trades on what you can build, and most owners are quoting the raw number in their head.

The math you run: lot SF times FAR gives maximum gross buildable. Acres times density gives maximum units. Whichever produces the smaller building is your binding constraint — and knowing which one binds tells you exactly what to argue for in a rezoning. Then multiply gross buildable by an efficiency factor (80–85% for multifamily, after corridors, lobbies, stairs and mechanical) to get net saleable.

Then work backwards to the dirt. Net saleable times sale price per foot is gross development value. Subtract hard costs, soft costs (22% of hard is a reasonable placeholder), contingency, selling costs, and developer profit — and profit is not negotiable to a developer; below about 15% of GDV most of them walk. What's left is the residual land value, and that is what the land is actually worth.

Ask the seller: a zoning verification letter from the municipality, because a listing's zoning claim is not evidence · survey with topography, since grade costs real money · any entitlement approvals, plats or pending applications · utility availability letters, because no sewer capacity means no project · Phase I, since vacant lots were rarely always vacant · concurrency and impact fee estimates, frequently the difference between feasible and not.

Give the buyer: the highest-and-best-use study with buildable SF, unit count and the binding constraint named · price per buildable SF shown next to price per lot SF · the residual land value with the development budget visible, which proves the price is supportable instead of asserting it · and a realistic entitlement path and timeline.

And the owner conversation this unlocks: "Raw land on your corridor trades around [X] a foot. Entitled for what your site should be, it's [Y]. Let's make sure your kids inherit entitled land, not a rezoning project — and you can hold it as long as you want afterward."

The financing page — the one competitors cannot produce

Because you own a loan shop, every offering package can carry a page no other broker in the market can write: indicative terms and what a buyer would actually qualify for. That single page changes the deal, because buyers decide on leveraged returns, not on cap rate.

Three tests size every commercial loan, and the lowest of the three governs. LTV — roughly 70–80% multifamily, 60–70% industrial and retail, 60–70% gas (higher with SBA), 50–65% land. DSCR — NOI divided by annual debt service, with 1.20 to 1.25 typical; below 1.20 almost nobody quotes. Debt yield — NOI divided by loan amount, 8 to 10% typical, which lenders lean on when cap rates get thin. The workbook runs all three and tells you which one binds, which tells you instantly what to attack: the value, the income, or the lender.

What the lender asks for is on the Financing Sizing sheet by asset type — but the universal set is the rent roll, three years of operating statements and tax returns, the current tax bill, the insurance declaration, the purchase contract, title, survey, and on the borrower side a personal financial statement, schedule of real estate owned, and three years of personal returns.

And the promise that becomes your brand: a soft read inside 48 hours. The market benchmark is 48 hours for a soft quote and 14 days for credible terms, and deals quoted inside that window close at measurably higher rates. Beat the benchmark, and say out loud that you did.

The workbook — built into this page

The Lions Realty Underwriting Workbook lives inside this file. Nine sheets — multifamily, industrial, retail/NNN, gas station, land HBU, financing sizing, and printable ask/give checklists. 114 live formulas. Blue cells on yellow fill are the only cells you type in; everything else calculates. Copy a tab per deal and rename it the property address.

Every assumption in it — hard costs, cap rates, insurance, business multiples — is an illustrative Miami-Dade placeholder. Replace them with your own market data before anything goes to a client.

Regulators & Law — Who to Call, What to Watch

The agency directory, then asset by asset: why buyers want it, what can go wrong, the rules that govern it, and exactly who you call. Verify every phone number and requirement before you rely on it — agencies reorganize and codes change, and this page is a starting map, not legal advice.

The directory — what you need and who has it

What you needWhoWhat they actually give you
Owner, folio, assessed value, sales history, building sketchMiami-Dade Property AppraiserYour first stop on every trace. The sales history is where an LLC transfer reveals a human name.
Deeds, mortgages, liens, lis pendens, judgmentsMiami-Dade Clerk of Court — Official RecordsDeed images carry the grantee's mailing address — the only route into a trust.
Permit history, open permits, certificates of occupancyMiami-Dade RER Building Division, or the municipal building department if the property sits inside a cityOpen permits kill closings. Pull them before you list, not during escrow.
Recertification status, unsafe structure casesRER Building / municipal building departmentAn open recert is a six-figure liability you need to know about first.
Code violations, open enforcement, liensCode Compliance (county or city, by jurisdiction)Violations run with the land. Buyers inherit them.
Zoning verification, permitted uses, FAR, densityMiami-Dade Planning & Zoning (Chapter 33) or the municipality — City of Miami uses Miami 21A written zoning verification letter. A listing's zoning claim is not evidence.
Contamination, tanks, wells, wetlands, sanitary sewer, tree removalDERM — Division of Environmental Resources Management, within REREnvironmental records and open cases. The first call on any industrial, gas, or land deal.
Storage tanks, petroleum cleanup eligibility, discharge historyFlorida DEP — Storage Tank programRegistration, tank age, closure and discharge records. Gas deals live or die here.
Water and sewer capacity, availability lettersMiami-Dade Water & Sewer (WASD)No sewer capacity, no project. Land deals need this in writing.
Right-of-way, driveway cuts, plattingPublic Works (county or municipal)Access is an entitlement too.
Access onto a state roadFDOT District SixCorridor sites often need a state connection permit.
Life safety, sprinkler and storage occupancy reviewFire — county or municipal plan reviewGoverns what a warehouse tenant may actually store.
Tax bills, delinquency, tax certificatesMiami-Dade Tax CollectorDelinquent taxes signal distress — and a motivated seller.
Entity officers, registered agent, annual reportsFlorida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz)The LLC-to-human bridge. Officer search reveals an owner's whole portfolio.
Licensing, brokerage law, complaintsDBPR / Florida Real Estate CommissionChapter 475 governs everything you do.
Jurisdiction first, always. Before you call anyone, establish whether the property is in unincorporated Miami-Dade or inside a municipality — City of Miami, Hialeah, Miami Beach, Coral Gables and the rest each run their own building, zoning and code departments with their own codes. Calling the county about a City of Miami parcel wastes an afternoon, and quoting county zoning on a city parcel embarrasses you in front of a client.

Multifamily

Why buyers want it: the best financing in commercial real estate — agency debt is cheaper, longer and more leveraged than anything else on this page. Risk is spread across many tenants rather than one, rents reprice annually so it tracks inflation, and it is the easiest asset class to value and therefore the easiest to exit.

What goes wrong: it is genuinely management-intensive, and evictions in Florida take time and money. Two Miami-Dade-specific items dominate underwriting right now — insurance, which has reset the economics of small multifamily, and recertification capital, which arrives as a lump sum on a schedule you can look up. Expense creep is the quiet killer: taxes reset on sale, and a seller's frozen basis flatters every number on their operating statement.

Rules to watch: Florida's residential landlord-tenant law governs the leases, and local notice ordinances for rent increases and non-renewals vary by municipality — check the one your property sits in rather than assuming. Recertification is the big one: in Miami-Dade, buildings from 1983–1992 were due by the end of 2024 and then every ten years; buildings from 1993 forward are first due at 30 years, and coastal condos and co-ops of three or more stories within three miles of the coastline are first due at 25 years, then every ten. The state milestone inspection law folded into that schedule, and as of January 2025 recertifications use new report templates with added requirements including infrared thermography on electrical service at 400 amps and above. Fair housing applies to everything you write and say.

Call: the building department for recertification status and open permits · code compliance for violations · the property appraiser to confirm what taxes become after a sale, not what they are today.

Industrial / Warehouse

Why buyers want it: NNN structure means the tenant carries taxes, insurance and maintenance, so management is minimal. Leases run long, capital expenditure is low compared with retail, and logistics demand has been structurally strong. For an owner-user, an SBA 504 can put them in a building with far less down than an investor would need.

What goes wrong: single-tenant risk is binary — you are either 100% leased or 100% vacant, and re-tenanting an industrial building takes months, not weeks. Functional obsolescence is the silent value killer: low clear height, inadequate power, or a tight truck court permanently limits who can use the building. And environmental legacy is real — prior industrial uses leave things in the soil.

Rules to watch: environmental first and always — a Phase I to the current ASTM standard, and a Phase II if anything is flagged. DERM holds the county's contamination and tank records. Stormwater, sanitary connection and industrial waste permits run through DERM as well. Fire code governs what a tenant may actually store, which matters enormously for hazmat or high-piled storage. Access onto a state road runs through FDOT.

Call: DERM for contamination and permit history · the building department for the CO and permit record · fire plan review if the use is at all unusual · FDOT for corridor access.

Retail / NNN

Why buyers want it: recoveries push operating costs onto tenants, credit tenants produce bond-like income, percentage rent gives upside on strong performers, and the asset is visible and easy for a passive investor to understand. A grocery anchor in particular drives traffic to every other suite.

What goes wrong: tenant rollover is constant and expensive — budget real money per square foot for tenant improvements and leasing commissions, because retail rollover is the single most underestimated line in a pro forma. Co-tenancy clauses can let tenants reduce rent or terminate if an anchor leaves, and an exclusive-use clause in one lease can make a vacant suite unleasable to the obvious candidate. Parking ratios constrain what uses are even permitted. And e-commerce pressure is uneven — service and food retail hold up far better than goods.

Rules to watch: ADA Title III deserves a specific flag in Florida, where accessibility litigation against commercial properties is common — parking, ramps, restrooms and paths of travel. Zoning governs parking counts and signage, and a change of use can trigger a parking requirement the site cannot meet. Lease law is where the value actually sits, which is why estoppels are non-negotiable.

Call: zoning for parking and signage requirements and permitted uses · code compliance for open cases · the building department for permit history on prior tenant buildouts, which is where unpermitted work surfaces.

Gas Station / C-Store

Why buyers want it: strong cash flow from two streams, an essential use that survives recessions, genuine barriers to entry since new stations are hard to permit, and an owner-operator can finance it with SBA leverage no investor deal would get. Real estate plus business means two ways to build value.

What goes wrong: this is the highest-liability asset class on the page. Environmental exposure is the whole story — contamination liability can exceed the value of the property, which is exactly why most banks decline the category and why stations sit on the market for a year. Tanks are a replacement cost with a clock on them. Fuel margins are volatile and the business is labor-intensive around the clock. Brand and supply agreements restrict who can buy and how they operate.

Rules to watch: Florida DEP's storage tank rules govern registration, construction, monitoring, closure and discharge reporting, and registration obligations follow a change of ownership — that transfer is a real step in a closing, not a formality. Financial responsibility for tank systems must be demonstrated and evidenced. Discharges carry mandatory reporting deadlines. State petroleum cleanup programs have eligibility rules that can matter enormously to a buyer, and eligibility does not automatically follow the property, so confirm it rather than assuming. Federal franchise law governs branded supply relationships and their termination. DERM holds the county-level environmental record on top of the state file.

Practical rule: no environmental file, no deal. Phase I to current standard, Phase II if flagged, tank registration and age, last tightness test, financial responsibility certificate, and the supply agreement with its remaining term. Assemble that package before you market the property and you can actually sell it — which is precisely the argument for why the owner should list with you rather than the broker who cannot.

Call: Florida DEP storage tank program for registration and discharge history · DERM for the county environmental record · the building and fire departments for the canopy, dispensers and tank permits.

Land & Development Sites

Why buyers want it: no tenants, no toilets, no management — and the largest value-creation opportunity available, because entitlement can multiply what the dirt is worth without a shovel touching the ground. It is also pure optionality: hold it, build it, or sell it entitled.

What goes wrong: it carries with zero income, so taxes and interest bleed every month. Entitlement risk is real and slow — timelines run in years and approvals are never guaranteed. Financing is the hardest on this page, typically half to two-thirds of value with lenders wanting entitlements already in hand. Impact fees and concurrency can quietly make a feasible project infeasible. And environmental or wetland findings can stop a project outright.

Rules to watch: zoning and the future land use designation both govern, and they are not the same thing — a rezoning to match an existing FLU designation is a very different proposition from a comprehensive plan amendment. In the City of Miami the code is Miami 21, a transect-based code; unincorporated Miami-Dade runs on Chapter 33. Wetlands bring both DERM and federal jurisdiction into play. Tree preservation, historic designation, platting and concurrency each add time. Utility capacity must be confirmed in writing.

The Live Local Act is the biggest land-use story in Florida and it is your best reason to call a land owner. As amended in 2025, it lets qualifying affordable housing be built on parcels zoned commercial, industrial or mixed-use — and now on flexibly-zoned areas like PUDs, and on land owned by a house of worship regardless of underlying zoning. Qualifying projects get the highest density, height and floor area ratio allowed anywhere in the jurisdiction as of July 1, 2023, and administrative approval without a hearing. The tradeoff: at least 40% of units affordable at up to 120% of area median income for 30 years — 10% for religious institutions — and mixed-use projects are capped at 10% non-residential. There are height step-downs adjacent to single-family neighborhoods, and parking requirements drop by 15% within a quarter mile of transit. Many owners of commercially zoned land have no idea their site may now support residential density it never had. That is a phone call worth making, and it is a conversation no competitor is having.

Call: planning and zoning for a written verification letter and to confirm Live Local applicability · DERM for wetlands and environmental · WASD for capacity in writing · public works for platting and access · FDOT if it fronts a state road.

Cross-cutting — every deal, every asset

  • Florida repealed the sales tax on commercial rent, effective for occupancy periods beginning October 1, 2025 — state and local surtax both. The rate had been 6% at repeal. It does not reach short-term rentals under six months, self-storage, boat slips or parking, which remain taxable separately. This materially improves NNN economics for tenants and landlords, and it is a legitimate, useful reason to call every commercial owner in your territory.
  • FIRPTA — a buyer generally must withhold on the purchase price when the seller is a foreign person. In Miami this comes up constantly, it surprises sellers late, and flagging it early makes you look like the professional in the room. Send them to a CPA; do not advise on it yourself.
  • 1031 exchange timing — 45 days to identify, 180 days to close, with a qualified intermediary engaged before closing. A seller who closes without setting it up cannot retroactively fix it. Ask "what would you do with the money?" early, because the answer is usually an exchange and the clock shapes the whole listing.
  • Chapter 475 — Florida brokerage law. Transaction broker is the default relationship in Florida, single agency requires written disclosure, and Florida does not permit dual agency. Know which hat you are wearing and disclose it in writing.
  • Your dual role — when the brokerage lists and the loan shop finances the same deal, disclose it in writing on the file, never condition one on the other, and confirm with counsel what your specific structure requires. The neutrality you sell in Gear 4 only survives if the paperwork matches the sentence.
  • Calling compliance — 8am to 9pm local time, identify yourself and your firm every call, honor removal requests immediately and permanently, keep your own do-not-call list, and be careful with autodialers on cell phones.
  • Anti-money-laundering awareness — all-cash entity purchases draw scrutiny, and reporting obligations in real estate have been expanding. Know who your buyer is and confirm current requirements with counsel rather than assuming last year's rules still apply.
The honest boundary: you are a broker, not a lawyer, an accountant, an engineer, or an environmental consultant. Your value is knowing what to flag, when to flag it, and who to send them to — and that is genuinely valuable. The moment you start advising on tax treatment, lease enforceability, or contamination liability, you have taken on risk you are not insured for and given advice you are not qualified to give. Flag it, name the specialist, and stay in your lane. Clients trust that more, not less.

Sources for the items above

Commercial rent tax repeal and its exceptions — Cherry Bekaert RSM · Live Local Act 2025 amendments — Holland & Knight · Recertification schedule and 2025 template changes — Miami-Dade Building · Storage tank registration — Florida DEP · DERM environmental records — RER/DERM

Statutes, ordinances and agency structures change, and municipalities differ from the county. Treat this page as a map of where to look, confirm current requirements with the agency or with counsel before relying on any of it, and never present it to a client as legal advice.

Execution Runbook — What You Actually Do, By Asset

The laws tell you what exists. This tells you what to do — and just as importantly, what to skip. A twelve-unit apartment building does not need what a gas station needs, and treating them the same either wastes your seller's money or gets your deal killed.
This runbook is the sequence. The Order List tab is the instrument list. Built backwards from litigated Florida cases: for each asset class, the exact report, letter, search or endorsement by its real name, who issues it, and what day it belongs on — with the items the market routinely skips flagged, because that is where your leverage is.

The principle: proportionality

Every item below is marked one of three ways. Never skip means do not go to market without it. Conditional means there is a specific trigger — if the trigger is absent, you do not need it. Skip means it is not proportionate for this asset and ordering it anyway burns money and time for no benefit.

The instinct to run everything on every deal feels responsible and is actually a failure of judgment — it slows listings, costs sellers money they did not need to spend, and buries the two or three things that genuinely matter under a pile of paper nobody reads.

Pick the asset

The one thing per asset you never skip — memorize this table

AssetThe thing that kills the deal if you skip itWhy it, and not something else
MultifamilyRecertification status + a real insurance quoteBoth are six-figure surprises in Miami-Dade, both are knowable in an afternoon, and both reprice the deal. Environmental is usually not your issue here.
IndustrialPhase I environmentalPrior use is unknowable from the street, lenders require it, and a solvent finding can exceed the building's value.
RetailThe dry cleaner history checkOne hour of tenant history. If a cleaner ever operated there, everything about the deal changes — and the state program that would have covered it closed to new applicants in 1998.
Gas StationThe complete environmental and tank package — before you marketWithout it the property is unfinanceable, which means unsellable. The package is the product.
LandWritten zoning verification letterYou cannot price land without knowing what can be built. Everything on the HBU sheet depends on this one document.

If you remember nothing else from this tab, remember that row for whatever you are listing this week.

Who pays for what — the default split

ItemNormally paid byNote
Marketing package, photography, aerials, OMThe firmAbsorbed. This is your listing pitch — say it.
SurveyNegotiable, often sellerAn old survey is usually fine for marketing; an ALTA is a closing item.
Phase I environmentalUsually buyer, during diligenceException: gas stations, where the seller should fund it up front or the property cannot be marketed properly.
Phase IIBuyer, or negotiatedExpensive and slow. Who pays becomes a real negotiation point once a Phase I flags something.
Property condition / roof reportBuyerLenders often require one on larger deals regardless.
AppraisalBuyer (lender-ordered)Buyer pays but cannot choose the appraiser.
Recertification engineering + repairsSeller, usuallyOr it becomes a price adjustment. Better to know the number than to negotiate blind.
EstoppelsSeller collectsCosts nothing but effort, and the lender will require them anyway.
Municipal lien searchUsually buyer/titleOrder it early — unrecorded liens do not appear in a standard title search.
Zoning verification letterWhoever needs it firstOn land, order it yourself at listing. It is cheap and it is your entire pricing basis.

Costs and turnaround vary by vendor, scope and how busy the market is. The ranges in the runbook above are ballpark figures to help you set expectations and build a timeline — confirm real numbers with the vendors you actually use before you quote anything to a client.

The universal sequence — same on every asset

  • Listing signed → same week: pull the public record (violations, open permits, liens, environmental file), request the seller document package, and order whatever this asset's "never skip" item is.
  • Before you go live: resolve or disclose anything the record turned up. A known issue priced into the marketing is a non-event; the same issue discovered in week three is a renegotiation.
  • Marketing: in-place and pro forma labeled separately, every number sourced, and the financing page attached.
  • LOI / contract: short diligence period, meaningful deposit, and hand over the entire diligence package on day one — a buyer with everything immediately has no excuse to extend.
  • Diligence: buyer orders their reports. You chase turnaround times and keep both sides informed weekly, including when there is no news.
  • Closing: confirm the asset-specific transfer items actually got done — tank registration transfer, estoppels in file, open permits closed, deposits transferred.

Environmental & Records — What to Pull, What Can Bite

Environmental liability is the one exposure that can exceed the value of the property itself, and code violations transfer with the land whether anyone read them or not. This is the standing records request for every deal, then what changes by asset class.
Three things the case law audit added to this page. (1) A Phase I is All Appropriate Inquiries–compliant for 180 days from the site visit, not a year — and it must be certified to the entity that actually takes title, with a reliance letter. (2) ASTM E2600 vapor encroachment screening is non-scope — order it by name or you do not get it. (3) On a gas station, pull the FDEP Petroleum Restoration Program eligibility determination per discharge: the cap is per discharge, not per property, so a site with two prior discharges may have burned most of its eligibility before you ever saw it. The Order List tab has all three, with the date calculator.

Why this sits on you even though you are not the consultant

Federal law makes the current owner potentially liable for contamination they did not cause — liability is strict, shared among responsible parties, and reaches backward in time. A buyer's protection from that is not automatic. It requires having done "all appropriate inquiries" before closing, which in practice means a compliant Phase I environmental site assessment performed by a qualified environmental professional, plus ongoing obligations after closing.

The timing trap that catches people: a Phase I goes stale. The core components have a 180-day window, and the report can generally be carried to a year only with specific updates. A Phase I sitting in a seller's file from two years ago does not protect your buyer — it is useful background and nothing more. If closing slips past the window, it needs updating, and that is a conversation to have in week one rather than week eleven.

The current standard for these reports is ASTM E1527-21, which the EPA adopted for all-appropriate-inquiries purposes. If a report predates that standard, say so plainly rather than letting a buyer assume it qualifies.

Your job is not to interpret any of this. Your job is to make sure it gets ordered early, by the right person, and that nobody discovers a problem three days before closing. Flag it, name the specialist, stay in your lane — and look like the only professional in the transaction while you do it.

The standing records request — pull these on EVERY property, before you list

Not at contract. Before you list. Everything here is public record, most of it is free, and finding a problem while you still control the narrative is the difference between an adjustment and a collapsed deal.

  • Open code violations and enforcement cases — county and the municipality if the property sits in a city. Violations run with the land; the buyer inherits them.
  • Code enforcement liens, and specifically unrecorded municipal liens. This is the one that surprises people: some municipal charges and code liens do not appear in a standard title search, which is why a separate municipal lien search is ordered on commercial deals. Ask for it by name.
  • Permit history, plus open and expired permits. An open permit means work was started and never closed out. It must be resolved before transfer or it becomes the buyer's problem, and closing an old permit can mean bringing the work up to current code.
  • Certificate of Occupancy and Certificate of Use — and confirm the CO matches the use actually happening in the building today.
  • Unsafe structure cases and any open board actions.
  • Building recertification status and the date of the next one.
  • DERM environmental record — contamination files, tanks, wells, sewer connection and industrial waste permits, and any open environmental enforcement.
  • Florida DEP facility search — storage tanks, discharge incidents, cleanup sites.
  • Zoning verification letter in writing, confirming the use is legal and not merely tolerated.
  • Tax status — delinquency, outstanding certificates, special assessments.
  • Flood zone determination, and the elevation certificate if one exists.
  • Historic designation check — designation quietly removes the demolition option.
Make it a listing-intake habit and say so out loud to the owner: "Before we go to market I pull the county and city record on your property — violations, open permits, environmental, liens. Not because I expect something, but because if something's there I would rather we fix it now than have a buyer's attorney find it in week three and use it to renegotiate you." Sellers hear that as protection, and it is. It also means you never get blindsided in your own deal.

Environmental red flags visible from the street or the file

  • Prior uses, always. Pull historical aerials and old city directories. A site is only as clean as everything that ever operated on it, and the current tenant tells you nothing about 1974.
  • Floor drains in an industrial or automotive building — a classic pathway straight to soil or sewer.
  • Patches, bollards, vent pipes or fill ports in a parking area — the signature of a tank that may or may not have been properly closed.
  • Stained soil or pavement, stressed vegetation, drums or totes stored outside.
  • Any neighbor with a gas station, dry cleaner, plating shop, auto repair or industrial use. Contamination migrates. Your site can be the victim of the property next door, and that is still your buyer's problem to manage.
  • Chlorinated solvents — the dry cleaner and degreaser chemicals. These are the expensive ones because they create vapor intrusion risk, which can require mitigation inside occupied buildings and can affect the property even without soil contamination on site.
  • Pre-1980s construction — assume asbestos-containing materials until tested, which matters most at renovation or demolition, when notification and abatement rules apply. Lead paint is the parallel concern in older residential.
  • Florida-specific: moisture and mold in humid buildings, and defective imported drywall in construction from roughly 2001 to 2009.

Multifamily

Watch for: asbestos and lead paint in older buildings, which govern renovation cost more than they govern sale · moisture and mold, which is both a habitability and a litigation issue in this climate · defective drywall in 2001–2009 construction · sewer connection status, since some older properties still have septic or non-conforming connections that DERM will require resolved · and the structural side, where recertification is the capital event you can look up in advance.

Request: the standing list, plus DERM sewer connection permits · water intrusion and mold remediation history · the insurance claims history, which is where prior water and roof damage actually shows up · any asbestos or lead surveys already performed · and recertification reports if the building has been through one.

Florida requires a radon notice on sale and lease documents for buildings, so make sure the required language is where it belongs.

Industrial / Warehouse

Watch for: this is the class where prior use is everything. Metal plating, auto repair, printing, machine shops, chemical storage and anything involving degreasing all leave a legacy — and chlorinated solvents are the worst of them, because a solvent plume is expensive, slow to remediate, and carries vapor intrusion exposure. Tanks, both under and above ground. Floor drains and their discharge point. Outdoor drum and material storage. Stormwater discharge from the yard.

Request: the standing list, plus a full tenant use history going back as far as records exist · DERM industrial waste permit file · hazardous waste generator records if the operation ever used an EPA identification number · stormwater permit status · any prior Phase I or Phase II reports in the seller's possession, along with lab data rather than just the summary · a floor drain survey · and a tank closure assessment if tanks were ever removed.

A seller saying "there was never a problem" means nothing. Ask instead: "Has anyone ever done a Phase I here — and can I see it, including the appendices?" A seller who has one and won't share it is telling you something.

Retail — and the dry cleaner problem

Watch for: the single biggest environmental landmine in retail is a dry cleaner, current or historical, anywhere in the center. Dry cleaning solvent contamination is expensive, migrates, and can create vapor intrusion in adjacent suites. Also: gas or automotive uses on an outparcel, historical photo labs and printers, nail salons, and restaurant grease interceptors and oil separators.

The fact that changes how you underwrite this: Florida runs a state Drycleaning Solvent Cleanup Program that limits owner and property-owner liability for eligible sites — but the application period closed on December 31, 1998, and applications are no longer accepted. So a contaminated dry cleaner site that never got into the program has no state-funded cleanup path, and the liability sits with the parties. Before you put a value on any center with a dry cleaner in its history, find out whether the site is in the program. That single question can be worth more than everything else in your due diligence.

Request: the standing list, plus a complete tenant history for every suite going back decades — this is the whole exercise · the program eligibility status if a dry cleaner is or was present · DERM records for the parcel and the neighbors · grease trap and oil separator permits · and any environmental reports the seller or a prior lender ordered.

Gas Station / C-Store

Watch for: everything. This class is environmental first and real estate second. Tank age, construction and leak detection. Discharge history, including incidents that were reported and resolved — resolved is not the same as clean. Off-site migration, which creates liability to neighbors that survives the sale. Vapor recovery equipment and compliance. And the financial responsibility demonstration the state requires.

Request: the complete Florida DEP facility file, not a summary — discharge reports, compliance inspections, closure assessments · tank registration showing age and construction · the most recent tightness and leak detection records · financial responsibility certificate · a written determination of petroleum cleanup program eligibility, because eligibility does not automatically follow the property and a buyer assuming it does is buying a problem · Phase I, and Phase II if anything at all is flagged · DERM's county-level file on top of the state's · and the supply agreement with remaining term.

This is also your competitive moat, so use it. Assemble that package before you market and the property becomes financeable and sellable — which is precisely why the owner should list with you rather than with the broker who cannot place the loan or read the tank file. Most stations sit for a year because nobody does this work up front.

Land & Development Sites

Watch for: wetlands, which bring both county and federal jurisdiction and can stop a project outright · protected trees under the county ordinance, which are a real cost and a real delay · fill material of unknown origin, since vacant lots are where things get dumped · agricultural residue on former grove or farm land, where historic pesticide use leaves arsenic in the soil · archaeological and historic sensitivity · and flood zone and resilience, which increasingly affects both cost and financeability.

Request: the standing list, plus historical aerial photographs, which for raw land are more informative than any document · a wetland delineation or at minimum a jurisdictional determination · a tree survey · protected species screening if the site is undeveloped · geotechnical borings, which are not environmental but will tell you what the soil actually is · FEMA flood determination · and utility availability letters in writing.

And remember the reverse: on land, environmental findings do not just cost money, they change what is buildable. A wetland finding can cut the developable area and therefore the residual land value on your Land HBU sheet. Re-run the numbers rather than assuming the price survives.

How to say it to a seller without losing the listing

"Two things I do before we go to market, on every property. First I pull the public record — violations, open permits, liens, environmental. Second, if there's any history here that would make a lender ask questions, I'd rather we get an environmental report in hand now than have a buyer order one in week three and use whatever it says to renegotiate you.

I'm not expecting a problem. I'm removing the excuse. A buyer who has no surprises left has no leverage left either — and that's how we protect your number."

That framing does two things at once: it makes diligence sound like protection rather than suspicion, and it quietly tells the seller you run a real process. It is also, conveniently, true.

Sources

ASTM E1527-21 required for liability protection FL Drycleaning Solvent Cleanup Program DSCP — application period closed 12/31/1998 F.S. 404.056 — radon notice DERM environmental records Miami-Dade Building online services

Environmental law is technical, fact-specific and changes. Nothing here is legal or environmental advice — it is a checklist for knowing what to order and who to call. Every determination belongs to a qualified environmental professional and to counsel.

Comps Workbench

Without comps you have no compass — no data points to base any assumption on. This tab does two things: it tells you exactly what to set in iMapp before you pull, and then it does the entire Excel cleanup for you. Multi-folio detection, price per unit, outlier flagging — all of it, in about fifteen seconds instead of forty minutes.

The one principle: data set size is the whole game

The tighter your criteria, the fewer comps you get. The looser, the more. You are always tuning that dial toward a usable set — so pull, count, and adjust before you do any cleanup work.

What you pulledWhat it meansWhat to do
30+ raw salesHealthy. Maybe two-thirds survive cleanup.Pull it. You'll land around 20 good comps — a perfectly good data set.
10–20 good after cleanupWorkable.Proceed, but know each comp carries weight. Read them individually.
Under 10 goodToo thin to trust.Loosen a constraint — widen the geography, extend the date range, or drop the unit floor — or commit to a deep qualitative dive on every single one.
100+ raw salesToo loose; you're pulling other markets.Tighten the geography first, then the date range. Geography is almost always the right dial.

Step 1 · Pull Planner — pick the asset, get the exact setup

Step 2 · Drop the iMapp CSV here

Export from iMapp to CSV, then drag the file in — or paste the rows. No Excel import wizard, no column deleting, no sorting. Everything below happens automatically.

Drop the CSV here
or click to choose a file — nothing leaves your computer
…or paste rows instead

Column mapping — auto-detected. Fix anything it got wrong; only the fields your asset type needs are required.

Step 3 · The set

The comps

Untick a row to drop it from the stats. Rows flagged MULTI-FOLIO can be merged with one click — units, beds, baths, square footage and assessments are summed, and the recorded sale price is kept once rather than double-counted.

The method, in order — what the tool is doing for you

  • Geography first, always. Draw the boundary that defines a genuinely similar market — similar building stock, similar economics above all, similar zoning. In Little Havana that's a recognizable shape you could draw from memory. Variation inside it is fine; you sort that out later.
  • Then the use constraint, then the size floor (five units and up for multifamily), then the date window.
  • Always set a minimum sale price. This is the highest-value filter in the whole pull — it strips out quitclaim deeds, dollar transfers, and intra-family paper that would otherwise poison your median.
  • Set the date window at the last pricing regime change, not at a round number of years. Values in Miami-Dade have been broadly consistent since late 2022, so a 2023-forward window is defensible. If that gives you 80 sales, keep it; if it gives you 12, go back further.
  • Sort newest to oldest — both to organize and to make repeat buyers visible.
  • Hunt multi-folio sales. Same buyer, same date, same price, adjacent addresses means one transaction recorded across several folios — and if you leave it, you've counted one sale three times at a fraction of its real size. Consolidate: sum the units, beds, baths, square footage and assessments; keep the price once. Same buyer and same date but different prices is not multi-folio — that's an investor closing two separate deals the same day, and both are real comps.
  • Then price per unit (or per square foot for industrial, per land foot for land), and cut the extremes. Don't agonize over it — if a comp is 70 or 80 percent off the norm, it's telling you something you can't see from a tax record, and it doesn't belong in the set.
  • Then narrow toward your target. For multifamily, year built is the dominant value determinant — once the set is clean, cut the vintages far from your subject's. A 1948 fourplex and a 2019 build are not the same asset.

The land trick — proving it's really a land comp

Land is the one asset where the sale record lies to you, because a "land sale" often has a building sitting on it that nobody paid for. Two ways to prove the value is in the dirt, and the tool runs the first one automatically when you pick Land:

  • The assessment ratio. Divide the building assessed value by the total assessed value. A high ratio means you're looking at an improved-property sale and the price reflects the building — drop it. A low ratio means the value is in the land, which is what you're comping. The tool computes and sorts on this for you.
  • The square-footage sanity check. A thousand-square-foot structure on a twenty-thousand-square-foot lot is a land sale wearing a building. Look at building SF against lot SF and the answer is usually obvious without any arithmetic.

Where comps go — both doors

A comp set is not a valuation exercise, it's the raw material for one — and it feeds both sides of the business. On the brokerage side it's the BOV, the number that gets you a twenty-minute visit and the credibility to price a listing honestly instead of buying it. On the lending side it's the value input for LTV — you cannot size a refinance without knowing what the collateral is worth, and an owner who hears "here's what your building is worth and here's what that supports as a loan" in the same sentence is hearing something no other caller offers.

And the last instruction from the class matters more than any technique here: pull comps constantly, then hand them to your Team Leader and your teammates and ask them to tear the set apart. Comping is a judgment skill, and judgment only calibrates against other people's judgment. Practice makes perfect — you're going to do a lot of them.

Trace Board — Finding the Person Behind the LLC

The research workflow as a working board. Fill it in as you go, use the direct links, and it builds your Salesforce note for you at the bottom. One profile takes about eight minutes once the tabs are set up.

Reonomy — working the grid

The Trace Board below is how you go deep on one owner. Reonomy is how you go wide across a block — and the two feed each other. Use Reonomy to sweep a grid and harvest owners and loan data; drop into the Trace Board when a profile needs the full chase.

Reserve your seat before you log in. The Reonomy login is shared across the floor, so the seat sheet is the rule, not a courtesy — put your initials on the time slot you want. The sheet clears every day, so a slot you booked yesterday is gone: if you plan to use it today, you register today. Nothing wastes a research block faster than opening the tab and finding someone already in it.
Reonomy— ask a manager if you don't have access to the seat sheet yet
  • Search an address in your territory and the map comes up with your parcel as the blue dot. Every surrounding parcel is clickable — that's the grid.
  • Go straight to the Owner section. Property stats are there and they're useful, but the owner block with contact information is what you came for. Copy it into Salesforce and move to the next parcel.
  • If an owner isn't clickable, Reonomy simply doesn't have them. It's uncommon but it happens — don't burn time fighting it. That parcel goes to the Trace Board for the Property Appraiser → SunBiz → LexisNexis chase.
  • Work the grid parcel by parcel, in a pattern. The visited pages highlight as you go, so the map itself becomes your coverage record — you can see at a glance which properties you've researched and which you've skipped. Work a block until it's done rather than hopping around; systematic coverage is the entire point of farming a territory.
The debt tab is the real prize, and most people skip it. Reonomy carries recorded loan history going back decades — amounts, recording dates, and maturity dates. A mortgage coming due means the owner is facing a refinance or a need for cash, and that is the single most predictable trigger in commercial real estate. It is also, for you, the direct handoff to Gear 4: you now know the maturity before you dial, which means you can open the financing door with a date in your hand instead of a question. Log every maturity you find and set the task for nine months out.

Occupants and demographics are there too — occupants is worth a glance for the entities attached to a site, which can shortcut the SunBiz step. Taxes and demographics are inconsistent; don't build a workflow on them.

Your tab setup — do this once, every morning

Two Property Appraiser tabs (one for the subject, one for chasing mailing addresses — you will bounce between them constantly), LexisNexis on Comprehensive People, and SunBiz. That's the whole rig.

Property Appraiser — subject Property Appraiser — chase SunBiz — by entity name SunBiz — by officer name Clerk — deed images LexisNexis
Before you trace anything: search the name and the address in Salesforce first. A meaningful share of research time gets burned re-tracing a profile someone already did — or worse, building a duplicate account. If it's already there, mark the task reviewed, kill the duplicate, and move to the next one.

Batch your day first

In Salesforce, filter the list of properties still needing research, select ten, and mass-update the Nexus date to today. They'll surface in Today's Tasks and you work them one at a time. Batching the setup keeps the research block from turning into a browsing block.

Property Appraiser — the address gives you the entity

Paste the address. You get the owner of record, the mailing address, use code, and — the part most people skip — the sales history. If the property ever transferred from a personal name into an LLC, that history hands you the human being's name for free.

Watch for a $100 or $10 transfer. That's not a sale, it's a family or estate transfer — which means the people on the old deed are almost certainly the people behind the new LLC. It's the single most reliable shortcut on this board.

The mailing address is a lead, not a formality

If the mailing address isn't the subject property, run it through your second Property Appraiser tab. Very often it's the owner's home — and if it comes back homesteaded, you've confirmed where they actually live, which is what makes the people search work.

SunBiz — the entity gives you names

Search the LLC. Pull the managers, the registered agent, and then scroll the old annual reports — an earlier filing sometimes carries a name the current one dropped.

Abbreviations will fool you. "CREF1 LLC" and "CREF LLC" are completely different companies; "APT" might be filed as "Apartments" or not. If the exact string fails, shorten it and scan the list rather than concluding it doesn't exist.

Know a dead end when you see one. If the registered agent sits at an office suite or an accounting firm, that person is a CPA doing paperwork, not your owner. Note it and move on — don't spend twenty minutes tracing an accountant.

Deeds — the only way into a trust

Open the deed image from the sales history. Deeds state the grantee's address in the body — and trusts and trustees do not appear on SunBiz at all, so for any trust-held property the deed is your only path to a mailing address, and the mailing address is your path to the people.

LexisNexis Comprehensive People — search the ADDRESS, not the name

Put in the address plus city and state, and leave the name blank. You want everyone affiliated with that address — spouse, adult children, anyone sharing the household — not just the one name you already have.

Then work the shortcuts: Address Summary → Phone Summary → Relatives. Don't scroll the whole report.

Read the phone numbers by their year

Every number carries a date range. A number showing this year is live. A number last seen in 2018 is a wrong number you'll waste a dial on. And if a number appears under a different person's name, it isn't theirs — skip it. Collect two or three current ones rather than ten stale ones.

Read the family structure — it tells you who actually decides

Same address, both alive, same last name: an intact household, and either one can be your contact. Different counties or different states: they're not together, and the decision may run through a third party — usually an adult child.

Two adult children with different surnames from different relationships is worth flagging hard: that's a potential inheritance conflict, and when it surfaces you'll want relationships with both of them already in place.

If the person search comes up empty, flip to Comprehensive Business

Paste the entity name, city and state, pull the report, and scroll to executive officers. It's a different pathway to the same people, and it works when an uncommon name still returns nothing on the consumer side.

The portfolio trick — reverse the whole thing

Once you have a name on a building of any size, run it through SunBiz officer search as "Lastname Firstname" (the field is last-name-first, and getting it backwards returns nothing). You'll see every LLC they're an officer of. Take those entity names to Property Appraiser's owner-name search and their entire portfolio falls out.

Do this on every owner of a twenty-plus unit building without exception. Nobody gets to that size by accident — they have other assets, and you have just mapped a family's holdings in your territory in about four minutes.

The age rule — the most important thing on this board

Owner 75 or older: stop and track the children. At that age the owner frequently isn't running the property day to day anymore and may not be the final decision maker. Someone is managing it — an adult child, or professional management. And the things that actually trigger a sale are already on their mind: inheritance, restructuring a trust, simplifying the estate. Log the age, log the children with their own phone numbers, and treat the family as the account rather than the individual.

This is the Legacy motive arriving before anyone says the word, and it's why age belongs in the Salesforce note next to the phone number. An 86-year-old owner in another county with two adult children is not a cold call — it's an estate conversation waiting for the right year.

Fill this in as you work — it writes your Salesforce note

Close it out properly — this is where the work becomes production

  • Paste the note, and always stamp it: date, your initials, "Nexus done," and what you actually found. The person reading it in a year is you.
  • Update the owner field if the entity or the co-owner changed. Stale ownership is the reason a good number goes unused.
  • Mark the research task Completed, then use Save & New — never just Save. That's what carries you straight into creating the next task instead of leaving the lead without a next touch.
  • Create the Call Prospecting task with a real date on it. Research with no call scheduled is a hobby.
  • Found a property or a number that belongs to a teammate's territory? Build the task for them and note it. It costs you a minute and it's how a floor compounds — and it's the reciprocity that gets sent back to you.
  • Duplicate account? Delete the stale one rather than leaving two half-researched profiles for the next person to redo.

Where the trace meets the call

Everything on this board exists to make the first ten seconds of the call work. The name gets you the Gear 1 opener. The address is your credential. The deed date tells you the hold period before you ask. The age tells you which motive to listen for. And the entity and the portfolio tell you whether you're calling about one building or about a family's whole position in your territory — which is a very different conversation, and a much better one.

The Listing Agreement

One page. Most brokerages hand a seller seven. The philosophy is deliberate: get things done, don't tie people up and suffocate them with paperwork. You need to be able to explain any clause on this page to anybody, cold — tap one below and you'll have the words.

The document itself

The full sample agreement is built into this page. Open it to read or print, or save it as a file you can edit.

Sample only. This mirrors the structure and clauses described in training. It has not been reviewed by counsel and does not include every disclosure Florida may require of a brokerage relationship. Your attorney and Broker of Record approve the final form before any version reaches a seller.

The three things to say before a seller reads a word

1 · "It's one page." Say it out loud and let them see it. A one-page agreement does more to lower a seller's guard than any paragraph inside it. Most of what they're bracing for simply isn't there.
2 · "This never obligates you to sell." The single most powerful sentence at the table. Even if we bring you a ready, willing and able buyer at your number, you are not required to sell. Plenty of brokerages write agreements that do force that. Ours does not, on purpose.
3 · "You can cancel any time." True, with one fair condition — covered in clause I. Lead with the freedom, then explain the condition when they ask. Don't bury it and don't skip it.

Those three sentences are the same mechanism as a no-oriented question: they remove the fear of being trapped, which is the fear actually standing between a seller and a signature. A seller who knows they can walk is far more willing to start.

The header — fill it correctly

  • Seller's name: the entity that owns the asset, not the human you've been talking to. If title is in an LLC, the LLC is the seller — and the person signing must have authority to bind it. Your Trace Board work already told you who that is.
  • Term: six months. That's the lifetime of the agreement.
  • The grant: exclusive right and authority to find a buyer to purchase, lease, exchange or otherwise contract for the real estate.
  • The property: address, folio, and whatever detail is needed to identify it beyond dispute. Be specific here — on an assemblage, list every folio.
  • The price is a guideline. It sets the marketing number. It does not create an obligation to sell at it, or at all.
Where obligation actually comes from: the purchase and sale contract — which is between the buyer and the seller, not with us. That document will likely contain language obligating the seller to close. The listing agreement never does. Keep those two clearly separated when you explain it, because sellers routinely conflate them and that confusion is what makes them hesitate.

The ten clauses — tap any one

What it says, what it actually means, what the seller will push back on, and the words that answer it.
What it means

What they'll say

How you answer

The two clauses that decide the conversation

Clause A, exclusivity, is the one that cannot move. Not because we're greedy about it, but because it's what lets us market the property to everyone without holding anything back. If our fee depended on the buyer's source, we'd have to be careful who we showed it to — and careful marketing is bad marketing. Exclusivity is what makes maximum exposure safe, and maximum exposure is what produces the number. Say that, and it stops sounding like a restriction.

Clause B, the deposit clause, is the one built to be argued about. It matters far less than sellers think it does — it only applies if the deal goes to contract, the buyer defaults, and the seller keeps the deposit. Attorneys and experienced sellers love to fight it. That's fine. Every negotiation goes better when the other side gets to win something, and it's far better that they win this than that they start chipping at exclusivity or the term. Know what you're holding and know what you can hand over.

Before you concede anything: clear it with your Team Leader or Broker of Record. Knowing which clause is the designed give is not the same as having authority to give it.

How the agreement connects to the second door

The listing agreement is a brokerage document and it stands alone. If the same seller is also considering a refinance through the loan side, that's a separate conversation with separate paperwork and a separate disclosure — never bundle them, never condition one on the other, and put the dual role in writing on any file where both businesses touch the same client. The neutrality you sell in Gear 4 only survives if the paperwork matches the sentence.

Note: this page explains the firm's own agreement in plain language so you can discuss it confidently — it is not legal advice, and it doesn't cover every disclosure Florida requires on a brokerage relationship. Any question about interpretation, any requested modification, and any seller who arrives with an attorney goes to your Broker of Record before you answer.

Research — Why It Is the Whole Game

The manual's rule is five facts before every dial. Here's the case for why that rule is the difference between a 12% reach rate and a 30% one — and the sharpest way to run it.

The data behind the rule

Two numbers explain why research isn't optional. First: roughly 82% of decision-makers say the salespeople who call them are unprepared — it is the single biggest complaint people have about cold calls, ahead of volume, ahead of pushiness. Second: industry connect rates on cold commercial calling run somewhere between 8% and 16%, while this firm's target reach rate is 20–30%.

That gap is not talent and it isn't the script. It's that you're calling a verified human being at a verified number instead of dialing an entity's registered agent. Every hour in the research block is buying you the reach rate the ratios depend on. If your reach rate is under 20%, the problem is almost never your calling — it's your list.

The five facts, and what each one buys you

#What to knowWhat it buys you on the call
1Owner's first nameThe Gear 1 opener only works with a name. It's the pattern interrupt.
2Full address + asset typeYour credential in the first ten seconds. Proves this isn't a blast.
3Recent Lions Realty activity nearbyThe 8-block variation — the strongest call in the system.
4One current market factThe reason to call that isn't "do you want to sell."
5Ownership duration (deed date)Predicts the motive before you dial. See below.

Read the deed date before you dial and you'll know which motive to listen for. Owned 1–5 years: likely an active investor — lead with the buy side, Gear 1 lands hard. Owned 6–15 years: refinance and rent-gap territory — income and liquidity. Owned 20+ years: legacy and headaches, probably free and clear, and the highest-probability listing in your whole list. Owners who bought decades ago hold enormous embedded gains, are often tired, and frequently have heirs who don't want the building.

Peeling the LLC — the order that works

  • Reonomy for the property record and ownership entity, plus mortgage data — that's where the maturity date lives.
  • Sunbiz for the Florida entity: managers, registered agent, and the mailing address on the annual report.
  • LexisNexis to convert a name into a human — current phone, address history, associated people.
  • County records to verify the deed, the date, and the price actually paid.
  • When it's still a wall: the tax bill mailing address, the property manager's sign on the door, the attorney who filed the entity, or the tenant who knows who signs the lease.

When you reach them, never open with how you found them. Open with the address. "How did you get my number?" gets an honest, calm answer if it comes — see the objection map — but volunteering the trail makes an ordinary call feel like surveillance.

The discipline part

Research happens after 5 PM and on weekends. Never during Golden or Silver Hours. The manual says this plainly, and it's worth naming what's really going on: researching during calling hours is avoidance that feels like work. It's the most common way a good agent quietly stops being a caller. If you find yourself "just finishing one more lead" at 10:15 AM, that's the red flag, and the fix is to close the tab and dial.

The Ratios Calculator

Real estate looks like chaos from the outside. It isn't — it's a chain of ratios, and if you follow the steps you get a predictable outcome. Put your target in the top row and this works backwards to the only number you actually control: how many calls you make today.

Your targets

Compensation is your net — after the split with your Team Leader and after a co-broke when there's an agent on the other side. That typically lands between 2 and 2.5%. Start at 2% so you're looking at the worst case. And a million-dollar average listing is on the low side for this firm; use it now because it's a round number, and replace it with your own after ninety days when you know your submarket.

Your ratios

What the defaults mean. One in three listings sells in the worst case — the firm average is closer to one in two, and where you land depends entirely on whether you and your TL priced it competitively. Four to five appointments produce a listing. Roughly 30% of scheduled appointments cancel or reschedule away. Ten reaches produce one scheduled appointment. Thirty calls produce ten reaches. Forty-eight weeks assumes you take a week at Thanksgiving, a week at Christmas, and a couple more somewhere.

What that requires

Every no has a price

This is the whole mindset, and it is arithmetic rather than a slogan. You do not get paid for the yes — you get paid for the process, and every no is a paid step through it. Don't judge a call in a vacuum; judge the chain. The old line puts it best: if you knew you were ten thousand no's away from ten million dollars, how fast would you want to collect them?

What getting better is worth — same calls, more money

Here's the part that should change how you think about training. Hold your daily calls exactly where they are and improve two ratios — get better at the listing presentation so four appointments produce a listing instead of five, and get better at pricing with your TL so one in two listings sells instead of one in three. Nothing about your effort changes. Watch the income.

That is why the drills matter, why you shadow meetings, and why you take the comp set to your Team Leader and ask them to tear it apart. Effort sets the floor. Ratios set the ceiling.

Even a broken clock

Read the daily number at the bottom of the chain and notice how ordinary it is. Work only forty-eight weeks. Make the bare minimum calls. Hit nothing but average ratios on every single step. You still land on the outcome. That is the entire argument for the system — you do not have to be exceptional at any one thing, you have to be unexceptional at all of them, every day, without negotiating.

Cross-check against the manual: at these defaults you're attending roughly appointments a week — which is exactly the 3–4 kept appointments per week the onboarding manual sets as the standard. The two numbers were built independently and they agree.

And remember there's a second door

This calculator models the brokerage side only. Every "not selling" owner in those reaches is still a refinance prospect, and a 1% fee on a $2M refi is $20,000 from a conversation this chain counts as a no. Run the calculator to know your floor — then treat the loan side as the part that isn't in the model.

Your Numbers — and How to Diagnose Them

The golden ratios from the manual, plus the reconciled working math and a diagnostic tree so you can find your own weak link instead of guessing.

The chain

30Calls/day
→
150Calls/week
→
30–38Reaches
→
3–4Appts set
→
3–4Kept/wk
→
TLHandoff
Worth raising with your SM

The manual states "4 appointments per 10 reaches" alongside a weekly target of 3–4 appointments. Those two don't reconcile — at 30 dials a day you'd generate about 10 reaches a day, and a 40% appointment rate would produce roughly 20 appointments a week, not 3–4. The working number is the weekly one: 3–4 appointments per 150 calls, which is roughly one appointment per 40–50 dials, or about a 10% appointment-per-reach rate. That is a strong, realistic number for cold commercial owner calling. Use it to diagnose yourself — and ask your Sales Manager which reading is intended, because it changes what "a bad week" means.

The diagnostic tree — find the actual broken link

If this is off…The problem is almost never…It's this
Calls under 30/dayTimeYour list wasn't built the night before, or you're doing admin in Golden Hours. Build the list at night; the block is for dialing only.
Reach rate under 20%Your deliveryResearch quality. You're dialing entities, stale numbers, or registered agents. Fix the list, not the script.
Reaching but no appointmentsThe scriptYou're stopping at the first or second "no." Run all three, then the motive question — that fourth question is where appointments actually come from.
Appointments set but not keptBad luckYou skipped the Appointment Lock or the confirmation touches. Same-week meetings hold at roughly 54%; push a meeting out four weeks and it drops toward 32%. Book close and confirm.
Kept appointments, no listingsYouMotive intel wasn't captured or wasn't handed to the TL. Brief them in Salesforce before the meeting, every time.

Persistence — the real numbers

Measured across a very large modern calling dataset: roughly 93% of all connects happen by the third attempt and 98% by the fifth. That's your rule for a prospect who never picks up — five attempts, then rotate them into long-cycle follow-up rather than burning dials.

And ignore the line you'll hear repeated everywhere that "80% of sales require five follow-ups." It traces back to an organization that doesn't exist and has been debunked. The real edge is simpler and less glamorous: most callers quit after one or two attempts. Completing your five puts you ahead of the field without any cleverness at all.

The Calendar

Everybody wants to be their own boss until they find out freedom has a cost — and that most of us are terrible bosses to ourselves. At the start, the flexibility in this calendar is the thing most likely to end your career. Work the same eight hours you worked when someone else was watching.

Right now

The counter lives in this page only — it resets when you close it, which is the point. Salesforce is the record; this is the scoreboard for the next three hours.

The week

TimeMonTueWedThuFri
8:00–8:45Arrive · email & voicemail · call list up and ready · nothing left behind
8:45–9:00First dials — start before the meeting, not after
9:00–10:00CallsCallsCallsSales training
9:00–9:30, then calls		Calls
10:00–12:00Team meeting 10:00
last week · market · new listings — then calls		Golden hoursGolden hoursGolden hoursGolden hours
12:00–1:00Lunch / Salesforce logging — noon to one is the deadest connect hour there is

Friday PMPower Hour

Get in at 8:00, 8:30 at the very latest. That half hour is what lets you start dialing at 8:45 instead of "getting settled" until ten. On Monday you can comfortably put 10 to 15 calls down before the meeting starts — which means by the time most people have opened their laptop, half your morning quota is gone.

Friday's Power Hour exists to prove something to you: agents routinely do 30 dials in that single hour. The only reason it's possible is preparation — the list was built the night before. That's the whole lesson of the week in one hour.

One task at a time, in 90-minute cycles

Do not call, then research, then send an email, then answer a text, then call again. That pattern feels productive and produces almost nothing. Work in 90-minute blocks of a single activity, take a short break, then run another.

  • When you're calling, you're only calling. Need to send a property email after a conversation? Set the task and send it at the end of the day.
  • When you're researching, you're only researching. Two to three hours, straight through.
  • Research speed: expect about ten minutes per lead at the start. With experience it settles around five. The target never changes — enough leads tonight for 30 calls tomorrow.
  • If you genuinely have no numbers left to dial, it's acceptable to research during Silver Hours. It is never acceptable during Golden Hours.

If the morning has to move

The morning block is the priority because of what happens to it otherwise: start the day with a showing or a deal and you'll find the afternoon block is very hard to reclaim. Momentum runs one direction. If you genuinely must see a client in the morning, shift the block to the afternoon deliberately — don't just lose it. And anyone you couldn't reach before noon moves to the afternoon list automatically.

What the call data says about each block

TimeBlockWhat the data says
8:30–12:00Golden Hours — calls onlyThe strongest measured connect windows sit around 10–11 AM and 2–3 PM, so this block contains the best hour of the day. Guard it completely: no email, no research, no conversations.
12:00–1:00Admin / SalesforceNoon to 1 is the deadest connect hour measured — which makes it exactly the right hour for logging. The manual put admin here for a reason.
1:00–4:30Silver Hours + confirmationsContains the second-best window (2–3 PM). Connect rates fall off after 4, so push confirmation calls earlier in this block, not later.
After 5:00Research blockBuilding tomorrow's 30 is what makes tomorrow's reach rate possible. This is not overtime — it's the input to your most important ratio.
9:00 AMMorning huddleStating your number out loud is public commitment, which is one of the most reliably measured effects in behavioral research. Numbers spoken are harder to miss than numbers thought.

Day of week: Thursday tends to be the strongest day for connects, with Tuesday and Wednesday close behind; Friday is consistently the weakest. Don't reduce Friday's dials — but expect a lower reach rate and don't let it dent your confidence going into the weekend.

The finding that matters more than any of this: success rises steeply with call length — roughly 4% at two minutes, around 16% at five, close to 30% past seven. Keeping someone talking is worth more than any hour-of-day optimization. Which is exactly what the motive question in Gear 3 is designed to do.

What 30 a day actually adds up to

The number sounds arbitrary until you run it forward. Thirty dials a day is the whole business plan — everything else in this tool is about making those thirty land better.

PeriodDialsWhat that becomes
A day30Roughly 4–6 real conversations and 1 appointment-quality contact on a good day
A week150Enough conversation volume that your ratios start meaning something instead of being noise
A month~650A pipeline that no longer depends on any single call going well
A year~7,800You now know your market by owner name, and that is the actual asset
And the reason preparation is the constraint, not effort. Thirty dials inside one Power Hour is routine for agents who built the list the night before, and impossible for agents who did not. You are not limited by how fast you can talk — you are limited by how many numbers are sitting in front of you when the hour starts. That is why the research block after 4:30 is not optional and is not overtime. It is the input to tomorrow.

Ten minutes per lead at the start, about five once you are experienced. Thirty leads is therefore two to three hours of research at first and closer to ninety minutes later. Budget it honestly rather than discovering at 8:50 AM that you have eleven numbers.

Eat the frog — the honest version

The manual says the first three hours are for calling, and that the calls you most want to postpone are the ones you make first. The reason this rule exists is that every hour you delay the first dial, the call gets heavier, not lighter. Nobody has ever warmed up to cold calling by thinking about it at 11 AM. Dial the worst one first and the rest of the day is downhill.

The Appointment Lock & Follow-Up

Setting the appointment is half the work. Keeping it is the other half — and it's where most new agents leak production without realizing it.

The lock sequence, and why each step exists

1 · Confirm — "Great, [Name] — I'm looking forward to our meeting on [Day] at [Time]."

2 · Value — "I'll share market intel our current clients are using — who is buying in your area, the actual value for properties exactly like yours, and which ones are getting over-asking offers. Information you cannot find in public records."

3 · Remove pressure — "You can take those numbers and use them however you want — even if you never work with us. That way, when the timing's right, you'll already have a trusted contact ready."

4 · Final confirm — "Looking forward to seeing you on [Day] at [Time]!"

Step 2 is what makes it worth showing up for. A meeting with no stated payoff gets cancelled when something else comes up; a meeting that delivers information they can't get elsewhere doesn't.

Step 3 is the most important sentence in the script and it is mandatory. "Even if you never work with us" removes the fear of obligation, and fear of obligation is the number one silent killer of kept appointments. It's the same mechanism as a no-oriented question: people relax the moment refusing stays available to them.

Restating the day and time twice is not redundant — it's the thing that makes the appointment real in their head and in their calendar.

The number that should scare you

Meetings booked for the same week show up at roughly 54%. Push the meeting out four weeks and that falls toward 32%. Always book close. When someone offers you a date three weeks out, counter once: "I'd rather not have you waiting on stale numbers — anything this week or early next?"

Three touches, not one

  • Touch 1 — the lock, on the call itself, immediately.
  • Touch 2 — the confirmation email (Template 2), same day.
  • Touch 3 — the confirmation call the day before, during Silver Hours. Never skip this. A confirmed appointment that goes unconfirmed becomes a drive across Miami for nothing.

Voicemail — two, then stop

Voicemails roughly double the reply rate of the email that follows them, which is why you leave them. But each one also cuts your odds of catching that person live by around a quarter, because they start screening the number. So: two substantive voicemails per prospect, each paired with an email, then move them to long-cycle follow-up. A third and fourth message trains them to ignore you.

The one that gets callbacks: "[Name], it's [You] at Lions Realty Commercial — calling about [address]. [Nearby address] just traded at [number]. Thought you'd want to know what that means for yours. My direct is [number]. Again, [number]."

Lead with the address, give one real piece of information, say your number twice slowly, and stay under twenty seconds. Never leave a message that's only an introduction — that's the one that gets deleted at second three.

Never send without a callback date

Straight from the manual and worth engraving: the email is 5% of the value — the callback is 95%. "Send me something" without a date attached is how prospects disappear politely. Always: "What email should I use? And I'll put you on my calendar to follow up on [Day] — is [Day] morning or [Day] afternoon better?"

The 14-Day Report

Internally this is the "let me keep my job" report, and the name is the point. Every listing gets a recurring task the day it's signed, and every fourteen days the client hears from you. Do that and the hard pricing conversation becomes a routine one. Skip it, and three months of silence later you'll be having it with someone who no longer trusts you.

"The market sucks" is not a diagnosis

You'll hear it constantly — nobody's buying, nobody's selling, I've had it listed seven months. That isn't reality. Markets don't suck; you have not adjusted to the changes taking place in the market. Things are dynamic. Your job is to notice and adapt faster than the listing goes stale.

Stale pricing destroys leverage before the owner realizes it. By the time they figure out the price was wrong, it's too late — you've lost the listing, and the next agent takes it, slashes the price, and sells it.
